text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Drones, uncrewed ground vehicles, field robots, and laser weapons are the latest manifestations of the electro-centric military of the future. That seems to have lit a fire under the US Army. The Army has been adopting EVs at a pace that any snail can beat with one hand tied behind its back. However, suddenly they are interested in a new tactical vehicle that can deliver enough wattage to power up electronic systems and equipment, including drones and other weaponry, whether the vehicle is parked or in motion.

Another Step On The Long, Slow Journey To EVs

The Army is aiming to ditch its familiar but outdated High Mobility Multi-Wheeled Vehicles (Humvees for short) and introduce a new vehicle more suitable for the electrified war of the future. They have tapped Ford, GM, and the off-road specialist BC Customs to produced prototypes under the ISV-H (Infantry Squad Vehicle – Heavy) program.

Despite the “heavy” in ISV-H, the ISV-H program stipulates a lighter, more agile vehicle than the Humvee. In the interest of speedy delivery, the Army is also aiming to make use of vehicles already in production. A third ask is for a vehicle that Army staff can maintain and repair without relying on specialized or proprietary contracts, in other words, the right to repair.

As one of the three automakers to fit the bill, BC Customs seems closest to the bone. BC Customs won its contract in partnership with the North Carolina firm Raglan, which specializes in electric, hybrid, and other advanced propulsion systems with an eye on military applications. Raglan also cites “onboard power generation, storage, and distribution systems to support energy-intensive mission requirements” among its core capabilities.

In addition to the new collaboration with BCC, Raglan further notes that it holds contracts with the US Special Operations Command and the Air Force Global Strike Command, alongside other development programs supported by the Operational Energy Innovation Office.

What Is This Operational Energy Innovation Office Of Which You Speak?

The Operational Energy Innovation Office is of interest considering the sudden U-turn in federal energy policy last year, which emphasizes fossil fuels. However, the immediate impact of that policy has fallen primarily upon civilian users. The military world, not so much, and OEI is apparently still on task.

OEI comes under the Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War [aka the Department of Defense] for Energy Resilience & Optimization, which notes that its innovation programs “harness the latest science and technology to improve the Department’s energy and environmental performance, reduce costs, and advance mission capabilities.”

EVs, EVEVs, And BC Customs

The new contracts mark a key step in a competitive application process. Under its contract with the US Army, BC Customs states that it will “manufacture and deliver three (3) ISV-H vehicles’ utilizing Raglan electronic control and export power systems for Government evaluation as the competition advances toward a potential follow-on production award.”

For those of you keeping score at home, the contract comes under the Other Transaction Agreement program, which provides the Army with the ability to acquire new gear more quickly.

“The program has an approved Army Acquisition Objective of 606 platforms and is intended to provide critical operational capabilities, including exportable power to support tactical operations and onboard power to enable mission command while maneuvering,” BC Customs explains, with 606 platforms referring to the number of vehicles.

I’ve reached out to BC Customs to see if any propulsion angle related to EVs is in play. In the meantime, a look-see at BC Customs’s website indicates that the company is already anticipating off-road jobs for EVs, military or not.

BC Customs’s entry into the vehicle electrification scene is the new SXV-EV1, which the company describes as its first EV in its tactical fleet.

“BC Customs, dissatisfied with the industry’s standard direction for electric vehicles in hostile scenarios, designed the SXV-EV1 with the end-users in mind, ensuring a reliable and viable electric option for individuals serving in the field,” BC Customs states.

The SXV-EV1 is a collaboration with Hypercraft, which has this to say about the difference between its electro-tech and legacy energy platforms:

“Legacy propulsion is a tactical liability.

“High thermal signatures and predictable acoustic profiles are no longer just limitations—they are targets. On the modern battlefield, traditional logistical ‘tails’ are vulnerabilities that compromise mission integrity.”

“Our systems allow operators to modulate energy in real-time—transitioning from total acoustic stealth to maximum kinetic output through a single interface,” Hypercraft adds.

An EV With An On-Board Diesel Engine

Before you get too excited, the SXV-EVI is not a full battery-powered EV. It’s also not an extended range EV of the type first pioneered by General Motors through the short-lived Chevy Volt. The Volt provided EV-curious drivers with the experience of an all-electric powertrain, alongside the security blanket of an on-board gas tank. Once the car battery is spent, a gas-powered generator kicks in to cover the rest of the trip, making the old “range anxiety” canard irrelevant.

Nope, it’s not that, not exactly. BC Customs describes the SXV-EV1 as a dual-mode vehicle. Developed with Hypercraft, the SXV-EV1 hosts a diesel engine alongside an electric motor.

Diesel fuel aside, the SXV-EV1 is capable of moving around in full electric mode as needed. “This innovative design offers the range and durability of a diesel engine with the ability to seamlessly switch to silent mode for specified distances, ensuring adaptability in various operational scenarios,” BC Customs explains.

“The SXV-EV1 also features on-the-fly charging while driving and export power capabilities, transforming the vehicle into a mobile generator,” the company adds.

The technology is also available as a retrofit kit for the company’s existing SXV vehicles. “By making the SXV-EV1 technology accessible for retrofitting, BC Customs ensures that servicemen and women can benefit from the advancements in electric vehicle technology without the need for an entirely new fleet deployment,” the company emphasizes.

More EVs For The US Army

Among other signs of interest in EVs, in 2023 the the Annual Meeting and Exposition of the Association of the U.S. Army in October hosted a display of the Humvee Charge concept vehicle, a hybrid developed by Humvee manufacturer AM General. Not to be confused with General Motors, AM General made a point of using off-the-shelf elements to assemble the diesel-electric concept.

Readers, if you know whatever happened to the Humvee Charge, drop a note in the discussion thread. Meanwhile, the Army has sent out EV feelers in other directions, including a cab-less hybrid electric truck that can ferry supplies out to danger zones without putting drivers and crews in danger.

The Army has also been experimenting with anti-idling kits, which are battery retrofits that kick in to power on-board electronic systems while a vehicle is stationary, as a better-performing alternative compared to running a gas or diesel engine in idle mode. The Army points out that its vehicles are parked about 75% of the time when in use, so the fuel savings is substantial. So is the tactical advantage of silent running with a minimal heat signature.

The new M1E3 Abrams tank represents another move in the electrification direction. Unveiled in prototype form earlier this year at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit, the M1E3 sports a hybrid diesel-electric propulsion system.

The big question is, whatever happened to the JLTV program? JLTV (short for Joint Light Tactical Vehicle) was supposed to fulfill certain mobility needs for both the Army and the US Marine Corps, as indicated by the “Joint” in JLTV. The program did not necessarily call for full electrification, though GM’s Defense branch did produce an all-electric prototype.

Aside from contractor difficulties, one shortcoming surfaced back in 2022. As initially designed, the JLTV could generate only 12.8-14.6 kilowatts. In comparison, the ISV-H program asks for up to 60 kilowatts, enough to power up drones and electronic weapons as well as communications gear and other systems, whether the vehicle is in motion or stationary.

“Tactical vehicles are increasingly expected to do more than move troops from one point to another. They are becoming mobile nodes that can carry sensors, recharge systems, support command posts, and keep networks running closer to the front line. explains Colton Jones of Defence Blog.

“The Army is looking for a system that can move rapidly across long distances, deploy by air, sea, and land, and continue to support communications and battlefield systems while on the move,” Jones elaborates. “The vehicle is intended for use at division and brigade level, where mobile units increasingly need to operate in smaller, dispersed formations,” Colton elaborates.

Keep an eye on those other two automakers for more vehicle electrification activity. As reported by Defense Post last month, GM Defense already has an Infantry Squad Vehicle program under way based on the Chevy Colorado, which puts the Chevy Silverado in play as a hybrid EV, while Ford makes its pitch for a variant of its F-Series Super Duty pickup truck.

title: What's behind changing electric bills and what to do about it - The Detroit News
description:
When a summer electric bill arrives higher than expected, the reaction is usually the same: maybe rates went up.
Why summer bills can run higher Michigan summers are warm and humid.
That’s why summer energy costs show up on your electric bill, not your gas bill.
Since 2021, Michigan’s electric bill increases have totaled 7.8%, compared to a national average of 25.5%.
And a summer electric bill that’s higher than expected still stings, even if it’s lower than most of the country.
text:
When a summer electric bill arrives higher than expected, the reaction is usually the same: maybe rates went up. Maybe last month was just hotter than usual. Maybe a new fee got added.

Usually, the answer is simpler. And more fixable.

The difference between your rate and your bill matters a lot

Your energy rate is the price per unit of electricity, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), set through a formal, public regulatory process led by the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC). Utilities cannot change rates on their own. Every adjustment requires detailed review, consumer advocacy input and MPSC approval.

Your bill is something different: it reflects your actual usage multiplied by that rate, plus fixed delivery charges. As the U.S. Energy Information Administration notes, changes in usage often have a greater impact on monthly bills than changes in rates.

In other words, when bills are higher than expected, increased consumption is often the key factor.

Why summer bills can run higher

Michigan summers are warm and humid. Central air conditioning runs longer cycles when temperatures climb into the 80s and 90s with high dew points, working harder to remove moisture from the air. Add in that kids may be home all day, the garage refrigerator is running overtime, the dishwasher never seems to stop, and summer energy use can climb significantly compared to spring.

Unlike heating, which runs on natural gas in most Michigan homes, cooling runs entirely on electricity. That’s why summer energy costs show up on your electric bill, not your gas bill.

There’s also a timing dimension. On weekday afternoons (the peak demand window), electricity requires more generating capacity because millions of households are running AC simultaneously. Michigan has time-differentiated pricing to manage that strain: higher rates during on-peak hours (typically weekday afternoons) and lower rates in evenings and on weekends.

The good news: you can control this

Here’s the part that often gets lost in the frustration: usage is something you can influence. A few practical adjustments can make a real difference on your monthly bill:

Shift high-energy tasks such as laundry, dishwasher cycles and EV charging to evenings or early mornings, when it's cooler.

Raise your thermostat a few degrees during peak afternoon hours (typically 2 to 7 p.m. on weekdays) and use ceiling fans to extend your comfort without increasing AC run time.

Consider a smart or programmable thermostat that automates the scheduling for you.

Check with your utility about time-of-use rate programs that can reward you for shifting energy use to off-peak hours.

None of these requires a major investment. They’re about working with how the rate structure is designed, rather than against it.

Michigan’s bills are lower than most, but the pressure is real

It’s worth knowing what the data actually shows. According to the Michigan Public Service Commission, citing 2024 U.S. Energy Information Administration data, Michigan’s average monthly home electric bill ranks 15th-lowest in the nation, at $23 below the national average, $16 below Ohio and $13 below Indiana. Since 2021, Michigan’s electric bill increases have totaled 7.8%, compared to a national average of 25.5%.

That context matters, and it doesn’t minimize the pressure Michigan families feel. Groceries cost more. Gas prices have risen. And a summer electric bill that’s higher than expected still stings, even if it’s lower than most of the country.

Powering Michigan Forward was built to help families understand what’s actually driving their energy costs, identify practical ways to save and cut through the misinformation that makes an already complicated system feel even more confusing. The more you understand how the system works, the better equipped you are to make it work for you.

description:

text:
Introduction to Solid-State Battery Technology

Solid-state battery technology is emerging as a major next-generation energy-storage innovation because it replaces the conventional liquid or gel electrolyte used in many lithium-ion batteries with a solid electrolyte. This architectural change has the potential to improve safety, energy density, form-factor flexibility, and performance while supporting new battery designs for electric vehicles, consumer electronics, medical devices, wireless sensors, and other applications.

Unlike conventional lithium-ion cells, solid-state batteries can use solid electrolyte materials such as sulfide, oxide, and polymer systems. The technology is attracting significant research and development because manufacturers and end users are seeking batteries that can deliver higher energy density, improved safety, longer operating life, and potentially faster charging. MarketsandMarkets identifies increasing electric-vehicle adoption, demand for safe and high-density energy storage, progress in solid electrolytes, R&D investment, pilot manufacturing, and government-backed initiatives as major forces supporting market growth.

According to MarketsandMarkets, the global Solid-State Battery Market Size was valued at USD 0.26 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 1.77 billion by 2031, growing at a CAGR of 37.5% from 2025 to 2031. The rapid expansion reflects the transition from laboratory research and pilot-scale production toward commercialization and application-specific deployment.

History of Solid-State Battery Technology

The development of solid-state batteries is rooted in decades of research into solid ionic conductors, thin-film batteries, electrochemical interfaces, and advanced energy-storage materials. Early solid-state concepts were particularly relevant to small electronic devices and specialized applications where compact size, long life, and safety were more important than very high power output.

As demand for electric vehicles and high-performance portable electronics increased, research shifted toward larger-format solid-state cells capable of storing substantially more energy. This brought new attention to sulfide, oxide, polymer, and composite electrolyte systems, as well as manufacturing methods capable of producing reliable interfaces between solid materials.

The current stage is characterized by pilot production, automotive collaborations, materials innovation, process engineering, and efforts to reduce manufacturing cost. MarketsandMarkets identifies Blue Solutions, Solid Power, ProLogium Technology, Ilika, Factorial Energy, QuantumScape Battery, and LionVolt among notable players.

Benefits of Solid-State Batteries

Solid-state batteries offer several potential advantages over conventional battery architectures. The benefits depend on electrolyte chemistry, cell design, manufacturing process, operating conditions, and technology maturity.

Enhanced safety potential

Higher energy-density potential

Longer cycle-life potential

Faster-charging potential

Flexible and compact cell designs

Reduced leakage risk

Potential for wider operating windows

Current Market Size and Growth Trends of Solid-State Battery Industry

The global Solid-State Battery Market Size is entering a rapid commercialization phase. MarketsandMarkets estimates the market at USD 0.26 billion in 2025 and projects it to reach USD 1.77 billion by 2031, representing a 37.5% CAGR. This reflects the relatively early stage of the market and expectations that successful pilot programs and manufacturing scale-up will expand the addressable market.

Electric vehicles are a central demand driver. MarketsandMarkets reports that the EV application accounted for 33.0% of the market in 2024. By capacity, batteries above 500 mAh are expected to register the highest CAGR of 43.3%, while secondary batteries are projected to hold the largest share at 66.6% in 2025. Asia Pacific is estimated to dominate the market and is also identified as the fastest-growing regional market.

Key Drivers and Factors Influencing the Future of Solid-State Batteries

Several structural and technology factors are shaping the commercialization pathway for solid-state batteries.

Electric-vehicle electrification

Demand for safer energy storage

Materials and electrolyte innovation

R&D and pilot-scale investment

Manufacturing scale-up

Need for higher energy density

Government and regional initiatives

Emerging Trends in Solid-State Battery Technology

The industry is characterized by rapid innovation across electrolyte chemistry, electrode architecture, manufacturing, battery management, and cell integration. These trends are expected to influence the market as technology moves toward commercialization.

Sulfide electrolyte development

Oxide electrolyte development

Polymer and composite electrolytes

High-capacity cells above 500 mAh

Secondary battery expansion

Pilot-line automation

Interface engineering

AI-assisted materials discovery

Battery digitalization

Application-specific architectures

Opportunities and Challenges in the Solid-State Battery Market

Opportunities

Electric vehicles

Consumer electronics

Medical devices

Wireless sensors

Energy harvesting

Drones and aerospace

Defense applications

Smart textiles and wearables

Strategic automotive partnerships

Commercial-scale manufacturing

Challenges

High manufacturing cost

Complex solid-solid interfaces

Scale-up and yield challenges

Material sensitivity

Long-term validation requirements

Specialized supply chains

Competition from advanced lithium-ion technologies

Innovations and Advancements in Solid-State Battery Technology

Innovation is occurring across materials, cell architecture, manufacturing, and battery intelligence. The objective is to create cells that can combine high energy density with manufacturability, safety, reliability, and competitive lifecycle economics.

Future Applications and Industries that will benefit from Solid-State Batteries

The technology's future extends beyond electric vehicles. MarketsandMarkets covers consumer electronics, electric vehicles, medical devices, energy harvesting, wireless sensors, packaging, and other applications including drones, aerospace and defense, and smart textiles.

Electric vehicles: higher energy density and safety potential can support future EV platforms.

Consumer electronics: compact cells can support thinner and lighter connected devices.

Medical devices: small, reliable batteries can support long-life medical technologies.

Wireless sensors: miniature solid-state batteries can power distributed IoT and industrial sensors.

Energy harvesting: solid-state storage can complement compact harvesting systems.

Drones and aerospace: weight reduction and energy density can benefit unmanned and aerospace systems.

Defense: specialized cells may support compact, reliable power requirements.

Smart textiles: miniature battery architectures can support connected clothing and wearable electronics.

Regional Outlook for Solid-State Battery Innovation

Asia Pacific is estimated by MarketsandMarkets to dominate the solid-state battery market and is also identified as the fastest-growing regional market. The region benefits from established battery manufacturing capabilities, strong electronics and automotive supply chains, significant R&D activity, and government-backed initiatives.

North America remains a major innovation center because of strong R&D activity, battery startups, automotive partnerships, and investment in domestic battery manufacturing. Europe is also an important market, supported by automotive electrification, battery technology programs, and efforts to establish regional next-generation battery supply chains.

Role of Solid Electrolytes in Technology Innovation

The solid electrolyte is one of the defining elements of solid-state battery architecture. Its properties influence ionic conductivity, interface behavior, mechanical stability, temperature performance, manufacturability, and safety. Sulfide, oxide, and polymer approaches each involve different trade-offs, which is why the industry is pursuing multiple technology pathways.

Sulfide electrolytes can provide high ionic conductivity but may introduce processing and stability considerations. Oxide electrolytes can offer attractive stability characteristics but may require demanding manufacturing and interface engineering. Polymer electrolytes can provide flexibility and process advantages, while conductivity and temperature performance remain important development considerations.

Manufacturing Innovation and Commercialization Pathway

The transition from prototype cells to mass-produced solid-state batteries is one of the most important technology challenges facing the industry. Developers must establish repeatable processes that deliver consistent cell performance while maintaining acceptable production cost and yield.

Pilot manufacturing lines provide a bridge between laboratory research and commercial-scale production. They enable developers to identify process bottlenecks, measure yield, validate materials, optimize equipment, and develop quality-control procedures. Automation and digital manufacturing can further improve consistency by monitoring critical parameters in real time.

Solid-state Batteries and Sustainability

Solid-state batteries are being evaluated within the broader transition toward sustainable electrification. Their potential for higher energy density can reduce battery mass for a given energy target in some applications, while longer service life could improve lifecycle value. Sustainability benefits ultimately depend on material sourcing, manufacturing energy, durability, recycling pathways, and the complete supply chain.

Future ecosystems will therefore need to consider responsible sourcing, manufacturing efficiency, end-of-life recovery, recycling, and material circularity.

Competitive Landscape and Strategic Innovation

The competitive landscape includes established battery companies, specialist solid-state developers, automotive companies, material suppliers, research institutions, and technology partners. MarketsandMarkets identifies ProLogium Technology, Solid Power, Blue Solutions, Factorial, Ilika, QuantumScape Battery, and LionVolt as notable players based on technology capabilities, pilot-scale progress, and strategic collaborations.

Competition is increasingly shifting from laboratory performance toward commercialization capability. Companies must demonstrate scalable manufacturing, reliable interfaces, consistent cell quality, cost reduction, safety, and compatibility with customer requirements.

Future Outlook for Solid-State Battery Technology

The outlook is strongly linked to commercialization. The 37.5% projected CAGR reflects expectations of rapid expansion from a small 2025 base as pilot projects mature and applications move toward broader adoption. The technology is likely to progress through materials research, pilot manufacturing, validation, scale-up, and volume production.

The most important transition will be from technical feasibility to repeatable commercial economics. Developers need to optimize the entire value chain, from raw materials and electrolyte processing to electrode interfaces, cell assembly, formation, testing, pack integration, and recycling.

Conclusion: The promising future of Solid-State Battery Technology

Solid-state battery technology represents one of the most significant innovation pathways in next-generation energy storage. By replacing conventional liquid electrolyte architectures with solid electrolytes, developers are seeking improvements in safety, energy density, charging performance, durability, and design flexibility.

According to MarketsandMarkets, the global solid-state battery market is projected to increase from USD 0.26 billion in 2025 to USD 1.77 billion by 2031, representing a 37.5% CAGR. The market is supported by EV adoption, demand for safe and high-density storage, electrolyte innovation, R&D investment, pilot manufacturing, and government-backed initiatives.

At the same time, significant challenges remain. Solid-state batteries must demonstrate scalable manufacturing, competitive cost, consistent interfaces, long cycle life, reliable performance, and robust supply chains. Continued collaboration among developers, automotive manufacturers, material suppliers, equipment companies, research organizations, and policymakers will be important.

The future will be shaped not only by chemistry breakthroughs but by the ability to translate those breakthroughs into reliable, manufacturable, and economically viable products.

text:
BEIJING, Aug. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A news report by chinadiplomacy.org.cn on China's new Ecological and Environmental Code:

China's Ecological and Environmental Code embeds green development in law, showing how prosperity and environmental protection can advance together rather than as competing goals.

Economic development and ecological protection are no longer necessarily opposing objectives. With cleaner technologies and more sustainable growth models, countries increasingly have the opportunity to build competitive and resilient economies while reducing emissions and preserving the natural resources on which future prosperity depends.

China's newly adopted Ecological and Environmental Code offers the world a practical test of this proposition. By embedding ecological protection and green, low-carbon development into a comprehensive legal framework, China is moving beyond the old "develop first, clean up later" model. Its experience could provide valuable lessons for developing countries searching for a path toward industrialization that creates prosperity without sacrificing the environment.

Adopted on March 12, 2026, and scheduled to take effect Aug. 15, the Ecological and Environmental Code brings a broad range of environmental laws and regulations into a unified national framework covering pollution control, ecological conservation, green and low-carbon development and legal accountability. In doing so, China is seeking to shift environmental protection from a collection of individual policies into an integrated pillar of national development.

But the code represents something much larger than legal consolidation. It aims to institutionalize a fundamental transformation in China's development philosophy, moving beyond the outdated logic of development versus environment toward an economy in which ecological protection itself can become a source of innovation, investment, competitiveness and long-term prosperity.

That distinction matters well beyond China.

China's development experience is increasingly studied across the Global South. Developing countries are interested not in copying China wholesale but in understanding how it combined long-term planning, infrastructure investment, industrialization, technological upgrading and poverty reduction. The Ecological and Environmental Code could add another important dimension to that experience by testing whether green development can become part of modernization itself rather than a luxury pursued only after a country becomes wealthy.

China's green transition has been years in the making. Environmental protection has gradually moved from the margins of economic policymaking toward the center of the country's development strategy. The new code seeks to give that transformation greater legal coherence and permanence.

That matters because green transformation requires more than targets; it requires institutions. Businesses need predictable rules, investors need regulatory certainty, local governments need clearly defined responsibilities and citizens need effective environmental protection. By embedding these expectations within a more systematic legal framework, China is working to give its green transition greater continuity, accountability and credibility.

The larger shift is from environmental protection as a separate policy domain to green development as an organizing principle of economic modernization. Pollution control, ecological restoration, clean energy, industrial upgrading and climate action increasingly form part of the same development agenda. In this emerging model, protecting the environment and transforming the economy are not parallel projects; they are parts of the same project.

From 'Two Mountains' to national law

The timing of the code is particularly significant. It takes effect on Aug. 15, closely linking a new chapter in China's environmental law with an idea articulated more than two decades earlier.

On Aug. 15, 2005, Xi Jinping, then working in east China's Zhejiang province, put forward what became known as the "Two Mountains" theory, the idea that "clear waters and green mountains are as valuable as mountains of gold and silver." The principle has since become central to China's green development philosophy, the belief that ecological protection is not the enemy of prosperity but can become one of its foundations.

Twenty-one years later, the new code represents an effort to translate that philosophy more systematically into law.

At its core, the "Two Mountains" theory challenges the traditional assumption that countries must choose between protecting nature and creating prosperity. Instead, it advances a more ambitious proposition: ecological protection can itself become a form of economic development. When forests, clean water, biodiversity and healthy ecosystems are treated as valuable assets rather than obstacles to growth, conservation can generate livelihoods, attract investment and create new pathways to sustainable prosperity.

China has spent years experimenting with how this principle can work in practice. Anji County in Zhejiang province is perhaps its most prominent example. Once dependent on mining and environmentally damaging industries, the county shifted toward ecological restoration, tourism, sustainable agriculture and greener economic activities.

The significance of this transformation is not simply environmental. It illustrates how restoring ecological assets can create new economic opportunities. Moving away from environmentally damaging industries does not necessarily mean sacrificing jobs and growth if new industries and livelihoods can emerge from a healthier environment.

China's experiments have gone further by seeking to change the economic incentives surrounding conservation itself. Local initiatives have explored ways to assign value to forests, water resources, carbon sinks and other ecological assets through ecological-product valuation, green finance, carbon markets and related mechanisms.

The objective is straightforward but potentially transformative: if communities can generate sustainable income by protecting nature, environmental conservation becomes not merely a regulatory obligation but an economic opportunity.

Consider the logic of a forest. If its primary economic value comes from cutting down its trees, pressure for exploitation will always remain. But if a standing forest can generate jobs and livelihoods through tourism, sustainable agriculture, ecosystem services, carbon markets and green industries, the old choice between prosperity and preservation begins to dissolve.

That logic is often summed up as turning "green into gold," building an economy in which nature can become more valuable when protected than when it is destroyed.

When environmental policy becomes growth policy

This is where the traditional development-versus-environment debate becomes increasingly outdated.

The question is no longer simply how much environmental protection an economy can afford, but how much economic opportunity a green transformation can create. If cleaner technologies, ecological restoration and low-carbon industries generate investment, innovation, productivity and employment, environmental policy ceases to be a brake on growth; it becomes one of its engines.

China is already attempting to build such a green industrial ecosystem. Electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy, energy storage and green manufacturing have become increasingly important components of its economy. Environmental regulation can reinforce this transformation by encouraging businesses to adopt cleaner technologies while creating demand for new products, services and industries.

Another less-discussed dimension of green development is national resilience.

As a major energy importer of oil and gas, China remains exposed to volatility in international energy markets and disruptions to global supply chains. In an era of geopolitical uncertainty, renewable energy, electric mobility, energy storage and greater energy efficiency therefore serve more than environmental objectives. They can also reduce exposure to imported fossil fuels and strengthen energy security.

Seen from this perspective, green development is no longer a narrow environmental agenda; it is becoming a pillar of national development strategy. Ecological protection supports sustainability, clean industries drive competitiveness, technological innovation creates new sources of growth and reduced energy vulnerability strengthens resilience.

Environmental policy, industrial policy, innovation policy and energy-security policy increasingly intersect.

The Ecological and Environmental Code seeks to give this broader transformation a durable legal foundation. By bringing environmental protection, green development, industrial upgrading and legal accountability into a more integrated framework, China is attempting to ensure that ecological, economic and technological objectives reinforce rather than compete with one another.

Why the developing world should pay attention

For developing countries, this debate is particularly urgent. Many are among the most vulnerable to climate change, yet they also face enormous development pressures. They need reliable electricity, transport networks, housing, factories and millions of jobs. They must reduce poverty and raise living standards while confronting environmental degradation and increasingly severe climate risks.

They cannot simply stop developing, nor should they be asked to. The solution is not to abandon industrialization but to industrialize differently, with cleaner energy, greener technologies and stronger environmental governance. The goal is a development model in which prosperity and ecological sustainability advance together.

China's evolving experience offers one possible reference point, not a blueprint to be copied but a development approach worth studying. It combines environmental regulation with industrial upgrading, renewable energy development with energy resilience, and ecological restoration with new economic value generated from natural assets.

The broader lesson is that environmental policy need not sit outside the development strategy. It can become an integral part of it.

Every country, of course, has different institutions, natural resources, fiscal capacities and development priorities. China's experience should therefore not be treated as a universal formula. Its significance lies instead in challenging the assumption that developing economies must accept environmental degradation as the inevitable price of prosperity.

China's experiment poses a powerful question: what if the road to prosperity does not have to run through environmental destruction?

If green development can create jobs, industries, innovation and economic resilience while protecting the natural foundations of prosperity, then environmental protection is no longer simply a cost of development. It becomes an engine of development.

This is perhaps the most important idea embodied in China's Ecological and Environmental Code, and its most consequential lesson for the developing world.

title: The clean energy revolution has a mining problem - The Hill
authors: Susan Atkinson, opinion contributor, Susan Atkinson, opinion contributor
description:
Yet one essential truth is often missing from the conversation: there is no clean energy transition without mining.
The International Energy Agency has concluded that critical minerals are indispensable to clean energy technologies.
Copper, lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, rare earth elements, uranium, and other critical minerals are the building blocks of modern technology.
They are needed for electric vehicles, batteries, transmission lines, renewable energy systems, advanced nuclear technologies, and the defense systems that protect our nation.
If America is serious about energy independence, economic competitiveness, and national security, we must recognize that critical minerals are foundational to all three.
text:
Every electric vehicle, battery storage system, transmission line, wind turbine, solar installation, and next-generation nuclear reactor begins with materials extracted from the earth. Before America can build the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence, data centers, advanced manufacturing, and an increasingly electrified economy, we must first secure the critical minerals that make those technologies possible.

Americans increasingly agree on one thing: our future will require far more electricity than our past. Whether the priority is economic growth, energy security, national defense, or reducing emissions, meeting that demand will require a historic expansion of America’s energy infrastructure, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation.

Yet one essential truth is often missing from the conversation: there is no clean energy transition without mining. The International Energy Agency has concluded that critical minerals are indispensable to clean energy technologies.

Copper, lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, rare earth elements, uranium, and other critical minerals are the building blocks of modern technology. They are needed for electric vehicles, batteries, transmission lines, renewable energy systems, advanced nuclear technologies, and the defense systems that protect our nation.

The challenge is that while America is rapidly advancing new energy technologies, we have not moved with the same urgency to develop the mineral supply chains those technologies require.

The U.S. has significant deposits of many critical minerals, along with the engineering expertise, skilled workforce, and technological capabilities needed to develop them responsibly. From Nevada’s lithium resources and Arizona’s copper reserves to Wyoming’s rare earth potential and Idaho’s cobalt deposits, America has the resources needed to strengthen domestic supply chains.

The question is whether we have the ability to develop them in a timely and responsible manner.

Responsible mineral development and strong environmental protections are not competing goals. The objective should not be fewer safeguards — it should be a permitting system that is rigorous, predictable and capable of making timely decisions.

Today, developing a new mining project can take well over a decade. An often-cited S&P Global study found that mine development timelines in many jurisdictions routinely exceed 15 years. Companies often face overlapping reviews, lengthy litigation, and years of uncertainty before a shovel reaches the ground. The Congressional Research Service has documented the complexity of federal permitting under the National Environmental Policy Act. Environmental oversight is essential, but endless delay does not automatically produce better environmental outcomes. A permitting system without predictability discourages investment and leaves America increasingly dependent on foreign suppliers.

That dependence is not only an economic concern. It is a national security vulnerability.

The same materials needed for electric vehicles, batteries, transmission lines, wind turbines, and solar panels are also essential for fighter aircraft, advanced electronics, communications systems, and other defense technologies. America’s energy future and national security increasingly depend on the same mineral supply chains.

Today, China dominates much of the world’s processing and refining of critical minerals, giving Beijing significant influence over materials essential to modern industry and defense. America should not rely on geopolitical competitors for the resources needed to power our economy, strengthen our electric grid, and protect our nation.

Improving domestic mineral production will require more than identifying deposits. America must also invest in better mapping, research, processing capacity, and a new generation of engineers, scientists, and skilled workers.

Advanced technologies can help locate resources more efficiently and reduce unnecessary exploration. Better information can lead to more responsible development, good-paying jobs, and stronger domestic supply chains.

The U.S. also has a long history with strategic minerals. Domestic uranium production helped support America’s nuclear program during the last century, and as interest grows in advanced nuclear technologies and small modular reactors, reliable access to nuclear fuel will become increasingly important.

It makes little sense to embrace next-generation nuclear power while relying heavily on foreign sources for the materials needed to support it.

This is not an argument for weakening environmental protections. It is an argument for producing more of the minerals we need under America’s rigorous environmental, labor, and safety standards rather than outsourcing extraction to countries with weaker protections and less transparency.

Outsourcing mining does not eliminate environmental impacts. It simply moves them elsewhere while increasing our dependence on foreign suppliers. If America is serious about energy independence, economic competitiveness, and national security, we must recognize that critical minerals are foundational to all three.

The clean energy transition will depend not only on the technologies we invent, but also on whether we can responsibly develop the materials that make those technologies possible. America’s clean energy future does not begin with a battery, a solar panel, or a wind turbine. It begins beneath the ground.

text:
On August 17, 2026, farmworker advocates intensified calls for stronger heat protections in North Carolina after heat indexes in parts of the state climbed above 105°F, exposing agricultural workers to potentially dangerous conditions. Workers and advocates who gathered at the state capitol said long hours, limited access to cooling and the absence of mandatory state heat standards are putting field crews at risk. The debate matters beyond worker safety: North Carolina agriculture depends on a reliable labor force at a time when farms are already confronting drought, higher input costs, tariffs and pressure on commodity margins.

The National Weather Service issues heat advisories when combinations of temperature and humidity reach dangerous levels, urging people to reduce exposure to the sun and take precautions against heat-related illness. Yet agricultural workers often have little flexibility to leave fields when temperatures rise. Andressia Ramirez, an advocacy and civic engagement manager at Casa Azul de Wilson, described visiting a farmworker camp where a young man with a fever sat beneath a tree because it was cooler outdoors than inside his housing. North Carolina farmworker housing is not currently required to have air conditioning, making nighttime recovery from daytime heat another concern during prolonged heat waves.

Ramirez said the incident illustrates conditions that have become normalized for parts of the agricultural workforce. The issue is particularly important during a summer in which heat and drought are placing simultaneous pressure on workers, crops and farm businesses. Producers are already managing higher operating expenses, volatile commodity prices, tariffs and weather-related production risks. Adding labor protections can raise questions about compliance and costs, particularly for smaller operations. Advocates argue, however, that heat illness can also generate economic consequences through lost workdays, lower productivity, turnover and greater pressure on a supply chain that depends heavily on seasonal agricultural labor.

Heat Safety Debate Tests the Balance Between Workers and Farm Economics

At the federal level, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration provides guidance aimed at preventing heat illness, but advocates note that agricultural employees still lack a comprehensive, specific federal heat standard currently in force beyond broader workplace safety obligations. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health recommends measures including work-rest cycles, task rotation, hydration and limits on heat stress. Those recommendations provide a framework for employers but do not themselves constitute mandatory nationwide requirements. Seven states have adopted specific occupational heat standards, while North Carolina has not enacted comparable statewide rules, leaving the issue at the center of a growing policy debate.

Esmeralda Juarez, who works with the nonprofit NC Field, told reporters she began laboring in tobacco fields at age 13 and recalled headaches, stomach pain and nausea while working in extreme conditions. Her experience underscores a challenge frequently raised in agricultural labor discussions: workers who depend on daily wages may be reluctant to stop working even when they experience symptoms of heat illness. Advocates say access to water alone is insufficient, calling for shade, understandable safety training, acclimatization periods and scheduled opportunities to recover. Those measures could become increasingly relevant as extreme weather complicates planting, harvesting and livestock management across U.S. agriculture.

The economic dimension makes the North Carolina dispute more complicated. Immigrant workers represent an estimated 12% of the state's workforce, while a conservative estimate cited by the N.C. Budget and Tax Center places their annual economic contribution at roughly $60 billion. Agriculture remains one of the sectors most dependent on immigrant and seasonal labor. For growers, meanwhile, additional requirements arrive as crop insurance, input costs, financing expenses, drought and uncertain commodity prices shape operating decisions. The policy challenge is therefore not simply whether protections should increase, but how lawmakers can improve workplace safety while preventing compliance costs from falling disproportionately on already stressed farm operations.

For the broader U.S. farm sector, North Carolina offers a preview of a debate likely to intensify as heat waves become a more persistent operational risk. Precision agriculture and improved weather forecasting can help producers adjust field schedules, while sustainable agriculture practices may reduce some environmental stresses, but technology cannot eliminate human exposure during labor-intensive operations. Future farm policy discussions could increasingly connect worker protection, crop insurance, disaster assistance and farm profitability, particularly if extreme heat affects yields, livestock performance and harvest schedules. Co-ops, growers, contractors and policymakers may ultimately need coordinated strategies that treat workforce resilience as part of agricultural risk management.

text:
The 11th edition of the India EV Conclave brings CXOs, policymakers, and innovators together not just for handshakes or polite applause, but to address these fault lines head-on across battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure, raw material security, software-defined vehicles, and workforce readiness.

Auto EV Conclave 11th edition is not limited to what's happening in the EV industry today; its discussions focus on building what comes next.

Let's look into some core discussion points that will be the soul of the Electric Vehicle Conference and dominate the whole room.

Charging at scale:

Advt

Installing chargers is not enough for India’s EV growth; they need to be reliable, compatible, accessible, and affordable, all while staying connected to the electric supply, which can actually hold. But one question still stands: does India have enough charging infrastructure for a growing EV market?

“Infrastructure, investment, and the last-mile gap” are not only three words in a quote mentioned in the discussion points of the EV Industry Conclave, but they are also the choke points and main concerns one should look into.

Infrastructure: Is it built in a way that can help one when needed the most, or is it situated in a place that is easily accessible?

Investment: A big question that plays a vital role in building the EV industry: who will actually invest in charging networks in India? Will the government take the initiative, or will a private player step in?

Last-mile gap: Are chargers actually available where people need them? Well, this point actually tells you the gap, or you can say the difficulty in providing charging to people when they actually need it, or when they use their automobiles.

Build for Bharat:

Are Indian EV products actually being designed specifically for Indian road conditions and Indian budgets, or are they just built without being concerned about people's needs or wants?

Indian markets are different from other countries' markets, which is absolutely ok because it depends on budget factors and the condition of resources, such as roads and so on. India's most successful EV products are two-wheelers and three-wheelers.

So, what factors should the Indian EV industry consider before designing any product to better suit its needs? Some are:

Indian budget and low price

Road efficiency

Better battery backup

Battery protection against heat, dust, and water

Simple and strong repair

Fleet electrification:

Advt

The smartest and most underrated way to conserve resources such as petrol and diesel for longer is to convert a fleet of fuel powered vehicles into electric vehicles.

Let's do some fact talk. Fleet vehicles run more kilometers than fuel-powered vehicles and also have greater durability, which means every vehicle in the fleet saves more fuel than a privately owned vehicle.

So ideally, there are no drawbacks in converting vehicles into electric vehicles, and it's not harming the environment or your pocket. But before going into it few things you should know or also take care of:

A proper driver training program should be there before handing over the vehicle.

Battery health monitoring of the vehicle should be kept as a priority

The electric vehicle (fleet) should be designed around its operator schedule.

If a vehicle is being used continuously, it may require fast charging.

Related Read: From Revolution to Reality: Inside the room where India's EV future gets decided

Policy synergy or policy chaos:

India launched many policies like FAME II and PM E-DRIVE to support EV adoption, manufacturing, buses, and expanding the ecosystem of the EV industry.

But are these policies really becoming benefits for citizens, or are they creating chaos for everyone? Well, let's break it down a bit:

Some schemes promote the EV industry and give full support to it, but somewhere they are also making it confusing, increasing taxes, delaying subsidies, making eligibility requirements unclear, and so on.

Our panelist at the Electric Vehicle Conclave will be addressing these points and giving us checkpoints on what is actually happening around India.

Global learnings, Indian realities:

Learning doesn't have any boundaries, which is the best part of this. The Indian EV industry may not be the best yet and has many flaws, from battery technology to its manufacturing, but that doesn't mean every solution has to be built from scratch.

If we look at the kaizen philosophy of Japan, it tells us that you should keep making small, consistent improvements every day rather than waiting for a big breakthrough; it will help to detect mistakes or problems at an early stage, and finding their solution becomes easy.

India can adapt the same technique by looking beyond their EV ecosystem and learning from different countries that are facing similar problems and dealing with them. The endpoint isn't to just copy the solutions that are working for them at that time but to understand how they tackle the problem without making it a burden for them.

The discussion is not over yet; it's just a small trailer of something big that will unfold in the Electric Vehicle Conference. Come join us to be a part of this wonderful journey and experience extraordinary ideas, conversations, and innovations that will help to shape the future of the EV industry.

text:
Plan balances reliability, diverse resources and costs while helping communities in the Carolinas continue to build robust economies

Near-term actions serve our customers’ rising energy needs while keeping customer benefits, value and future optionality central to resource planning

GREENVILLE, S.C. – South Carolina is one of the fastest-growing states in the nation, attracting new residents, major employers and billions of dollars in economic investment. Meeting the state’s energy needs requires a reliable energy system that can support thriving communities while keeping costs as low as possible for customers.

Duke Energy’s 2026 Carolinas Resource Plan – submitted Aug. 14 to the Public Service Commission of South Carolina (PSCSC) – reflects execution already underway and highlights new opportunities to power South Carolina’s future.

The strategy is designed to maximize the value of existing assets while making prudent investments in additional diverse resources needed to serve the state’s growing population and economy.

Through an execution-informed planning approach, Duke Energy will continue adjusting to changing conditions while maintaining its focus on delivering safe, reliable and affordable energy for Palmetto State customers.

Our view: “South Carolina’s success depends on having the energy infrastructure in place to support new residents, new businesses and new or expanding industries,” said Tim Pearson, Duke Energy’s South Carolina president. “We’ve made significant progress executing the strategy outlined in previous resource plans, and this updated roadmap builds on that momentum and details the additional actions we need to take now to keep the Carolinas powered reliably and affordably as the region grows.”

A plan for South Carolina: Consistent with previous resource plans and supportive of South Carolina energy policy goals under the 2025 Energy Security Act (Act 41), the latest plan advances new generation, new energy storage and renewables opportunities, evaluates future nuclear generation options, maximizes energy efficiency and maintains flexibility to adapt as customer needs, technology and market conditions evolve.

What’s in the plan?

Key elements include:

Natural Gas: Natural gas is a major near-term reliability resource, with uprates completed, multiple combined cycle (CC)/combustion turbine (CT) projects advancing, approval for a 1,400 megawatt (MW) new combined cycle facility in Anderson County secured, and turbine supply agreements executed with delivery beginning from GE Vernova in Greenville.

Storage: The company is scaling battery storage execution, with storage projects in service, equipment secured, interconnection activity underway, and an RFP for 400 MW of standalone storage in South Carolina.

Solar: Solar procurement and construction remain active, including completed facilities, projects under construction, and RFPs for solar and solar paired with storage.

Nuclear: Existing nuclear assets continue to be maximized through license renewals, uprates, and fuel-cycle work, while the company evaluates potential new nuclear options and considers sites in Cherokee County, S.C., and Stokes County, N.C.

Grid Edge: Grid Edge programs are treated as a core execution tool to reduce, shift, and shape demand through energy efficiency, demand-side management, load curtailment, customer programs, and storage demand response.

To explore more details of the Carolinas Resource Plan, visit duke-energy.com/CarolinasResourcePlan.

Our view: “As South Carolina continues to grow, we’re continuing our investment not only in new energy resources, but also in programs and technologies that help customers use energy more efficiently and save money,” Pearson said. “From energy-efficiency programs to demand-response initiatives and our grid modernization strategy, this plan provides customers with more value while ensuring we have the reliable energy infrastructure needed to support the state’s future.”

Maximizing value for customers: Duke Energy continues to use every tool available to manage costs for our customers while delivering the high quality of service they expect.

Through its proposed resource mix, the company is maximizing the value that tax credits provide customers and finalizing the recently approved combination of Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress – efforts that together will deliver more than $5 billion in cost-saving benefits to the customers and communities the company serves.

Duke Energy has also applied for loans from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) that represent potentially billions of dollars in customer savings as the company strengthens the electric grid.

What’s next: The PSCSC will hold a hearing on the resource plan in April 2027 and issue an order by June 2027.

Duke Energy Carolinas, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 20,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 2.9 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 24,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.

Duke Energy Progress

Duke Energy Progress, a subsidiary of Duke Energy, owns 13,800 megawatts of energy capacity, supplying electricity to 1.8 million residential, commercial and industrial customers across a 28,000-square-mile service area in North Carolina and South Carolina.

Duke Energy

Duke Energy (NYSE: DUK), a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C., is one of America’s largest energy holding companies. The company’s electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky, and collectively own 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. Its natural gas utilities serve 1.6 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio and Kentucky.

Duke Energy is executing an energy modernization strategy, keeping customer value at the forefront as it invests in electric grid upgrades and efficient generation resources to strengthen the system and serve growing energy needs.

text:
X-energy to get another $1 billion: During its second-quarter earnings call on Thursday, CEO Clay Sell said the DOE notified X-energy that it would receive an additional $1 billion in cost-shared funding for its Long Mott project. The company wants to build four Xe-100 reactors at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations, a chemical production facility in Seadrift, Texas. It would be the first advanced reactor deployment of its kind at an industrial site in North America.

Combined with the $1 billion X-energy has already received from DOE, the company will have received roughly $2.15 billion for the Seadrift project, Sell said. X-energy will be required to follow the same cost-share requirements as in the earlier allocation.

“Our project with Dow is important not only because it is our initial deployment but because of the unmatched versatility for nuclear energy that it represents,” Sell said.

He highlighted other key second-quarter moments and developments for the company during the call, including the following:

Entering into long-term agreements for high-assay low-enriched uranium enrichment services with Centrus Energy Corp. and General Matter.

Entering into an agreement with SGL Carbon to expand manufacturing capacity for nuclear-grade graphite.

Receiving an $11 million economic development grant from Tennessee to support its TRISO-X fuel fabrication campus in Oak Ridge.

Acquiring roughly 70 acres adjacent to its Oak Ridge campus to expand its TRISO-X footprint.

With regard to Long Mott, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is expected to complete its construction permit review later this year, with a permit issuance decision likely in the first half of 2027, according to Sell. X-energy is also expected to submit its construction permit application to the NRC in the first half of next year for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility project in Washington state with Amazon and Energy Northwest.

Lastly, an announcement of a 1-GW project with an unnamed utility is coming “in the near future,” Sell said.

TerraPower, South Korean companies reach deals: TerraPower is looking to strengthen its ties with South Korea and has reached agreements with Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC) and SK Innovation to develop and commercialize the Natrium reactor in the United States, Korea, and select international markets. This comes after TerraPower officials—including founder and chair Bill Gates and president and CEO Chris Levesque—traveled to South Korea to meet with Prime Minister Seong-sook Han and leaders from the Export-Import Bank of Korea, HD Hyundai, HDEC, and SK Innovation.

Under the agreement reached with HDEC, the Korean company will be TerraPower's engineering, procurement, and construction contractor and will build up to eight of its Natrium reactors with completion, price, and performance guarantees. TerraPower is currently constructing its first Natrium reactor—a 345-MWe sodium-cooled fast reactor with molten salt heat storage to temporarily boost power output to 500 MWe—in Kemmerer, Wyo.

TerraPower’s term-sheet agreement with SK Innovation clears a pathway for Korea's first Natrium plant, along with plans to expand internationally. The two companies will explore opportunities to collaborate on engineering and digital innovation solutions, including digital twin technology and artificial intelligence, the news release said.

“Today marks a pivotal moment for TerraPower as we embark on a new chapter of international collaboration with Korea’s leading organizations,” Levesque said. “Combining TerraPower’s innovative advanced nuclear technology with Korea’s nuclear construction and operational expertise will strengthen our global cooperation and accelerate the deployment of a Natrium fleet that will transform the world's energy landscape.”

title: The hidden link between Europe's housing crisis and energy poverty
description:
With housing costs surging across Europe, EU-funded researchers are showing how tackling energy poverty and inequality together could fix fragmented housing policy.
“My view is that affordable housing and energy, which are usually treated as separate policy fields, should be thought of together,” said Janoschka.
“The housing cost overburden in Greece is the highest in the EU, and a substantive part of that is energy costs,” said Meriç Özgüneş, housing policy coordinator at Housing Thessaloniki, the city’s social rental agency.
Dr Anne Kantel, an energy policy researcher at the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research in Karlsruhe, coordinates the EU-funded HouseInc project.
“When we talk about housing policy, we’re not just talking about any housing, but quality housing related to people’s well-being,” said Kantel.
text:
With housing costs surging across Europe, EU-funded researchers are showing how tackling energy poverty and inequality together could fix fragmented housing policy.

As cities across Europe sweltered under a heatwave in June 2026, professor Michael Janoschka was focused on a longer term problem: how to make homes affordable and energy-efficient in a continent facing a housing crisis.

Janoschka has spent much of his career studying how rising house prices, property speculation and urban inequality are reshaping European cities.

Today, as professor of regional science at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany, he is leading an international team investigating how housing affordability and energy poverty can be tackled together rather than as separate policy challenges.

“Europe has an ageing, often energy-inefficient housing stock,” said Janoschka. “Housing affordability is not only about rent or mortgage payments, but also about heating and, more and more, cooling.” For him, rising prices and energy use are part of the same crisis.

House prices have soared in the past decade, and almost 10% of EU citizens face a “housing cost overburden” – spending more than 40% of disposable income on rent, mortgage and utilities. Meanwhile, nearly 10% of Europeans cannot keep their homes warm enough, and summertime cooling is a growing concern too.

Rethinking policy with communities

As part of the EU-funded PREFIGURE project, researchers, municipalities and housing organisations from eight European countries have joined forces under Janoschka’s lead to explore the link between housing and energy, and how they can be made both more affordable and inclusive.

Together, they have studied 16 local initiatives involving the provision of affordable housing and energy for vulnerable groups, including lower-income households, older people, refugees and people without a home.

They looked at what municipalities, local organisations and residents are already doing to tackle the pressures of housing affordability and energy poverty in their neighbourhoods.

“My view is that affordable housing and energy, which are usually treated as separate policy fields, should be thought of together,” said Janoschka. The researchers argue that housing should be viewed as more than simply providing a roof over people’s heads. It also shapes health, economic well-being and social cohesion.

To understand how widespread these challenges are, the researchers also surveyed around 30 000 households across Europe. They are now analysing the survey results to understand how successful local approaches could be adapted elsewhere through “learning communities” comprising networks of residents, public officials and researchers.

Solutions on the ground

The German city of Karlsruhe, for example, has run a cooperative housing programme for 20 years, offering renovation subsidies and giving homeless people access to vacant apartments, alongside the creation of energy-efficient homes. According to Janoschka, the programme has significantly reduced homelessness.

The researchers are now exploring whether these lessons can transfer to Thessaloniki in northern Greece, which has 35,000 vacant homes.

“The housing cost overburden in Greece is the highest in the EU, and a substantive part of that is energy costs,” said Meriç Özgüneş, housing policy coordinator at Housing Thessaloniki, the city’s social rental agency.

The agency has recently been renovating 40 long-empty homes for vulnerable communities, with people moving in since last December. It aims to add 60 more within three years and hundreds more after that.

“The PREFIGURE work has provided us with inspiring stories and a deeper understanding of potential strategies and financing approaches,” said Özgüneş. The Thessaloniki scheme offers tenants both long-term social rental contracts and energy-upgraded homes.

In Barcelona, another initiative – WikiHousing – is taking community participation a step further. It brings together young people aged 18 to 30 from diverse backgrounds to work alongside architects and builders to help design, prefabricate and eventually manage energy-efficient public housing.

As they learn practical construction skills, the project is also creating an open-source model that other cities can adapt to develop affordable, low-carbon homes.

Inequality, energy and place

While the team led by Janoschka has focused on identifying successful local housing initiatives, another European research team has been investigating why many vulnerable communities continue to miss out on affordable, energy-efficient housing.

Dr Anne Kantel, an energy policy researcher at the Fraunhofer Institute for Systems and Innovation Research in Karlsruhe, coordinates the EU-funded HouseInc project.

Working with local authorities, researchers and community organisations across Europe, the team is exploring how housing inequality is shaped by energy costs, market forces, policy, climate change and access to transport, public services and social support.

“When we talk about housing policy, we’re not just talking about any housing, but quality housing related to people’s well-being,” said Kantel.

The team ran four case studies involving marginalised groups from Eastern Europe: migrants in Germany, Roma communities in Czechia and Romania, and Ukrainian refugees in Italy.

Through interviews, focus groups and hands-on trials, residents worked with local authorities, NGOs and researchers to discuss potential innovations.

The researchers have also been surveying almost 15,000 households across eight countries to map where these gaps in housing and energy access are most acute, and building an atlas cataloguing existing fixes, such as social rental agencies or community-based renovation schemes, that other cities could draw on.

Falling through the cracks

The research found that these marginalised communities often face structural discrimination.

Roma people frequently lacked official residency status or lived in self-built homes on land they did not own, raising the risk of displacement. Meanwhile, Ukrainian refugees in Italy struggled with short-term funding that prevented them settling, finding work or integrating.

In both cases, homes often lacked energy efficiency measures, forcing tenants to rely on old electrical or heating appliances.

“A recommendation that came out of this is that there needs to be some stability and longevity in such programmes,” said Kantel. “Local authorities also need support and training to assess local needs and help people in targeted ways.”

In the Vogelstang district of Mannheim, Germany, home to many residents with a migrant background and living in energy-inefficient buildings, people reported struggling to heat and cool their homes affordably. However, many in the municipality have not picked this up as a separate problem.

For Kantel, that finding is revealing. It shows how issues like energy poverty can slip through the cracks when departments work in silos, without collaboration and exchange. “In Europe, I think there’s a need to redistribute resources better and invest in local capacity building,” she said.

Integrated housing strategy

Kantel’s broader argument is that municipalities need to consider a whole area’s buildings and infrastructure, not just individual homes, when planning housing strategy.

“The housing becomes part of the area’s infrastructure,” she said. “Measures can’t just stay at the household level, they need to go to the building and neighbourhood level.”

Ultimately, the two research teams reach the same conclusion: making homes greener will not automatically make them fairer.

Housing policies need to be designed alongside the people they are intended to help, so that Europe’s green transition does not leave its most vulnerable citizens behind.

This article was originally published in Horizon the EU Research and Innovation Magazine.

Research in this article was funded by the EU’s Horizon Programme.

text:
X-energy to get another $1 billion: During its second-quarter earnings call on Thursday, CEO Clay Sell said the DOE notified X-energy that it would receive an additional $1 billion in cost-shared funding for its Long Mott project. The company wants to build four Xe-100 reactors at Dow’s UCC Seadrift Operations, a chemical production facility in Seadrift, Texas. It would be the first advanced reactor deployment of its kind at an industrial site in North America.

Combined with the $1 billion X-energy has already received from DOE, the company will have received roughly $2.15 billion for the Seadrift project, Sell said. X-energy will be required to follow the same cost-share requirements as in the earlier allocation.

“Our project with Dow is important not only because it is our initial deployment but because of the unmatched versatility for nuclear energy that it represents,” Sell said.

He highlighted other key second-quarter moments and developments for the company during the call, including the following:

Entering into long-term agreements for high-assay low-enriched uranium enrichment services with Centrus Energy Corp. and General Matter.

Entering into an agreement with SGL Carbon to expand manufacturing capacity for nuclear-grade graphite.

Receiving an $11 million economic development grant from Tennessee to support its TRISO-X fuel fabrication campus in Oak Ridge.

Acquiring roughly 70 acres adjacent to its Oak Ridge campus to expand its TRISO-X footprint.

With regard to Long Mott, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is expected to complete its construction permit review later this year, with a permit issuance decision likely in the first half of 2027, according to Sell. X-energy is also expected to submit its construction permit application to the NRC in the first half of next year for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility project in Washington state with Amazon and Energy Northwest.

Lastly, an announcement of a 1-GW project with an unnamed utility is coming “in the near future,” Sell said.

TerraPower, South Korean companies reach deals: TerraPower is looking to strengthen its ties with South Korea and has reached agreements with Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC) and SK Innovation to develop and commercialize the Natrium reactor in the United States, Korea, and select international markets. This comes after TerraPower officials—including founder and chair Bill Gates and president and CEO Chris Levesque—traveled to South Korea to meet with Prime Minister Seong-sook Han and leaders from the Export-Import Bank of Korea, HD Hyundai, HDEC, and SK Innovation.

Under the agreement reached with HDEC, the Korean company will be TerraPower's engineering, procurement, and construction contractor and will build up to eight of its Natrium reactors with completion, price, and performance guarantees. TerraPower is currently constructing its first Natrium reactor—a 345-MWe sodium-cooled fast reactor with molten salt heat storage to temporarily boost power output to 500 MWe—in Kemmerer, Wyo.

TerraPower’s term-sheet agreement with SK Innovation clears a pathway for Korea's first Natrium plant, along with plans to expand internationally. The two companies will explore opportunities to collaborate on engineering and digital innovation solutions, including digital twin technology and artificial intelligence, the news release said.

“Today marks a pivotal moment for TerraPower as we embark on a new chapter of international collaboration with Korea’s leading organizations,” Levesque said. “Combining TerraPower’s innovative advanced nuclear technology with Korea’s nuclear construction and operational expertise will strengthen our global cooperation and accelerate the deployment of a Natrium fleet that will transform the world's energy landscape.”
