title: N.C. Coastal Resources Commission to revisit N.C. 12 protections, septic systems, and ...
description:
The North Carolina Coastal Resources Commission (CRC) will meet in Manteo Aug. 26-27, with oceanfront erosion, protections for vulnerable sections of N.C. Highway 12, and new regulations addressing septic systems exposed by erosion among the major issues on the agenda.
The Coastal Resources Advisory Council will meet first at 10 a.m. Aug. 26, followed by the Coastal Resources Commission at 1 p.m.
Members of the public can attend the CRC meeting in person or online, according to the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality.
The full CRC meeting begins at 1 p.m. Aug. 26, with an in-person public comment period scheduled for 1:30 p.m.
The commission reconvenes at 9 a.m. Aug. 27 and is scheduled to adjourn at approximately 4 p.m.
text:
The North Carolina Coastal Resources Commission (CRC) will meet in Manteo Aug. 26-27, with oceanfront erosion, protections for vulnerable sections of N.C. Highway 12, and new regulations addressing septic systems exposed by erosion among the major issues on the agenda.

The two-day meeting at the Dare County Government Complex comes as shoreline erosion continues to affect homes, roads, and infrastructure throughout the Outer Banks, and several of the commission’s scheduled discussions have direct ties to Hatteras and Ocracoke Islands.

The Coastal Resources Advisory Council will meet first at 10 a.m. Aug. 26, followed by the Coastal Resources Commission at 1 p.m. The CRC will reconvene at 9 a.m. Aug. 27. The Dare County Government Complex is located at 954 Marshall C. Collins Drive in Manteo. Members of the public can attend the CRC meeting in person or online, according to the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality.

One of the most locally significant items is a proposed rule change that would give the N.C. Department of Transportation greater flexibility to use larger, alternative sandbag systems to protect state-maintained public roads from erosion.

Under current CRC rules, temporary erosion-control structures are generally subject to restrictions on sandbag color, individual bag dimensions, and the overall size of the structure. NCDOT has sought and received three variances since 2020 allowing alternative systems for roadway-protection projects along N.C. 12 on Ocracoke Island, at Mirlo Beach in Rodanthe and near the Pea Island Visitor Center, according to the CRC’s fiscal analysis and briefing document.

The systems approved through those variances used 50-foot-long white, tetrahedral structures containing individual baffled cells. The proposed rule would exempt sandbags used to protect state-maintained public roads from the existing color and individual bag-size limitations, and would increase the maximum size of the overall erosion-control structure from a 20-foot-wide base and 6-foot height to a 30-foot-wide base and 10-foot height.

The proposal would not change existing sandbag standards for private oceanfront property owners or other non-roadway uses. NCDOT would also still be required to apply for a major CAMA permit, including agency review and public notice, but qualifying projects would no longer have to go through the additional CRC variance process solely because of the alternative bag dimensions or color.

According to the fiscal analysis, the variance process currently adds an average of two to four months between a permit denial or conditioned permit and CRC approval of a variance. DCM said the proposed amendment is intended to reduce those delays when erosion threatens road support, transportation access or infrastructure.

qThe proposed rule is not yet in effect. The CRC approved the proposed rule language in February for fiscal analysis, and the N.C. Office of State Budget and Management approved that analysis July 23. At its Aug. 26 meeting, the commission is scheduled to consider approving the fiscal analysis, another step required before the proposed rule can move forward through the state rulemaking process.

Another issue with particularly strong ties to Hatteras Island is a proposed amendment governing septic systems that become exposed or repeatedly inundated as the shoreline moves landward.

Division of Coastal Management staff said the issue was initially identified through recurring septic-system failures in Rodanthe and Buxton, where erosion has caused systems to become exposed on the public beach or repeatedly inundated by ocean water, according to the CRC’s Aug. 5 septic-system briefing document.

Under the current regulatory framework, septic systems within an Ocean Hazard Area of Environmental Concern may, in some circumstances, continue to be repaired in place under state onsite-wastewater regulations without CAMA review. DCM said that can leave systems in vulnerable locations where waves, tides, overwash and continuing erosion result in repeated damage or failure.

The proposed amendments would not prohibit routine septic-system maintenance, establish new site requirements, or automatically require an exposed system to be relocated. Routine maintenance of septic tanks, pump tanks and components of ground absorption systems would continue to be allowed without a CAMA permit.

However, once a system is waterward of the applicable vegetation line, measurement line or pre-project vegetation line, repair or replacement would require CAMA permit review. That review would give DCM an opportunity to evaluate conditions at the site and determine the appropriate course of action under the commission’s Ocean Hazard rules.

DCM said the amendments are intended to interrupt a cycle in which systems become exposed on the public beach, are repaired following storm damage or tidal inundation and subsequently fail again during future erosion and storms. The agency said the proposal could also facilitate relocation of vulnerable septic systems farther from the active beach when opportunities arise.

The proposal has been under development for several years. An earlier version was approved by the CRC in April 2023, but rulemaking was delayed. More recently, DCM coordinated with the N.C. Department of Health and Human Services and participated in a stakeholder meeting in Dare County with federal and local government representatives, health departments, industry organizations, environmental organizations and other interested parties.

The CRC will consider whether to advance proposed septic-system rule changes during its Aug. 27 meeting. The amendments would not take effect immediately and would have to complete the state rulemaking process before becoming effective.

Perhaps the broadest Outer Banks-related discussion will occur the morning of Aug. 27, when commissioners are scheduled to spend approximately two hours discussing oceanfront erosion and North Carolina’s approach to hardened shoreline structures.

The discussion comes after the CRC Science Panel presented a draft report in June examining the effects of hardened structures on sandy, open-ocean shorelines. According to the commission’s oceanfront erosion briefing document, the draft recommended maintaining a cautious approach to any expansion of hardened structures, requiring comprehensive evaluations of proposed projects, avoiding projects where adverse effects cannot be mitigated, and requiring long-term monitoring, maintenance and mitigation plans for ocean shoreline modifications.

Commissioners subsequently requested additional information, including a closer look at policies in other coastal states, a review of Reef Balls as offshore breakwaters and the addition of known oceanfront erosion hotspots to the Science Panel report. Dr. Laura Moore is scheduled to provide an update on the final report, while DCM staff will discuss other states’ approaches to hardened structures and the history of North Carolina laws and rules governing shoreline armoring.

The issue is particularly relevant to the Outer Banks, where erosion has repeatedly threatened oceanfront homes, N.C. 12 and other infrastructure.

North Carolina generally limits hard erosion-control structures along the oceanfront. Groins, breakwaters, seawalls, bulkheads, and revetments are generally prohibited, with certain statutory and regulatory exceptions, while beach nourishment and temporary measures such as sandbags remain among the state’s primary erosion-response tools. The General Assembly has also authorized a limited number of terminal groins.

The discussion comes amid renewed debate over North Carolina’s approach to shoreline hardening. DCM’s briefing materials include a comparison of coastal-armoring policies in states including Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, Florida and South Carolina, providing commissioners with examples of how other states regulate seawalls and other erosion-control structures.

The Aug. 27 erosion briefing also includes an update on North Carolina’s effort to modernize its Inlet Hazard Area boundaries and oceanfront and inlet erosion rates, another issue with potential significance for barrier-island communities.

The existing Inlet Hazard Area boundaries have remained largely unchanged since they were adopted in 1979. In May, the CRC approved updated boundaries, erosion rates, and associated rule amendments, formally beginning the rulemaking process. The updated methodology would result in some hazard areas expanding and others contracting compared with the original designations.

A required fiscal analysis is still being completed and must be reviewed and approved before the proposed rules can move to public hearings. DCM currently anticipates the updated boundaries, erosion rates and associated rule changes could take effect no earlier than spring 2027.

Commissioners will also receive an update on recent state legislation, including funding to update North Carolina’s roughly decade-old Beach and Inlet Management Plan.

The 2026 state budget allocated $373,884 for the update, with an interim report due Dec. 1, 2026, and the final updated plan due July 1, 2027, according to the CRC’s legislative briefing. DCM plans to coordinate with other state agencies and require the contractor selected for the project to engage relevant nongovernmental organizations and other stakeholders during the update.

Other agenda items include an update to the Coastal Habitat Protection Plan; rulemaking involving man-made ditches and upland marina basins; amendments addressing the repair and replacement of certain piers; and an update on the state’s electronic CAMA permitting system.

The Coastal Resources Advisory Council’s Aug. 26 meeting will also focus heavily on shoreline policy, with a 45-minute discussion of hardened structures and the Science Panel report beginning shortly after the 10 a.m. meeting starts. Public comment for the advisory council is scheduled for approximately 11:20 a.m.

The full CRC meeting begins at 1 p.m. Aug. 26, with an in-person public comment period scheduled for 1:30 p.m. The commission reconvenes at 9 a.m. Aug. 27 and is scheduled to adjourn at approximately 4 p.m. Agenda items and times are subject to change.

name: American Energy
title: Winning the Critical Minerals Race | Energy Intelligence
description:
Rare earth elements may capture headlines because of their defense applications, but they are only one category within a wider group of critical minerals that underpin modern manufacturing, energy security and advanced technologies.
From electricity grids and utility-scale battery storage to artificial intelligence data centers, the modern energy economy is becoming increasingly dependent on secure supplies of processed critical minerals.
In other words, the race for critical minerals is increasingly shaping both military power and future energy systems.
Additionally, the Department of Energy’s recent $500 million initiative to boost critical minerals processing is a step in the right direction.
But what if tariffs can help protects jobs and preserve US-based critical minerals production?
text:
In March 2026, reports surfaced that the US holds only a two-month supply of rare earth elements critical for the guidance systems and radar technologies driving our defense operations. The recent concerns surrounding rare earth supply are symptomatic of a broader challenge facing the US. Rare earth elements may capture headlines because of their defense applications, but they are only one category within a wider group of critical minerals that underpin modern manufacturing, energy security and advanced technologies. Among these minerals is silicon — the foundational input for semiconductors, solar cells and next-generation batteries. From electricity grids and utility-scale battery storage to artificial intelligence data centers, the modern energy economy is becoming increasingly dependent on secure supplies of processed critical minerals. In other words, the race for critical minerals is increasingly shaping both military power and future energy systems.

This vulnerability underscores the importance of Project Vault, the new US strategic critical minerals stockpile, and the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement (Forge), a US-led initiative to coordinate allied investment and cooperation on critical mineral supply chains. Additionally, the Department of Energy’s recent $500 million initiative to boost critical minerals processing is a step in the right direction. These initiatives signal that Washington finally recognizes that military strength energy security and industrial competitiveness are impossible without material dominance. However, the US is successfully stockpiling the "what," while overlooking the "how" of domestic production. In short, we are building the factories, but can we survive a price war?

Building Resilience Beyond Stockpiles

While Project Vault secures minerals, and Forge aligns geopolitical allies, the US will remain strategically fragile until it implements structural market mechanisms that provide long-term support and prevent — or at least deter — other nations from weaponizing supply chains to bankrupt American manufacturers.

The current crisis is not a result of a lack of domestic talent but decades of predatory pricing by state-backed actors. For years, China has utilized massive subsidies, weaker environmental standards and allegedly forced labor to flood global markets with cheap critical minerals, deliberately driving prices below the cost of production for Western firms to eliminate competition.

US allies are watching. The EU is looking for answers as it faces the same threat, while the US has a more integrated trade and industrial policy. But as developed as that policy is, US-led initiatives such as Pax Silica — a partnership with allies to secure the supply chains underpinning AI, from critical minerals to semiconductors — and Forge are only as strong as the domestic industrial base that anchors them.

Silicon and Strategic Supply Chains

For instance, if the US cannot maintain its own production of silicon (a needed ingredient for aluminum, solar, electric vehicle batteries and chemicals) and ferrosilicon (a specialty steel ingredient), along with other critical minerals, its commercial partners will eventually be forced to look elsewhere for their industrial sourcing, undermining the very trade bloc we seek to lead. That has implications well beyond manufacturing. The same supply chains increasingly determine who builds the solar industry, battery storage, electricity grids and other technologies central to the global energy security.

One existing mechanism for creating a level competitive field is tariffs. Some critics argue that tariffs lead to higher costs for US consumers and manufacturers who rely on cheap raw materials. But what if tariffs can help protects jobs and preserve US-based critical minerals production?

When considering these weighty factors, consider that a market is not free if one participant is a state-backed monopoly using unlimited capital to destroy its competition. Likewise, the cost of slightly higher material prices today must be weighed against the far greater strategic and economic costs of a weaponized supply chain tomorrow.

The US has a good foundation to deal with this challenge. One of its advantages is its tariff regime, which must remain predictable, executable and accurate to maintain integrity against dumped goods. This mechanism must deter foreign actors that flood the market with materials priced below fair-market value. Doing so provides increased certainty for private capital to invest in multidecade projects, such as high-purity silicon plants. In this context, the objective is not to shield domestic industries from competition but to ensure that it occurs on fair terms. Predictable and enforceable frameworks are particularly important for capital-intensive segments, where project lifecycles span decades.

From Stockpiles to Industrial Strategy

But we should also expand the scope of the Project Vault’s $12 billion reserve to include long-term offtake agreements for domestic producers. By guaranteeing that the US government will support US-based production capabilities for high-purity silicon and other critical minerals at a sustainable price, we derisk the massive capital expenditures required to build state-of-the-art metallurgical sites.

Several African countries are leveraging these types of commitments. Trafigura’s offtake agreement with Ghana’s Heath Goldfields for the Bogoso-Prestea Gold Mine will provide 700,000 ounces of gold. In Madagascar, NextSource Materials extended its offtake agreement with Mitsubishi Chemical Corp. to supply 9,000 tons of graphite per year. The most striking example is Bannerman Energy’s five-year agreement with two Tier-1 North American generation companies to supply an aggregate 1 million pounds of uranium from the Etango Uranium Project in Namibia.

Prioritizing R&D tax credits specifically for the purification and advanced processing stages of the mining value chain is another option. While mining is important, the true bottleneck is processing. Policies are needed that incentivize industry to address the deficit in processing needed to produce high-performance materials found in aerospace and medical technology. Currently, the US has the Section 45X advanced manufacturing production credit on the books, but the nation’s domestic producers need more of these specialized benefits expanded and to include longer term dates. As currently structured, the credit is scheduled to phase out starting in 2030 before expiring at the end of 2032.

Third, the Forge partnership must be used to create a preferential trade zone where members agree to common labor and environmental standards. This allows the US to compete on a level playing field. If a foreign producer gains a price advantage by ignoring environmental protections, a carbon and quality adjustment should be applied at the border to equalize the cost for domestic producers. This framework should be guided by the goal of reestablishing US manufacturers’ market share to historic levels. Advancing a trade framework that protects core American businesses will provide manufacturing executives with the confidence they need to expand.

Lastly, the US should formalize the Sovereign Risk Insurance Fund discussed by US Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. Such a measure would protect American companies from the policy whiplash of future administrations, ensuring that a 20-year investment in a domestic mine or refinery isn't rendered worthless by a sudden shift in federal priorities. It also creates the regulatory certainty that high-tech manufacturing craves.

To strengthen US energy security and industrial resilience — and maintain its strategic position in an increasingly electrified global economy — we must first recognize the industrial and manufacturing realities of a critical minerals value chain and support an expansion of more domestic processing. We cannot afford to be a nation that designs the future but lacks the materials to build it.

title: Rising Outage Costs Are Reshaping Energy Storage ROI
description:
Between 2018 and 2024, the number of major U.S. outages rose 29%, from 4,666 to 6,533, and the average outage lengthened from 9.6 hours to 11.8 hours.
Rising outage costs and falling storage prices are, in effect, two lines on the same graph moving in opposite directions, and that shift changes the shape of the storage conversation.
The ROI Calculation Has Been Missing a Cost An energy storage project evaluated only on utility savings can look very different from one evaluated against the financial consequences of losing power.
For businesses, ORNL calculates outage costs using lost production and direct interruption costs, offset by any energy savings realized during the outage itself.
The more useful comparison is increasingly total resilience cost against expected interruption loss, not battery cost against electricity savings alone.
text:
For years, the business case for energy storage at commercial and industrial facilities has largely been built around what happens when the grid is working: reducing demand charges, shifting consumption away from expensive hours, or participating in demand-response programs. The cost of what happens when the grid is not working has been harder to fit into that same calculation, and new data from Oak Ridge National Laboratory makes the omission increasingly difficult to defend.

What the Outage Data Shows

Researchers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory found that major U.S. power outages cost customers an average of more than $67 billion annually between 2018 and 2024, with the total reaching $121 billion in 2024 alone. Commercial and industrial customers absorbed an average of $6,031 per outage in 2024, and businesses in every state saw average per-outage costs above $4,000. Between 2018 and 2024, the number of major U.S. outages rose 29%, from 4,666 to 6,533, and the average outage lengthened from 9.6 hours to 11.8 hours. In one South Carolina county the lab examined, the estimated loss reached $140,000 per non-residential customer for a single outage.

At the same time, the technology companies can use to offset some of that exposure has become considerably cheaper. BloombergNEF found that battery packs for stationary storage averaged $70 per kilowatt-hour in 2025, down 45% from 2024 and the steepest decline of any battery segment the firm tracks, making stationary storage the least expensive lithium-ion category for the first time. Lithium-ion pack prices across all applications averaged $108 per kilowatt-hour. Rising outage costs and falling storage prices are, in effect, two lines on the same graph moving in opposite directions, and that shift changes the shape of the storage conversation.

The ROI Calculation Has Been Missing a Cost

An energy storage project evaluated only on utility savings can look very different from one evaluated against the financial consequences of losing power. A $6,031 average outage does not by itself justify a battery, but the cost belongs in the model, alongside the broader tradeoffs resilience spending already faces against other capital priorities.

For businesses, ORNL calculates outage costs using lost production and direct interruption costs, offset by any energy savings realized during the outage itself. That makes the data particularly relevant to finance teams, because the loss is not an abstract measure of inconvenience but an attempt to put a dollar figure on interrupted operations. A manufacturer losing production for several hours, a distribution center unable to move inventory, and a data center supporting continuous workloads do not carry the same outage exposure, and neither do facilities in regions with different reliability histories. The more useful comparison is increasingly total resilience cost against expected interruption loss, not battery cost against electricity savings alone.

Falling Battery Prices Widen the Resilience Case

The other side of that calculation is moving quickly, though the direction matters more than the headline number. BloombergNEF's $70/kWh figure reflects battery-pack pricing, not the fully installed cost of a storage system; companies still have to account for power conversion equipment, engineering, construction, controls, permitting and financing, and U.S. costs can run higher than global averages because of tariffs and supply-chain conditions. Still, BNEF's broader project-cost data shows the benchmark levelized cost of electricity for a four-hour battery storage project fell 27% in 2025 to $78 per megawatt-hour, its lowest level since the firm began tracking the technology in 2009, driven by lower pack prices, stronger manufacturer competition and improved system design.

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) is making a related argument about microgrids: facilities typically install them because they cannot tolerate significant outages, but the same systems can generate value during normal operation through time-of-use rate arbitrage, demand-charge reduction and optimized dispatch of onsite generation and storage. A resilience asset no longer has to sit idle waiting for an emergency to justify its cost, which changes how the investment should be modeled from the outset.

Finance and Facilities Need the Same Model

This is where the storage decision becomes less about technology and more about capital allocation. Facilities teams know which operations cannot tolerate an interruption, and finance teams know what those interruptions actually cost. Energy teams bring a third piece to the table: utility tariffs and the savings available on the grid-connected side. Those numbers need to be evaluated together rather than built into separate business cases that never meet, particularly as facilities also weigh the operational readiness steps utilities are already asking them to complete before peak season.

DOE's Federal Energy Management Program approaches resilience the same way through its Customer Damage Function Calculator, a free tool built to help facility owners establish the financial cost of a grid outage as the first step toward evaluating the avoided costs tied to resilience investment. For corporate buyers, that logic points to a more useful question than "what is the battery payback." The better question is what it costs a given facility when power disappears, how often that is likely to happen, and how much of that exposure a resilience investment can realistically avoid, a question that matters even more for organizations exposed to the longer restoration timelines that can follow when neighboring grid regions face simultaneous strain.

Storage will not pencil out everywhere. Batteries cannot protect every load indefinitely, and system design has to reflect outage duration, critical loads and available generation. But the hurdle has changed: with outage losses rising while stationary-storage costs fall, excluding reliability from the ROI calculation can make the cheaper investment on paper turn into the more expensive decision over the life of the facility.

title: Africa's Renewable Manufacturing Opportunity: The Continent Moves Beyond Importing ...
description:
Solar panels, batteries, inverters and other technologies have largely been imported, even as demand for clean energy has grown across the continent.
This creates the potential for renewable-energy manufacturing and electric-mobility industries to develop alongside one another.
Another major Egyptian project, the Obelisk solar development, involves a 1 GW photovoltaic plant and a 200 MWh battery-storage system.
The African Development Bank notes that AfCFTA could boost intra-African industrial trade by 35.7% by 2045.
Africa has some of the world’s fastest-growing energy markets, abundant renewable resources and a young workforce.
text:
For years, Africa’s renewable-energy expansion has depended heavily on equipment manufactured elsewhere. Solar panels, batteries, inverters and other technologies have largely been imported, even as demand for clean energy has grown across the continent.

That picture is beginning to change.

A new wave of investment is creating opportunities for Africa to participate more deeply in the manufacturing side of the energy transition, potentially allowing countries to capture more of the economic value generated by their rapidly expanding clean-energy markets.

READ ALSO: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline: Opportunity, Risk and the Renewable Challenge

One of the most significant developments is emerging in Morocco, where the African Development Bank has approved a €100 million loan to Gotion Power Morocco for the development of an integrated lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone. The project is expected to produce 10 gigawatt-hours of battery cells and packs in its first phase, with plans to eventually expand capacity to 100 GWh. The bank also plans to mobilise an additional €141 million from financial partners.

The project is particularly significant because battery manufacturing sits at the centre of several fast-growing industries, including electric vehicles, renewable-energy storage and industrial power systems. By developing production capacity locally, Morocco is positioning itself not simply as a consumer of clean technologies but as part of the global supply chain.

The country’s position is also strengthened by its established automotive manufacturing base and access to European markets. This creates the potential for renewable-energy manufacturing and electric-mobility industries to develop alongside one another.

Elsewhere, African countries are building large renewable-energy projects that could create demand for increasingly sophisticated domestic supply chains.

In Egypt, for example, the African Development Bank approved financing in July 2026 for the first phase of the 500 MW Dandara solar project, which includes a 100 MWh battery-storage system. The total project cost is expected to exceed $290 million.

Another major Egyptian project, the Obelisk solar development, involves a 1 GW photovoltaic plant and a 200 MWh battery-storage system. The project is expected to generate about 2,772 GWh of electricity annually once fully operational and create around 4,000 jobs during construction.

These investments demonstrate the scale of the market that African manufacturers could eventually serve.

The opportunity extends beyond assembling solar panels. A deeper industrial ecosystem could include battery components, mounting structures, cables, electrical equipment, inverters, transformers and other components required by renewable-energy projects.

That would have implications far beyond the energy sector.

Local manufacturing can create skilled employment, strengthen industrial capabilities and reduce exposure to international supply disruptions and currency fluctuations. It can also encourage technology transfer and provide African companies with opportunities to move into higher-value areas of production.

The African Continental Free Trade Area provides another important opportunity. As regional markets become more integrated, manufacturers can potentially produce in one African country and sell across multiple markets rather than being restricted to relatively small national markets. The African Development Bank notes that AfCFTA could boost intra-African industrial trade by 35.7% by 2045.

However, building competitive manufacturing industries will require more than investment announcements. Reliable electricity, efficient ports, transport infrastructure, technical skills, access to finance and predictable industrial policies will all be important.

Africa also needs to avoid replacing one form of dependence with another. The objective should not simply be to assemble imported components, but progressively develop local capabilities across the value chain.

The opportunity is considerable. Africa has some of the world’s fastest-growing energy markets, abundant renewable resources and a young workforce. If these advantages are combined with strategic industrial policies and investment, the continent could capture a larger share of the global clean-energy economy.

Africa’s renewable-energy story may therefore be entering a new phase — one in which the continent is not only installing the technologies of the energy transition, but increasingly helping to manufacture them.

title: America Has a Power Problem. Private Capital Is the Solution. - Yahoo Finance
description:

text:
When President Trump released his America First Investment Policy, the document made clear that welcoming investment and strengthening America's capital markets would be central to economic growth.

His data center infrastructure order has since followed the same logic, targeting the rapid development of transmission lines, natural gas infrastructure, substations, and new power generation needed to support America's AI expansion.

This is supply-side economics working as intended.

Government removes unnecessary barriers and creates an environment where private businesses have an incentive to invest.

Unfortunately, progressive groups that call themselves consumer advocates have adopted a different model: block the investment, slow the progress, and dress obstruction up as protection.

This has come to the detriment of America's ratepayers.

Regulators Must Clear the Way for New Investment as Demand Increases

America's electricity system was built during an era of relatively stagnant demand. That era is over. Between 2005 and 2019, electricity demand increased only about 0.1% annually.

Between 2020 and 2025, the rate jumped to roughly 1.7% annually, with data centers helping drive the acceleration, and is expected to continue rising in the coming years. Demand is expected to keep rising.

Artificial intelligence requires extraordinary amounts of electricity. So does the domestic manufacturing base Trump is rebuilding. Private infrastructure funds, pension funds, utilities and institutional investors control trillions of dollars of capital are looking for exactly this kind of long-duration investment.

That alignment of need and capital is a genuine opportunity — unless regulators are pressured into treating every private investor as a threat.

FERC Is Helping Remove the Bottlenecks

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has a real job to protect competition, ensure electricity rates remain just and reasonable, and determine whether transactions subject to federal review are consistent with the public interest.

FERC's job is not to treat private capital as inherently suspect. Recently, the Commission has said as much.

In late May, FERC authorized Blackstone Infrastructure's acquisition of TXNM Energy, concluding that the transaction was consistent with the public interest and finding no evidence of adverse effects on rates or competition.

FERC has also approved Southwest Power Pool's new consolidated transmission and interconnection process.

Commissioner David Rosner said in his concurrence the reform would "get transmission built smarter and connect new generation faster."

Progressive advocacy groups have routinely opposed most of these types of transactions. Their argument, stripped of its consumer-protection framing, is that private ownership of utilities is itself a problem. That is an ideological position, not a legal or economic one. FERC was right to reject it.

AES Is the Test Case for What Comes Next

The same fight is now playing out over the proposed acquisition of AES Corporation by a consortium led by Global Infrastructure Partners and EQT. AES serves roughly 1.1 million customers through regulated utilities in Indiana and Ohio and is positioned directly in the path of growing power demand from technology companies.

The transaction would bring substantial private capital to expand infrastructure and support demand growth in the years ahead.

Opponents, including Public Citizen, are raising the same alarms FERC already dismissed in the Blackstone-TXNM case. The pattern is familiar: whenever private capital moves toward American energy infrastructure, the same organizations appear to slow it down, using ratepayer protection as the justification.

Regulators should scrutinize utility acquisitions. If a transaction threatens competition, harms customers, weakens a utility financially or shifts inappropriate acquisition costs onto ratepayers, regulators should act. But private capital itself is not evidence of consumer harm. New electricity generation still requires financing.

Making investment harder does not protect consumers. It makes America's energy challenge more expensive and hands the advantage to competitors abroad who are not slowing down.

The Real Consumer Threat is Falling Behind

President Trump understands the connection between energy and economic growth. Lower-cost, abundant energy combined with private investment can increase productivity, strengthen manufacturing and fuel broader prosperity.

America needs trillions of dollars of new investment to win the global competition for energy, manufacturing and artificial intelligence.

Progressive groups claiming to speak for consumers are, in practice, undermining that investment. FERC should protect consumers and enforce the law. But it should recognize that reflexive opposition to private capital is not consumer protection. It is obstruction dressed up in populist language.

The AES transaction represents exactly the kind of long-term investment deal America needs, and FERC should approve it.

_______________

Michael Busler is a public policy analyst and a professor of finance at Stockton University in Galloway, New Jersey, where he teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in finance and economics. He has written op-ed columns in major newspapers for more than 35 years.

title: A 155-ton reactor vessel near Bologna runs on molten lead with electric heaters standing in ...
description:
America already built most of a plutonium fuel plant once.
America’s answer was the Mixed Oxide Fuel Fabrication Facility at the Savannah River Site: take the warhead plutonium, blend it into reactor fuel, burn it in power plants.
And there is one detail in the wreckage that deserves its own sentence: the failed American plant was modeled on France’s Melox facility.
“Fuel supply constraints are a key throttle to advanced reactor development,” Oklo CEO Jacob DeWitte said in the announcement.
He founded Newcleo after selling his previous company, nuclear medicine firm Advanced Accelerator Applications, to Novartis for $3.9 billion.
text:
Dress rehearsals are supposed to be the boring part. You run the whole show with nothing real at stake, you find out what leaks, and nobody gets hurt. Newcleo has spent 2026 doing exactly that with a 155-ton reactor vessel in the hills near Bologna, where electric heaters stand in for uranium and molten lead does everything the real coolant would do. But the French company has now filed the paperwork that points at opening night. On August 6, it handed the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission a plan for licensing a factory that would turn recycled plutonium into reactor fuel on American soil.

And if that idea sounds vaguely familiar, it should. America already built most of a plutonium fuel plant once. It cost billions, took over a decade, and the government walked away from the half-finished building. More on that in a minute.

The rehearsal reactor was only ever half the story

Quick recap for anyone who missed the earlier chapters. Newcleo is building PRECURSOR, a full-scale non-nuclear demonstrator at Italy’s ENEA Brasimone Research Centre. The vessel weighs a little over 20 metric tons empty and passes 155 once the molten lead and internals go in, and it was lowered into place in late May. Electric heaters play the role of the fuel, and a Fincantieri turbine will make actual electricity from a reactor with zero uranium anywhere in the building.

It is a clever way to de-risk the scary part of a lead-cooled fast reactor, which is the lead itself. Molten lead eats steel, which is why the Swedish company chasing the same coolant needs three different alloys in one machine just to keep its pump impeller alive. Prove the metallurgy first, add atoms later.

But a lead-cooled fast reactor without fuel is a very expensive kettle. Newcleo’s reactors are designed to run on MOX, a blend of uranium and plutonium recovered from spent fuel. The company describes itself as the leading Western private firm pursuing licenses to make that fuel for advanced reactors, which is a polite way of saying nobody is actually doing it yet. So it decided to build that part of the supply chain itself, and this month it told American regulators how.

Two filings in five weeks, and the second is the bigger ask

In July, Newcleo submitted a Regulatory Engagement Plan to the NRC for its commercial reactor, the 200-megawatt LFR-AS-200. On August 6 came the second one, this time for a US facility that would manufacture MOX fuel from recovered or surplus nuclear materials, according to World Nuclear News. The company had opened pre-application talks with the NRC back in February, so this is the paperwork catching up with the conversations.

A Regulatory Engagement Plan is not a license application. It is the document before the document, laying out which technical topics the company expects to hash out with NRC staff, what it plans to submit, and roughly when. The point is to surface the hard questions early, before anyone commits to a formal application that takes years to review.

“This submission to the NRC is a concrete step to advance our MOX fuel facility in the U.S., building on the work of over 100 engineers with decades of industrial experience,” said Stefano Buono, Newcleo’s CEO, in the company’s announcement. The company has not announced where the American plant would go.

The US filing leans on homework already done in Europe. In July, France’s nuclear safety authority ASNR judged the safety program for Newcleo’s planned French MOX plant satisfactory, and the company runs a testing center in Chusclan called FASTER, where prototypes of the fuel manufacturing line are already installed and running in a non-nuclear environment. Same philosophy as the Italian rig: rehearse everything, then go nuclear.

America has been down the MOX road before, and it did not end well

Here is where the story gets uncomfortable for anyone with a long memory and a South Carolina zip code. Under a 2000 agreement, the US and Russia each committed to disposing of surplus weapons-grade plutonium, 68 metric tons between them. America’s answer was the Mixed Oxide Fuel Fabrication Facility at the Savannah River Site: take the warhead plutonium, blend it into reactor fuel, burn it in power plants.

Construction started in 2007 with a 2016 start-up in mind and an original estimate of $4.9 billion. It did not go to plan. By 2018 the National Nuclear Security Administration terminated the contract, and the agency later said finishing the plant would have taken until 2048 and cost $17 billion. The Post and Courier put the money actually spent at $5.4 billion on the half-built plant alone, roughly $8 billion counting the wider program. The government switched to diluting the plutonium and burying it, and the abandoned MOX building is being repurposed to make plutonium pits. Which are nuclear weapon cores. The factory meant to unmake warheads will now help make them.

And there is one detail in the wreckage that deserves its own sentence: the failed American plant was modeled on France’s Melox facility. The next company proposing to make MOX on American soil is French. The design crossed the Atlantic once and sank; now the whole firm is coming over instead.

The fuel would come out of the plutonium nobody wants

The material side of this got moving in May. The Department of Energy selected five companies for advanced negotiations under its Surplus Plutonium Utilization Program, which would hand designated surplus plutonium to industry and let it become advanced reactor fuel, under US security and safeguards rules.

One of the five is Oklo, the NYSE-listed reactor startup, and its partner in the bid is Newcleo. Oklo would lead the plutonium work while Newcleo brings the fuel experience and potential project capital, all of it still subject to definitive agreements. The two companies pitch it as disposition through use: the plutonium already exists, so fission it into electricity instead of guarding it forever.

“Fuel supply constraints are a key throttle to advanced reactor development,” Oklo CEO Jacob DeWitte said in the announcement. He is not wrong. You can design the finest fast reactor on Earth and it will sit there doing nothing without fuel, and the enrichment supply chain for advanced reactors is years behind the reactor designs themselves. Leftover weapons plutonium is, in the coldest possible accounting, a shortcut.

A Nasdaq ticker before the first watt

All of this is happening while Newcleo goes public. The company signed a definitive merger agreement with NewHold Investment Corp. III on May 27, and in early August the SEC declared the registration statement effective, per the joint announcement. NewHold shareholders vote on September 17, and if it closes as planned in the second half of 2026, the combined company trades on Nasdaq as newcleo plc under the ticker NWCL.

Buono has done the Nasdaq run before. He founded Newcleo after selling his previous company, nuclear medicine firm Advanced Accelerator Applications, to Novartis for $3.9 billion. This one has raised about $780 million in private funding and employs more than 900 people across Europe and the US, per the company. Between Oklo on the NYSE and Newcleo headed for Nasdaq, both halves of the plutonium partnership would be publicly traded before a single gram of that surplus material becomes fuel.

So where does this actually stand? A Regulatory Engagement Plan is a roadmap, not a permit, and the formal license application it leads to typically takes years of NRC review. The American plant has no announced site. The Italian demonstrator is still scheduled to finish installation this year, and it will stay proudly uranium-free the whole time, because that was always the point. What changed this month is smaller and stranger than a groundbreaking: the company that got famous for practicing nuclear power without the nuclear part has now told American regulators, in writing, exactly how it wants to handle the real thing. The last people who tried left a $5.4 billion shell in South Carolina. Newcleo gets to decide how that story ends the second time.

From: Mercom India

SunScout Holding Limited, a clean-technology company developing autonomous solar-powered robotic mowers and related solar energy solutions, has raised $15.5 million through its initial public offering.

The company offered 3.1 million Class A ordinary shares at $5 per share.

SunScout’s Class A ordinary shares began trading on the NYSE American and NYSE Texas under the ticker symbol ‘SNSC’ on August 12, 2026.

Dominari Securities served as the lead underwriter, and Revere Securities served as a co-underwriter. Ortoli Rosenstadt has acted as U.S. counsel to SunScout, and Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li has served as U.S. securities counsel to the underwriters.

Founded in 2020 and headquartered in Palmerston North, New Zealand, SunScout designs, manufactures, and distributes autonomous robotic lawn mowers powered by integrated solar energy systems. SunScout’s solar division develops, constructs, and operates solar energy projects ranging from commercial rooftop installations to utility-scale power plants.

The company plans to use the proceeds from the offering to establish a manufacturing plant in Austin, Texas. The company also plans to allocate the proceeds toward marketing and promotion, product development, inventory, repayment of one loan, working capital, and a payment related to its acquisition of Brightway Energy under a membership purchase agreement.

SunScout has granted the underwriters a 45-day option to purchase up to an additional 465,000 Class A ordinary shares at the public offering price of $5 per share, less underwriting discounts.

Solar public market financing in 1H 2026 totaled $2.2 billion in 17 deals, a 371% increase compared to $467 million in five deals in 1H 2025, according to Mercom’s Annual and Q4 2025 Solar Funding and M&A report.

text:
South Korean battery maker Samsung SDI has acquired General Motors’ 49.99% stake in SynergyCells, taking ownership of the $3.5 billion manufacturing facility currently under construction in New Carlisle, Indiana.

The buyout converts the 680-acre facility into Samsung SDI’s first wholly owned battery production plant in North America. Originally designed to produce nickel-rich prismatic cells for GM electric vehicles starting in 2027, the plant will now pivot toward manufacturing energy storage systems (ESS) to capture demand in the US power grid market.

The partners attributed the structural shift to macroeconomic headwinds and a broader slowdown in North American electric vehicle adoption.

“The ownership change was made in consideration of market changes since the joint venture was announced, including the slower-than-expected growth of EV demand,” read a joint statement by Samsung SDI and General Motors.

GM and Samsung SDI also signed a concurrent agreement to jointly develop prismatic cells for potential future vehicle applications.

“While reflecting recent market changes, this acquisition decision is to continue the strategic partnership with GM. We will continue our commitment to an electrified future with the partner, while utilizing the plant to proactively respond to the fast-growing ESS market in the US,” Samsung SDI said in the official statement.

Background:

First announced in April 2023 and finalized in August 2024, SynergyCells was projected to deliver an initial annual capacity of 27 gigawatt-hours (GWh), expandable to 36 GWh. However, physical construction stalled earlier this year as automakers across Detroit re-evaluated capital allocation following sluggish EV sales growth and changing federal subsidy frameworks. While the building shell in Indiana is complete, production equipment has yet to be installed, allowing Samsung SDI the flexibility to adjust cell architecture for grid storage applications.

text:
Oʻahu runs on more electricity per capita than almost anywhere else in the United States — and demand is climbing faster than it has in twenty years. Electrification of cars, buses, and industrial systems is pushing the island’s isolated grid toward a reckoning that mainland utilities rarely face: there are no neighboring states to borrow power from when supply runs short.

Hawaiian Electric just filed one of the largest energy procurements in state history in response to that pressure — targeting nearly 1,650 gigawatt-hours of variable renewables and hundreds of megawatts of storage across Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi Island, and Maui. What fuels will keep the lights on during the transition remains an open question.

An island grid under pressure

Oʻahu isn’t a typical electricity market. Home to nearly one million residents, the island accounts for more than 70% of all electricity generated across the Hawaiian archipelago — a concentration of demand on a single, isolated grid that creates challenges mainland utilities simply don’t encounter.

If regulators agree to expand the scope of the competitive procurement, the Japan-based conglomerate’s LNG project could be considered alongside other bids.

The pressure is more acute right now because of the pace of change. Electricity demand is growing at its fastest rate in two decades. More EVs, more electric buses, more industrial processes switching off fossil fuels — all of it lands on the same grid, at the same time.

Oil still dominates that grid. Hawaiʻi is consistently one of the most expensive electricity markets in the country, and oil-fired generation is a primary reason why. Reducing that dependence isn’t just an environmental goal — it’s an economic one. The state has also set a legally binding target of 100% renewable electricity by 2045, which creates urgency and a clear direction even when the path involves difficult trade-offs.

What Hawaiian Electric is actually asking for

The Integrated Grid Planning RFP is the centerpiece of Hawaiian Electric’s response. The solicitation seeks nearly 1,650 GWh of variable renewable energy — primarily solar and wind — spread across Oʻahu, Hawaiʻi Island, and Maui.

That’s not all. The RFP also includes 465 MW of grid-forming resources, meaning solar generation paired with battery storage, plus 111 MW of firm generating capacity capable of producing power around the clock. Projects are targeted to come online between 2031 and 2034, an accelerated timeline by the standards of large-scale energy infrastructure.

Separately, Hawaiian Electric is seeking regulatory approval to expand firm generation procurement on Oʻahu by up to an additional 500 MW. The company framed this as a request for a “transparent, Commission-supervised forum” — one that evaluates firm generation needs without pre-determining the size or fuel type required.

The reliability puzzle: retiring old plants while keeping the lights on

Renewable energy goals and grid reliability don’t always move in the same direction. Solar and wind are variable — they produce power when the sun shines and the wind blows, not necessarily when demand peaks. That’s the core tension Hawaiian Electric is working to manage.

The plan addresses this by accelerating the retirement of aging oil-fired power plants while adding modern firm generation capable of producing electricity 24/7. The logic is straightforward: you can’t retire old plants safely unless dependable replacements are already in place.

To evaluate what those replacements should be, Hawaiian Electric plans to launch a request for proposals covering all fuel types — liquid and gaseous — by the end of 2026. That process will assess proposals on price, sourcing, and environmental impact within a competitive framework. CEO Scott Seu described the approach as one that must deliver efficiency, reliability, lower emissions, and least cost — all at once, not in sequence.

LNG enters the conversation — and the controversy

Liquefied natural gas has emerged as one possible answer to the firm generation question, bringing with it a notable dispute over process. Hawaiian Electric has acknowledged that LNG could be a beneficial option if it delivers value to customers — but insists any such pathway must go through the PUC’s transparent evaluation process.

That position is already being tested. An affiliate of a Japan-based energy conglomerate has announced plans to build what would be the largest power plant on Oʻahu, fueled by LNG, and notified the PUC that it intends to seek approval outside the standard competitive bidding structure.

Hawaiian Electric pushed back publicly. Seu stated that the company believes in “an open competitive process as opposed to a sole-source, multibillion-dollar contract without seeing what else is out there.” More options are welcome — just not through a process that bypasses competition.

What comes next for Hawaiʻi’s energy future

The RFP is now open to developers. The Public Utilities Commission is overseeing the process under docket number 2024-0258, and the competitive clock is running. The most consequential near-term decision, though, may belong to the PUC itself.

If regulators agree to expand the scope of the competitive procurement, the Japan-based conglomerate’s LNG project could be considered alongside other bids. If they don’t, the landscape shifts considerably. That single regulatory call will shape who competes, on what terms, and ultimately what gets built — and Hawaiian Electric has framed this procurement as one of the most significant energy decisions the state will make, not just for the next decade but for generations. The outcome will reveal whether Hawaiʻi can honor its 100% renewables mandate while keeping a rapidly electrifying economy reliably powered. The islands are watching. So is the rest of the country.

title: The Critical Minerals Bull Market Is Here as China Puts Its Arsenal Back in Play
description:
Copper has become the clearest evidence that the critical minerals contest is shifting from securing future deposits to controlling present flows.
Critical minerals sit within a dual-use system because the same materials, equipment and process knowledge may serve semiconductors, civilian electronics, drones and weapons.
(Reuters; United States Department of Energy) The emerging critical minerals economy is consequently less a free market than a network of managed channels.

https://bit.ly/4wtt5WX August 11, 2026 – Should the U.S. Department of Energy Become a Critical Minerals Toll Processor?
text:
“November 10 is not simply an export control deadline. It is the day the West discovers whether it has built anything that China cannot interrupt. Deposits, subsidies and press releases are not supply chains. Until we can mine, separate, refine and manufacture qualified products at commercial scale, Beijing will retain the ability to decide who receives critical minerals, in what form and on what terms.” — Jack Lifton, Co-Chair, Critical Minerals Institute (CMI)

The most revealing signal in copper this week was not the headline price, but the premium buyers were paying for metal available immediately. On the London Metal Exchange, the cash-to-three-month spread widened to approximately US$434 a tonne, its steepest backwardation in five years, while the August contract traded as much as US$370 above September—the widest one-month spread since the 2021 squeeze. Cash copper remained near US$14,500 a tonne as exchange inventories declined for a 42nd consecutive session. These figures do not prove that the world has exhausted its copper. They show that deliverable metal is becoming scarce in the locations and forms consumers require. Tariff expectations, warehouse movements, stockpiling, export policy and competition between the United States and China are dividing a nominally global market into regional pools. Copper has become the clearest evidence that the critical minerals contest is shifting from securing future deposits to controlling present flows.

Policy has helped create the physical divide. Copper has migrated toward the United States as traders position for tariffs and toward China as inventories there tighten, drawing liquidity from the warehouses that ordinarily balance regional shortages. The International Energy Agency identifies a deeper vulnerability: China accounted for more than 90% of the growth in global copper smelting capacity between 2005 and 2025, lifting its share from roughly 15-50%, while utilisation outside China fell below 70%. The West can therefore add mine supply without proportionately reducing its processing exposure. Copper’s squeeze is not simply a warning about too few mines. It is a warning that inventory geography, midstream economics and trade policy can create scarcity even where metal still exists elsewhere in the system. (Reuters; International Energy Agency)

The Democratic Republic of the Congo sharpened that lesson by prohibiting exports of copper and cobalt concentrates, subject to possible one-year waivers in strategic circumstances. Most Congolese copper already leaves as refined cathode, while cobalt is generally exported as hydroxide rather than concentrate, so the immediate loss of global supply may be smaller than the market reaction implied. The order nevertheless pushed copper higher because it arrived in an already tight physical market. Kinshasa’s objective is to compel more domestic processing and retain more mineral value, continuing a policy that previously softened only when local smelting was insufficient. Ivanhoe Mines Ltd. (TSX: IVN), whose Kamoa-Kakula complex is jointly owned with Zijin Mining Group Co., Ltd. (SSE: 601899; HKEX: 2899) and the Congolese state, has previously received exemptions while building local smelting capacity. Consuming nations are no longer the only governments directing mineral flows; producer countries are increasingly using access to ore as industrial policy. (Reuters; Reuters analysis)

Rare earths reveal the same contest in a smaller market with more concentrated leverage. European erbium prices have risen by more than 50% since June and Chinese prices by roughly 40% as buyers accumulate material before the November expiry of the suspension covering parts of Beijing’s expanded export-control regime. Erbium is used in fibre-optic communications, lasers and infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence (AI) data centres; holmium and ytterbium have also attracted precautionary buying. The importance lies less in the absolute size of these markets than in what the price movement says about expectations. Industrial customers are purchasing insurance against a political decision that has not yet been made. The November deadline is affecting costs months in advance, demonstrating that export controls exercise influence even while suspended. Uncertainty changes inventories, contract terms and capital allocation before any licence is denied. (Financial Times; InvestorNews)

China’s proposed expansion at Bayan Obo adds an important qualification. Annual mining capacity would rise by 50%, from 10-15 million tonnes, through an investment exceeding 500 million yuan, or about US$74 million. The expansion is principally intended to increase iron ore output; rare earths are recovered as a by-product and remain governed by quotas. More ore does not automatically mean more separated rare earths for export. China possesses sufficient geological and industrial depth to increase feed availability while retaining administrative control over how much rare-earth material reaches domestic and international customers. Extraction, quotas, processing, domestic allocation and export licences can be adjusted independently. Beijing can support its manufacturers with scale while preserving the option to ration foreign access, a more sophisticated form of industrial policy than simple supply restriction. (South China Morning Post) (South China Morning Post)

Enforcement is becoming as consequential as the written rules. Chinese authorities have detained several Japanese nationals, including senior executives of companies operating in China, in investigations involving alleged violations of dual-use export restrictions. Corporate offices have faced inspections and employees have been questioned, while Tokyo has warned companies to exercise greater caution. Critical minerals sit within a dual-use system because the same materials, equipment and process knowledge may serve semiconductors, civilian electronics, drones and weapons. For multinational manufacturers, the risk now extends beyond delayed shipments and licence denials to personnel, internal controls, customer due diligence and decisions about whether technical employees should travel to China. That raises the cost of operating even when material remains available and strengthens the relative position of Chinese downstream producers operating inside the domestic allocation system rather than at its external boundary. (South China Morning Post; Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China)

Japan’s response must extend beyond identifying another conventional supplier. Tokyo and Washington are advancing plans for what would become the world’s deepest undersea rare earth mine near Minamitorishima, where mineral-rich mud lies roughly 6,000 metres beneath the Pacific. Japan has demonstrated that sediment can be recovered from that depth, and its bilateral framework with the United States provides for coordinated financing, stockpiling and processing. The deposit lies within Japan’s exclusive economic zone and may contain heavy rare earths that are especially difficult to source outside China. Its commercial logic remains unproven. Mining at six kilometres must overcome engineering, environmental, lifting, dewatering, separation and cost challenges before it can provide qualified products. The project is best understood as a long-term strategic option, not near-term relief. It also reinforces a recurring InvestorNews point: a resource becomes strategically meaningful only when it can be converted repeatedly and economically into material customers can use. (The Japan Times; Associated Press; White House; InvestorNews) (AP News)

Malaysia and Australia are pursuing a nearer-term route through cooperation on rare earth processing, residue management and domestic neodymium magnet manufacturing. Malaysia’s objective is to build a value chain extending from separation into finished magnets rather than remain solely a processing location. Lynas Rare Earths Limited (ASX: LYC) and South Korea’s JS Link, Inc. (KOSDAQ: 127120) provide an industrial template: JS Link plans a 3,000-tonne-per-year sintered neodymium-iron-boron magnet factory near Lynas’s Kuantan complex, supported by an A$50 million Lynas investment and a feedstock arrangement extending to 2038. The project connects separated material, manufacturing expertise, an industrial site and prospective customers. It also illustrates why allied supply chains will not be purely national. Australia contributes resources and processing capability, South Korea magnet expertise, and Malaysia the industrial location and political licence to operate. The emerging alternative to China will be a negotiated network of specialised jurisdictions, not a duplicate supply chain contained inside one border. (The Edge Malaysia; Reuters)

The United States is responding with unprecedented financial breadth. The White House says the administration has signed or approved 160 mineral transactions worth nearly US$40 billion since January 2025. A further package announced on August 7 included a conditional loan of up to US$1.4 billion for Sila Nanotechnologies, Inc., US$400 million for Sunrise Energy Metals Limited (ASX: SRL) and its Australian scandium project, and US$150 million for Niron Magnetics, Inc. Although framed as a revival of American mining power, the portfolio reaches far beyond extraction into batteries, magnets, processing, technical education and enabling infrastructure. The analytical challenge is to distinguish the scale of commitment from the speed of delivery. These projects occupy different stages of technical maturity, financing and customer qualification. Public capital can absorb risks private markets will not, but it cannot eliminate the sequence in which a resource must become a stable process, a specification-compliant product and then a dependable industrial input. (White House; Reuters; InvestorNews) (Reuters)

MP Materials Corp. (NYSE: MP) offers the clearest evidence that government support is already changing corporate economics. Its second-quarter results included US$17.6 million of price-protection income, bringing cumulative federal support payments to US$110.9 million. Revenue from processed rare earths nearly quadrupled to US$94.4 million after the company stopped sending material to China for processing, while its Texas magnet operations generated US$16.5 million of revenue and US$7.5 million of adjusted profit. Washington has accepted that a strategically necessary producer cannot immediately compete against Chinese prices shaped by scale, sunk infrastructure and state policy. A price floor buys time for domestic processing and magnet capacity to mature. It also changes the test of performance: the relevant question is whether supported capacity advances toward qualified, repeatable and increasingly competitive production, rather than whether subsidy disappears quickly. (Reuters)

Defence procurement is beginning to provide the missing demand signal. Lockheed Martin Corporation (NYSE: LMT) is negotiating with NioCorp Developments Ltd. (NASDAQ: NB; TSX: NB) for scandium and with Teck Resources Limited (TSX: TECK.A; TSX: TECK.B; NYSE: TECK) and 5N Plus Inc. (TSX: VNP) for germanium. The reported preliminary NioCorp arrangement covers 15 tonnes of scandium annually, roughly one-quarter of current global demand, while pricing and contract duration remain obstacles in the germanium discussions. This is industrial policy conducted through the customer rather than the mine. A long-term defence offtake can validate a project, support financing and establish a reference price in markets too small and opaque for ordinary futures contracts. It also exposes a circular problem: manufacturers hesitate to redesign products around materials that are not reliably available, while producers cannot finance capacity without assured demand. Government pressure on prime contractors may be needed to break that circle, but contracts must still distribute technical, volume and price risk credibly. (Reuters; InvestorNews)

Two less celebrated decisions expose how difficult execution remains. The United States Department of Commerce will prohibit exports of lithium-ion battery black mass and tungsten-bearing scrap for one year beginning August 27th, retaining potentially valuable feedstock for domestic recyclers. American facilities cannot presently process all of it, however, and several recycling companies have entered bankruptcy. The Defense Logistics Agency separately cancelled a tender for almost 36 million pounds, or roughly 16,000 tonnes, of battery-grade lithium carbonate worth as much as US$300 million without publicly explaining the decision. Keeping feedstock at home is easier than creating a profitable recovery system; announcing a stockpile is easier than designing procurement terms suppliers can accept across a volatile five-year market. Project Vault and related reserve proposals may protect manufacturers from interruption only if purchasing, storage, quality control, rotation and release rules are aligned with actual industrial demand. Otherwise, stockpiling relocates scarcity without building productive capability. (Reuters; Mining.com; InvestorNews)

Private finance is being recruited into the same architecture. Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC) has announced an 18-month Critical Infrastructure Finance Initiative intended to mobilise US$250 billion by July 4, 2027 — for digital, energy, power and core infrastructure, including critical minerals and mining. JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM) and Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS) have each announced longer-term US$1.5 trillion programmes covering strategic industries. These figures should not be confused with committed equity for mines: they include lending, capital markets services, advisory mandates and investment across data centres, generation, transmission, semiconductors, transport and natural gas. Their importance is nevertheless substantial. Critical minerals are being absorbed into mainstream infrastructure finance because artificial intelligence, defence manufacturing and electrification cannot be financed separately from their materials and power systems. The constraint is shifting from capital availability in the abstract to the supply of bankable projects with permits, customers, proven technology and credible construction plans. (Bank of America; Reuters)

Recent Canadian developments show what that transition looks like at a smaller scale. Ucore Rare Metals Inc. (TSXV: UCU; OTCQX: UURAF) closed a C$69 million bought-deal offering largely to advance its Louisiana Strategic Metals Complex, directing capital toward separation capacity rather than another resource estimate. Natural Resources Canada invited Defense Metals Corp. (TSXV: DEFN; OTCQB: DFMTF; FSE: 35D) to submit a full proposal for work moving the Wicheeda project’s concentrator, hydrometallurgy and solvent-extraction programme toward feasibility, although the invitation is not yet a funding commitment. First Phosphate Corp. (NASDAQ: PHOS; CSE: PHOS; OTCQX: FRSPF; FSE: KD0) moved its American depositary receipts to the Nasdaq Global Market after securing C$4.84 million in non-repayable federal contributions for road and power planning at Bégin-Lamarche. None guarantees commercial production, but each addresses a recurring obstacle between Canadian geology and North American industrial supply: processing, infrastructure or access to deeper capital markets. (Ucore Rare Metals; Defense Metals; First Phosphate Nasdaq uplisting; First Phosphate infrastructure funding)

The energy system is being folded into this industrial strategy. X-Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: XE) may receive up to an additional US$1 billion from the United States Department of Energy for its advanced reactor project with Dow Inc. (NYSE: DOW) in Seadrift, Texas, bringing available public support since 2021 to as much as US$2.15 billion under a 50-50 cost-sharing structure. The proposed four-reactor installation is intended to provide electricity and industrial steam to Dow’s petrochemical complex in the early 2030s. Its relevance to critical minerals extends beyond uranium and advanced reactor fuel. Western separation, refining, recycling and magnet plants require dependable electricity, industrial heat and infrastructure at prices capable of competing with established Asian systems, while data centres increase both power consumption and mineral demand. The same public balance sheet is therefore being asked to support mines, processors, reactors, transmission and manufacturing, turning energy policy and critical minerals policy into one capital-allocation problem. (Reuters; United States Department of Energy)

The emerging critical minerals economy is consequently less a free market than a network of managed channels. China controls quotas, licences, domestic allocation and enforcement; the Democratic Republic of the Congo uses export rules to demand local processing; the United States deploys price floors, loans, procurement pressure, export restrictions and strategic reserves; Japan combines stockpiling with frontier resource development; Malaysia bargains for downstream manufacturing; and private banks fold minerals into national infrastructure mandates. The risk is no longer that Western governments will fail to act. It is that they will finance the chain in the wrong order, compete for the same scarce output or retain materials they cannot yet process. Copper’s backwardation is the immediate market warning, while erbium’s rise ahead of November is the diplomatic warning. Durable advantage will belong not to the country announcing the largest mine or financing programme, but to the industrial system capable of moving material through extraction, separation, fabrication and qualification without a politically vulnerable break. (International Energy Agency; Financial Times; InvestorNews)

About the Critical Minerals Institute (CMI)

The Critical Minerals Institute (CMI) is a global think tank and central hub for the critical minerals ecosystem, connecting companies, capital markets, and policymakers. Through its monthly CMI Masterclasses, twice-monthly Critical Minerals Report (CMR) and CMR Podcast episodes, bespoke research, and board-level advisory services, CMI delivers actionable intelligence spanning exploration finance, supply chains, industrial policy, and geopolitics.

CMI tracks 12 leading national and multilateral critical minerals lists and applies a rigorous comparative process to independently select and maintain its proprietary CMI Watchlist. Materials are evaluated against one another based on strategic importance, supply-chain concentration, geopolitical exposure, substitutability, and relevance to defense, technology, and economic security. Through its strategic partnership with the Critical Minerals Platform (CMP), CMI offers Platinum members access to independent mineral pricing, market forecasts, corporate intelligence, and global supply-chain data.

CMI also organizes its flagship annual event, CMI Summit 6. Held under the theme Critical Minerals Diplomacy in a Fragmented Global Economy, the Summit brings together government leaders, institutional investors, policymakers, and industry executives from around the world. CMI Summit 6 will take place May 17–18, 2027, at Toronto’s Fairmont Royal York.
