title: Florida residents stopped trusting the grid and started building their own "safety nets" before ...
description:
With total U.S. electricity demand projected to rise rapidly over the coming decade, that deficit becomes increasingly dangerous.
Now, a quiet shift across Florida homes and businesses is unfolding—one that centralized utility planners are failing to predict.
Natural gas fueled roughly 75% of state electricity generation in 2024, creating extreme exposure whenever supply chains face storm disruptions or price shocks.
Driven by data centers, industrial expansion, and electrification, U.S. power demand is projected to climb 21% by 2030 and 39% by 2035.
Why Florida residents feel grid stress more than most No state relies on its residential sector like Florida.
text:
Florida stands as America’s second-largest producer of electricity, yet it cannot power itself independently. The state routinely draws power from neighboring regional grids to cover the gap. With total U.S. electricity demand projected to rise rapidly over the coming decade, that deficit becomes increasingly dangerous.

This tension peaks every year between June and November, when hurricane season transforms widespread blackouts from a statistical risk into an annual certainty. Now, a quiet shift across Florida homes and businesses is unfolding—one that centralized utility planners are failing to predict.

A grid under pressure from two directions

Florida’s energy infrastructure conceals significant vulnerability. Natural gas fueled roughly 75% of state electricity generation in 2024, creating extreme exposure whenever supply chains face storm disruptions or price shocks.

Across Florida, electrical contractors report multi-year growth in pre-storm infrastructure spending by property owners unwilling to rely on utility promises.

This localized risk aligns with a broader national crunch. Driven by data centers, industrial expansion, and electrification, U.S. power demand is projected to climb 21% by 2030 and 39% by 2035. Nationally, operators hold just 26 gigawatts of reserve capacity above reliability requirements—a thin 3% buffer that is continually narrowing.

While planners focus heavily on new gas plants, utility solar, and transmission lines, they overlook a critical dynamic unfolding directly on the customer side of the meter.

Why Florida residents feel grid stress more than most

No state relies on its residential sector like Florida. Households consume 54% of all electricity used statewide—the highest share in the nation. Nearly every home runs air conditioning, and 90% rely on electric heating.

Consequently, power failures trigger immediate public safety crises. When severe storms destroy distribution lines, outages instantly threaten food supplies, medical equipment, and essential climate control.

With Florida experiencing more hurricane landfalls than any other state, prolonged blackouts are an expected annual reality. Living through them shifts how residents view public utilities, prompting proactive investment.

Solar is rising, but so is the demand it must meet

The generation mix is evolving. Wind and utility solar produced a record 17% of U.S. electricity in 2025, reaching 19% with small-scale solar included. Florida ranked third nationally in solar generation, behind only California and Texas.

However, power consumption is expanding in parallel. Population growth, expanding digital infrastructure, and electrified systems continuously absorb new generation as fast as it comes online.

Thus, utility solar expansion alone cannot eliminate operational risk. Reliability margins remain tight, leaving the central grid vulnerable.

Property-level resilience: The demand signal planners are missing

Standard forecasting models miss crucial bottom-up decisions. Across Florida, electrical contractors report multi-year growth in pre-storm infrastructure spending by property owners unwilling to rely on utility promises.

EV charger installations have similarly grown, reflecting a broader mindset shift: consumers are actively moving from hoping the grid holds to preparing for when it fails.

Because utility forecasts prioritize centralized plant construction, this uncaptured demand growth creates an expanding blind spot for grid operators.

What Florida’s pattern means for grid planning everywhere

Florida offers a vital case study for storm-exposed regions nationwide. Property-level resilience decisions draw from the same tight capacity margin as utility demand. Planners who fail to track these signals will miscalculate baseline grid requirements.

text:
North Carolina's fast-growing data center industry is meeting stronger neighborhood-level resistance as more residents say they do not want such projects close to home during the AI-driven expansion.

Here's what to know

According to NC Newsline, a statewide survey conducted at the end of July found that 53% of North Carolinians opposed data centers in their communities.

Another 20% supported them, while 27% said they were unsure.

That was a clear change from Elon University's March poll, which found 44% opposed, 24% supportive, and 32% undecided.

Opposition spanned multiple voter groups. Jason Husser, director of the Elon Poll, said the survey showed majorities of Democrats, independents, and women against local data centers, along with pluralities of Republicans and men.

The industry's support numbers fell despite a pro-data-center lobbying group spending $367,272 on a North Carolina advertising campaign focused on the business and economic upsides of data centers.

Husser said the issue carries extra weight because it is unfolding close to where people live.

"It's not just a debate in Raleigh that can be far away for people," he said. "It's a debate in their local county seats."

More background

The poll comes as communities across North Carolina grapple with what large data center projects could mean for land use, power demand, water consumption, noise, and local budgets.

More than 20 local governments in North Carolina have put moratoriums in place on new data center development, while they evaluate the issue and decide which rules should apply to future proposals.

At the same time, some local officials have pushed back against moratoriums, arguing that data centers could generate valuable property tax revenue. The debate has become increasingly visible at county meetings and in city halls across the state.

Data centers support cloud computing, online services, and AI tools that can help optimize electricity systems, improve renewable energy forecasting, and boost efficiency. But they can also consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, strain local infrastructure, raise concerns about pollution and higher utility costs, and fuel broader worries about security, misuse, and unintended social consequences as AI expands.

What's being done?

Many communities appear to be trying to slow the process rather than stop it outright.

Moratoriums can give local governments time to study likely impacts, hear from residents, and write zoning or permitting rules that fit local infrastructure and development goals.

Husser told NC Newsline he was not surprised that the advertising push has struggled to win people over, especially when residents are focused on how projects could affect their own neighborhoods.

Public hearings, planning board meetings, and county commissioner sessions can shape whether projects move forward, what restrictions apply, and how benefits and burdens are distributed.

In cases like this, local rules around water use, energy demand, buffering, and tax agreements can directly affect everyday life.

As Husser put it, "We've seen in the past that grassroots NIMBY movements can move the needle more than significant corporate spending, particularly when people are skeptical of those corporations to begin with."

title: After a 2-year wait, will Ohio's largest solar project get the OK? - Canary Media
description:
The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County and three of its townships.
Oak Run Solar would bring 800 megawatts of solar and 300 MW of energy storage to a state that has become increasingly hostile to clean energy, even as mounting electricity demand increases power prices and threatens grid reliability.
The OPSB’s staff has already weighed in: Its Aug. 7 brief asks the full board to confirm Oak Run’s permit.
“The project represents a significant opportunity for long-term economic investment in Madison County while supporting Ohio’s growing energy needs,” Samantha Sawmiller, senior development manager for the Oak Run Solar Project, told Canary Media.
The Ohio Supreme Court’s multiple opinions on May 26 in the Oak Run case may also suggest a growing partisanship among some of its members.
text:
Following a key legal deadline last Friday, the stage is now set for the Ohio Power Siting Board to make a final decision about whether the state’s largest solar and energy storage project to date can move ahead.

The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County and three of its townships.

Oak Run Solar would bring 800 megawatts of solar and 300 MW of energy storage to a state that has become increasingly hostile to clean energy, even as mounting electricity demand increases power prices and threatens grid reliability.

Though the county and townships filed their appeal with the Ohio Supreme Court in October 2024, it was not until this past May that the court weighed in. A majority of the seven justices rejected all objections to the project except one.

To deal with that issue, the court sent the case back to the board with instructions for regulators to ​“more thoroughly address the Oak Run project’s visual impacts,” specifically by reviewing photo simulations or artist’s sketches of how the project’s proposed substations would look from public vantage points.

On July 28, Ohio regulators heard testimony on this narrow issue. Briefing wrapped up last Friday.

Once the full board reviews the transcript, briefs, and other filings, it will issue a decision. The OPSB’s staff has already weighed in: Its Aug. 7 brief asks the full board to confirm Oak Run’s permit.

The board is under no obligation to vote according to its staff’s recommendation, and there is no specific deadline for it to act. Any additional appeal could also eat up more time.

“The project represents a significant opportunity for long-term economic investment in Madison County while supporting Ohio’s growing energy needs,” Samantha Sawmiller, senior development manager for the Oak Run Solar Project, told Canary Media. ​“We respectfully await the Ohio Power Siting Board’s decision.”

Oak Run’s saga demonstrates the difficulty of developing clean energy in Ohio. In recent years, the state has blocked 5.3 gigawatts of wind and solar projects and garnered a reputation as the place ​“where wind and solar projects go to die.”

Since 2021, the General Assembly has enacted multiple laws that create extra hurdles for new solar and wind, but not for fossil fuel projects.

Meanwhile, the OPSB has played a central role in restricting solar’s growth, especially for grandfathered projects exempted from local government bans under those state statutes.

In March, the OPSB denied permits for the proposed 94-MW Crossroads Solar Grazing Center in central Ohio. Last month, it asked the state Supreme Court to dismiss an appeal from the developer of the planned 175-MW Kingwood Solar installation, whose permits the regulators denied in 2022. The project’s interconnection agreement has expired while it awaits a court decision — a fact the board used to justify its request for dismissal.

The Ohio Supreme Court’s multiple opinions on May 26 in the Oak Run case may also suggest a growing partisanship among some of its members. Previously, the court’s members had generally shown more deference toward the OPSB’s expertise on its factual findings.

When those opinions are pieced together, six of the court’s seven justices found fault with the OPSB’s grant of the permit because the developer’s visual evidence didn’t include renderings of the project’s three substations.

Three of those justices found that was the only shortcoming. Three others also sided with the local governments and would have required more evidence on issues dealing with water, wildlife, and fears about the safety of battery storage.

Jennifer Brunner, the court’s only Democrat, would have affirmed the OPSB’s decision in its entirety, based on the case record’s other evidence.

Taken together, the opinions ​“added more confusion to an already uncertain legal environment” for utility-scale renewables, said Karin Nordstrom, a lawyer with the Ohio Environmental Council, which is a party in the case supporting the project.

“Ohio is facing a massive energy crunch and ever-rising energy prices [and] really needs a clear substantive standard for reviewing these proposed projects,” she added. ​“And that’s not what we got from the court in this case.”

Testimony at the July 28 hearing was relatively brief. Lauren Devine, director of permitting and environmental matters for Savion, the project developer, said the company had the consulting firm EDR do additional work to show how public vantage points would look with the planned substations.

Gordon Perkins, a division manager with EDR, reported on that new work and its photo simulations with the substations included. The substations ​“would not contribute to visual impacts that were not already identified” in the group’s earlier review of the Oak Run project, he said, adding that the developer would take various steps to minimize visual impacts.

Mark Bellamy, a utilities specialist on the technical staff that advises the OPSB, reported that he had reviewed the consultant’s new report and concluded that Oak Run’s aesthetic appearance would be consistent with that of other solar farms — hence the staff recommendation to greenlight the project.

The local governments’ sole witness was Errol Gattis, a resident of London, Ohio, who said he’d be able to see the project from his yard and porch and objected to EDR’s choice of vantage points.

Ohio’s rules don’t require consideration of a project’s expected appearance from every possible angle, however. And state law doesn’t guarantee that viewsheds won’t change, said Tom Bullock, executive director for the Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, a consumer watchdog group that promotes clean energy and is not part of the case.

An Aug. 7 brief filed by the opponents’ lawyer, Jack Van Kley — a longtime renewable-energy opponent in the state — took issue with the vantage points for the visual analysis and argued that the developer should have provided the materials as a supplement to the company’s project application, complete with various steps for public participation.

Those stances are similar to arguments that the Ohio Supreme Court rejected in its Oak Run ruling in May, about the general approach for a visual analysis and whether regulators had properly found that the developer’s application was complete. Moreover, the court didn’t order a supplement to the application, just the review of additional material on a single issue.

“This was the evidentiary hearing that is very narrowly focused on the simulations for the substations,” said Christine Pirik, a lawyer for the developer, when Van Kley tried to use the argument to block admission of the additional evidence into the case record.

Administrative Law Judges David Hicks and Isabel Marcelletti sided with the developer and the siting board’s staff, noting their belief that the hearing process complies with the court’s directive.

Filings by the OPSB’s staff and the Ohio Environmental Council, which advocates for clean energy, also took issue with Van Kley’s arguments. ​“The Local Governments’ alleged procedural violations apply to service requirements for an application, not supplemental evidence submitted on remand,” lawyers Karin Nordstrom and Chris Tavenor wrote in the council’s Aug. 14 reply brief.

The clock is ticking for Oak Run, as lawyers for the developer noted in a May 18 court filing: ​“Oak Run is now in dire need to have the appeals process come to a close as soon as possible.”

“Should the Project fail due to the lengthy time for considerations, Oak Run will lose its significant financial investment and the community and state of Ohio will lose the employment and financial benefits that would result from construction and operation of the Project,” including about $250 million for local governments, its filing said.

title: Hochul wants to build more nuclear power than the U.S. has in 30 years - Times Union
description:
Kathy Hochul is pushing New York headlong into building more nuclear power capacity in the coming years than the entire country has added over the last three decades.
​Most of the country’s nuclear plants — which make up roughly 20% of U.S. electricity generation — were built between the 1970s and 1990s.
The last two nuclear reactors built in the U.S. — both at the same site in Georgia — were collectively $17 billion over budget and years late.
“I’m not anti-nuclear, and I’m not advocating shutting down existing operating nuclear plants,” said Allison Macfarlane, who chaired the Nuclear Regulatory Commission from 2012 to 2014.

text:
ALBANY — Gov. Kathy Hochul is pushing New York headlong into building more nuclear power capacity in the coming years than the entire country has added over the last three decades.

At a time when lawmakers and governors across the political spectrum are increasingly open to boosting nuclear energy supply, but not crafting solid plans, she’s set a firm target to add 5 gigawatts of new energy production — enough electricity to supply nearly 4 million homes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The hope is that a bounty of reliable power would spur economic development, stabilize soaring utility bills and propel New York into an era with plentiful clean electricity. Augmenting the state’s nuclear fleet would add roughly $50 billion in benefits to the electric grid by 2050, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority.

But the vision could sputter under the technology’s immense costs and protracted regulatory timeline. A spate of new reactors could require $15 billion to $24 billion in public subsidies, a state analysis found. That analysis doesn’t include additional payments residents may have to make if projects go over budget. The first new nuclear facility may not be complete until 2039, meaning it will do little to address present affordability and electric grid reliability challenges.

The initiative by New York comes as a bevy of federal tax credits and low-cost loans have been rolled out in recent years to bring new reactors online affordably and meet rising power demand, including from AI-driven data centers.

​Even with renewed enthusiasm, it’s been a challenge to get nuclear plants under construction.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“We’re in the middle of an often proclaimed renaissance in nuclear power,” said David Victor, a University of California San Diego professor who researches reducing the electric grid’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We have a lot of talk about building new reactors — and not a lot of doing.”

The next two decades may determine whether Hochul’s push is justified or whether nuclear power remains mired in controversy and cost overruns that have historically hindered the industry’s growth. Despite some of the concerns that have heightened the stigma surrounding the industry, including safe storage of radioactive waste, nuclear plants can produce enormous amounts of steady power for decades and with no greenhouse gas emissions. They also operate around the clock, unlike wind and solar projects.

​Most of the country’s nuclear plants — which make up roughly 20% of U.S. electricity generation — were built between the 1970s and 1990s. A powerful antinuclear movement grew during that period and gained momentum after incidents that included the meltdown at the Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania. Public backlash was so strong on Long Island that a nuclear facility completed there in 1984 never operated commercially.

The last two nuclear reactors built in the U.S. — both at the same site in Georgia — were collectively $17 billion over budget and years late. Last year, voters ousted incumbents from the Georgia Public Service Commission after they had hiked utility rates to pay for the new facilities.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

‘The objective at hand’

Some energy sector experts and environmentalists question the focus on building new nuclear plants when solar and wind farms are cheaper and take less time to build.

“I’m not anti-nuclear, and I’m not advocating shutting down existing operating nuclear plants,” said Allison Macfarlane, who chaired the Nuclear Regulatory Commission from 2012 to 2014. “I’m just practical. And if you’re talking about spending public money, you shouldn’t be talking about wasting public money when there’s an easier available alternative.”

But Hochul’s vision for the state’s energy system is one of abundance, where nuclear plants complement a swath of new wind and solar farms to meet New York’s ambitious mandate to utilize 100% clean energy by 2040.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nuclear is one of the only energy sources that can operate nonstop while producing no greenhouse gas emissions — which are linked to both warming the planet and negative public health outcomes. In 2024 alone, the emissions avoided by operating the four existing reactors upstate were equivalent to removing 3.5 million cars from the road, according to Brattle, an energy research firm.

Indian Point, a Westchester County plant, provided New York City with around 25% of its electricity needs until a public pressure campaign eventually led to its closure in 2021. The use of fossil fuels to offset that loss has increased, and more than 85 percent of electricity being supplied to New York City and Long Island is from gas and oil.

Every gigawatt of nuclear power — enough energy to supply 750,000 homes — can, in some cases, provide the same benefit to the grid as three gigawatts of wind, solar and battery storage, according to the Energy Research and Development Authority.

“Anyone that’s out there pushing for one specific technology, whether it be just nuclear or just renewables, isn’t necessarily serious about achieving the objective at hand,” said Richard Barlette, director of state government affairs at Constellation Energy, which operates all of New York’s nuclear plants. “Because at the end of the day, the (state’s climate) goals are so lofty you need every clean resource at your disposal.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Hochul is only looking to build new reactors in communities that want them, making Constellation a likely partner. Both Wayne and Oswego counties — where the existing nuclear plants are — have expressed interest in getting new facilities.

Building additional reactors at existing locations takes advantage of “low-hanging fruit,” because necessary heavy rail lines and water access are already onsite, Barlette said. Constellation also has already secured a grant to study putting a new reactor at one of the plants in Oswego County.

How to pay for it

Even with willing developers and communities, building new nuclear facilities is fraught with pitfalls — especially for a governor so committed to affordability, a tension Hochul has acknowledged.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“I look at projects like the very expensive nuclear project they did in Georgia,” Hochul said. “I’m working hard to make sure that we don’t get sucked up into those high costs.”

No matter how efficiently New York gets nuclear off the ground, residents will likely be on the hook for billions in subsidies to keep the plants commercially viable. The state’s current fleet of nuclear and renewable energy producers already receive subsidies, and they amount to roughly 10% of the typical residential utility bill.

What remains to be seen is how innovative state and energy sector leaders can be in bringing down the cost of new nuclear so those future subsidies are as minimal as possible.

President Donald J. Trump has ratcheted up financial programs for nuclear developers, and the Inflation Reduction Act signed by President Joe Biden in 2022 created significant tax credits for nuclear projects.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

How to cover the remaining billions that the federal government won’t guarantee is where development can get expensive for New Yorkers.

To make financing a new nuclear facility feasible, taxpayers may have to pay some added costs if a project comes in over budget, according to a report by the state Energy Research and Development Authority and Public Service Commission report.

“If you’re thinking about building a big new reactor in New York, you’re not just looking at (whether) people (are) saying nice things about your project right now,” said Victor, the University of California professor who is also on the advisory council of the Institute for Nuclear Plant Operations. “It’s, will those nice things hold when the project has cost overruns, which seems likely.”

Barlette, the Constellation Energy official, wouldn’t say whether state taxpayers would have to cover potential construction overruns for the company to invest in new nuclear projects. Holtec, a major nuclear developer, said in filings submitted to the Public Service Commission that state taxpayers could bear additional costs in the event construction goes over budget.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Where does this public support come from? It comes from the people,” said Assemblywoman Jo Anne Simon, a Brooklyn Democrat who opposes Hochul’s plan. “You spread that out across all the ratepayers, and everybody’s going to get a very significant hike.” Simon is sponsoring legislation that would institute a moratorium on public subsidies for new nuclear plants.

The state can also take some amount of ownership in new plants or provide grants to lower their costs, the Energy Research and Development Authority report stated. Hochul already tasked the New York Power Authority, a state-run entity that owns and operates power plants, to develop at least one gigawatt of the new nuclear reactors.

Hochul has suggested power-intensive businesses, like Micron’s chip fab complex near Syracuse, could receive electricity in exchange for covering some of the costs.

A spokesman for Micron wouldn’t say whether the company is interested in such an agreement but noted the company is generally supportive of the governor’s nuclear energy targets.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The most commercially viable reactor is the design constructed in Georgia. Each can consistently power 750,000 homes. Smaller designs are entering the market now but are extremely expensive and less tested.

​States are hoping that as more nuclear plants are built, both the nascent small reactors and established large-scale designs can become less expensive.

​The next generation of large reactors could be roughly 40% cheaper than the Georgia plants if a robust workforce is in place and the companies developing the projects are on firm financial footing, a 2024 Massachusetts Institute of Technology study estimated. Hochul has already dedicated $40 million to enlisting a workforce for the next generation of reactors.

But the history of nuclear development in the U.S. doesn’t show a steady decline in costs for new reactors. Throughout the 1950s and early 1960s, plants became progressively cheaper, according to a study from researchers at the Breakthrough Institute, an environmental research center. Since the late 1960s, costs for new facilities have largely escalated.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

None of the four reactors built in the U.S. over the last 30 years were on time or on budget.

‘Looking out for your safety’

​A core component of how expensive new facilities will be is how quickly they can get built. Projects have to be under construction by 2033 to fully take advantage of Biden-era tax credits. But that timeline is tighter than it looks because the federal approval process can take roughly six years.

​Hochul has encouraged the Trump administration to speed up the regulatory process. But the push puts her in a potentially vexing situation as some former regulators have raised concerns that changes under consideration by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission undermine safety.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nuclear plants have limits on how much radiation an employee or member of the public can be exposed to every year. ​In July, the nuclear commission proposed rules eliminating a requirement that nuclear facilities keep radiation exposure to employees far below those top annual limits.

Workers at nuclear plants received an average of roughly 3% of their annual radiological exposure limit in 2024, according to commission data.

Part of the reason plants keep exposure levels so low is because of the standard the commission is seeking to remove, said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety with the Union of Concerned Scientists.

If New York is going to provide subsidies to new reactors, they should “be put toward making the plants safer, instead of allowing the industry to cut costs,” he added.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

David Brenner, a radiation expert from Columbia University, said the proposed changes are “not unreasonable” because the commission already has rules setting the maximum amount of radiation an employee or member of the public can safely receive.

“Radiation does get a rather bad rap,” Brenner said. “The very word radiation makes people nervous.”

But the world is full of radiation, including from medical devices like X-ray machines and natural sources like fruit. It’s estimated that living near a nuclear power plant for a year exposes a person to roughly the same amount of radiation as eating a banana.

Hochul said that new nuclear reactors will be built with “safety at the forefront” and under “rigorous environmental standards.” Hochul’s administration is still reviewing the commission’s proposal, a spokesman said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

‘Has got people excited’

The nuclear industry has long been plagued with concerns over safety.

​But in the upstate communities where plants have been in operation for more than 50 years, the technology is widely popular. About 60% of Oswego County residents support building new nuclear reactors while 12% are opposed, a survey from Jefferson Community College found. Communities in that region are used to running annual safety drills and have thousands of employees working at the existing plants on a temporary or permanent basis.

​Local officials are hoping the power from new facilities will support economic development nearby.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Newsletter

Sign up for the Capitol A.M. Roundup newsletter

Get a free roundup of New York government and political news, delivered weekdays to your inbox.

Sign up here

​Hochul, when discussing the challenges of keeping New Yorkers employed and fostering economic development, often references the closure of manufacturing plants in western New York that took place during her childhood. Adding nuclear energy is about spurring an “upstate ecosystem surrounding innovation,” she said. Large businesses like Micron and GlobalFoundries already have plans to build massive facilities upstate.

​“There’s been over the last few decades some loss of manufacturing,” said Philip Church, the Oswego County administrator. “But nuclear and its employment has been steady, and so it’s a major player in our economy, a major employer. The prospect of having additional one or two plants here has got people excited.”

​Building new reactors in willing communities reduces the risk of catastrophic public backlash like what happened with the plant on Long Island or Indian Point. But Hochul’s vision is a colossal test of whether New Yorkers can reap the benefits of nuclear energy without suffering from significant overruns at a time when affordability is everything.

text:
The steel structures market in China is estimated at 100 million tonnes

In 2026, China’s steel structures sector is expected to see steady growth in demand, which remains one of the key pillars of domestic steel consumption, with an annual volume of around 100 million tonnes. However, the market is undergoing a clear structural shift: away from traditional civil engineering towards the new energy sector, high-tech manufacturing and infrastructure. This is reported by BigMint.

Sheet and processed sheet steel account for 60–70% of the total volume of steel used in steel structures. Due to the ongoing contraction in the residential construction sector, the main drivers of growth are renewable energy projects, industrial facilities, data centres and transport infrastructure.

Key areas of consumption:

Industrial construction and IT. Thanks to the development of industrial parks, cold-storage logistics centres and data centres, the use of all-steel frames – which ensure rapid assembly – is expanding.

Energy infrastructure. This sector is expected to become the strongest driver of growth. The production of solar mounting systems, wind turbines and substations is significantly increasing demand for hot-rolled and galvanised coils, as well as heavy plate.

Transport and urban infrastructure. The construction of bridges, railway stations and sports facilities ensures stable consumption of heavy sections and pipes, although this depends on funding schedules.

At the same time, the qualitative structure of consumption is changing: the share of high-strength steel grades (above Q355), weather-resistant and corrosion-resistant alloys is growing. In the long term, China’s decarbonisation policy and the development of prefabricated construction will contribute to a further increase in the share of steel structures in the country’s total crude steel consumption.

name: EPA
title: The Case Against Gas-Powered Leaf Blowers Has Only Grown Stronger
authors: Mark Nevitt, Michael Herz, Cameron Kay, Jolie McLaughlin, The Regulatory Review
description:
Three years later, nearly every major development has strengthened the case for phasing out gas-powered leaf blowers.
Two-stroke engines—the technology underpinning gas-powered leaf blowers—have been phased out of virtually every other industry due to their debilitating impacts on worker health.
In July 2025, Montgomery County, Maryland, banned the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, with a violation resulting in a $500 citation.
Imagine visiting Yosemite, Yellowstone, or the Grand Canyon without the fear of gas-powered leaf blowers disturbing your peaceful enjoyment.
The case for banning gas-powered leaf blowers is clear.
text:
Evidence on the harms of gas leaf blowers has sparked contests over regulatory authority.

I argued in a February 2023 essay in The Regulatory Review that regulators should ban gas-powered leaf blowers due to their enormous environmental, public health, and hidden labor costs. Three years later, nearly every major development has strengthened the case for phasing out gas-powered leaf blowers. State and local governments are acting. Industry is fighting back through state preemption laws and constitutional litigation. And a recent federal court decision has exposed the decades-long failure of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to enforce the Noise Control Act.

Electric alternatives have improved substantially, and the consumer price differential of gas-powered equipment has narrowed. While the political and legal terrain is growing more contentious and complicated, the underlying case for regulation is more powerful than ever. Consider that a consumer-grade, two-stroke gas-powered leaf blower emits more pollution in 30 minutes than a Ford F-150 Raptor traveling 3,900 miles from Alaska to Texas.

Two-stroke engines—the technology underpinning gas-powered leaf blowers—have been phased out of virtually every other industry due to their debilitating impacts on worker health. Yet two-stroke engines remain commonplace in the landscaping industry, raising enormous environmental justice concerns, as half of all landscape workers nationally are Latino.

According to the 2020 National Emissions Inventory published by EPA, lawn and garden engines emit nearly 22,000 tons of fine particulates into the air—as much pollution as produced by 234 million cars annually.

The noise pollution alone from gas-powered blowers is staggering. Gas-powered blowers routinely exceed 100 decibels, equivalent to standing beside a jet engine at takeoff. Permanent hearing loss begins at 85 decibels. These harms are concentrated and borne disproportionately by low-wage workers and neighbors who have little practical recourse.

Several state and local governments have acted since 2023. California enacted the most sweeping action: a statewide ban on the sale, though not the use, of all new gas-powered lawn equipment, effective 2024. Virginia is a Dillon’s Rule state where local governments have only the powers explicitly given to them by the state. There, the Virginia Attorney General issued a legal opinion in 2024 granting localities the authority to amend noise ordinances to prohibit gas-powered leaf blowers. Soon after, Alexandria, Virginia, voted to phase out gas-powered leaf blowers in favor of electric equipment. In July 2025, Montgomery County, Maryland, banned the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, with a violation resulting in a $500 citation.

City-level action has also accelerated. Portland, Oregon voted unanimously in 2024 to phase out gas-powered leaf blowers starting in 2026, with a complete ban by 2028. Seattle banned contractor use by 2025 and homeowner use by 2027. Baltimore enacted an ordinance restricting gas blower use to a two-month fall window, with a full ban taking effect at the end of 2026. Lexington, Massachusetts, enacted a commercial ban effective March 2025, with residential use to follow in 2026.

State governments are acting as well. Colorado prohibited state agencies from using gas-powered push and handheld lawn equipment during summer months beginning in June 2025. The law also requires the University of Colorado to report annually on gas equipment use to the state Air Pollution Control Division.

This regulatory momentum has also stimulated a coordinated countermovement. Landscaping industry groups have partnered with state legislators in Texas in 2023, in Georgia in 2024, and in Florida in 2026 to enact preemption laws prohibiting local governments from banning gas-powered equipment. The framing is familiar: Local restrictions, the argument goes, impose unfair burdens on small businesses. But these preemption laws reallocate regulatory authority away from the governments most directly affected by noise and localized air pollution. Communities experiencing the harms lose the ability to tailor regulations to local conditions.

Georgia enacted a law in 2024 preempting local governments from imposing a ban on gas-powered lawn equipment. This legislation strips Atlanta and other Georgia municipalities of the authority to address a demonstrable public nuisance within their own borders. For Atlanta, a city with a stunning tree canopy that is known as a “City in a Forest,” the “ban on bans” legislation is particularly incongruous and harmful.

The backlash has also arrived in court. In 2023, a group of landscaping companies sued Montclair Township, New Jersey, after the township enacted a gas-powered blower ban, arguing that the ban violated the U.S. Constitution’s Takings and Supremacy Clauses, and the U.S. and New Jersey Constitution’s Equal Protection Clause. Although a federal district court dismissed this claim and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit upheld the decision, the litigation demonstrates the extraordinary steps that vested interests will take to challenge leaf blower regulation.

Litigation may be beginning to move in the other direction—a “backlash to the backlash.” Homeowners in some jurisdictions may consider bringing nuisance claims against landscaping companies under state law. Georgia nuisance doctrine, for instance, defines a nuisance as “anything that causes hurt, inconvenience, or damage to another”—without regard to whether the underlying act is otherwise lawful. Given that gas-powered blowers routinely exceed 100 decibels, nuisance law offers a plausible theory of liability and takes on increased importance as state legislators prohibit municipal action. But litigation is a costly and unpredictable substitute for regulation, and any relief would be ad hoc at best.

In the interim, I assess that three categories of actors can address the harms of gas-powered lawn and garden engines without waiting for Congress or state legislatures.

First, colleges and universities represent the most tractable near-term opportunity. Most large universities operate significant grounds maintenance programs, employ sustainability offices, and face competitive pressure from on campus environmental interests, including students, faculty, and staff, that reward emissions reductions. Here, the University of Southern California (USC) deserves special recognition. A letter from a professor to USC’s president put an end to gas-powered leaf blowers on campus over a decade ago, resulting in USC’s campus being certified as a “green zone” by the American Green Zone Alliance. USC remains one of the few major universities to have comprehensively phased out gas-powered leaf blowers. The field appears wide open for other universities to act.

Second, state and local governmental officials can limit the use of gas-powered lawn equipment on state and local lands. For example, New York State’s Department of Environmental Conservation committed to converting its lawn maintenance equipment to zero-emission models. And Charleston, South Carolina, transitioned its city fleet entirely to electric and manual tools. More municipal and agency administrators can follow suit.

Finally, federal agencies have direct authority over the lands they manage. The National Park Service maintains iconic public properties and operates a substantial fleet of landscape maintenance equipment. An executive order directing federal land management agencies to phase out gas-powered equipment would generate real emissions reductions, signal a national norm, and require no legislative action. That such an order never came from the Biden Administration remains a missed opportunity. Meanwhile, federal regulation has remained limited to incremental emissions standards despite EPA’s authority under the Clean Air Act over nonroad engines. Although the current Administration is unlikely to pursue this authority, it remains available to future administrations. Imagine visiting Yosemite, Yellowstone, or the Grand Canyon without the fear of gas-powered leaf blowers disturbing your peaceful enjoyment.

The gas-powered leaf blower has become an unlikely but revealing test case for environmental regulation in an era of federal retreat. Some state and local governments have demonstrated the political leadership to act. The industry has responded with preemption campaigns and litigation. Congress and the executive branch have done nothing. What remains is a patchwork—regulations that are protective in California, prohibited in Georgia, and contested in a growing number of courtrooms.

Increasingly, the debate is no longer whether gas-powered leaf blowers should be regulated but who gets to decide—the federal government, state legislatures, local communities, or private litigants.

That patchwork will not hold indefinitely. The underlying harms to air quality, worker health, and to the peace of residential neighborhoods are irrefutable. The question is whether communities will continue to bear the costs while legislators stall in the face of industry opposition, despite mounting evidence of environmental and public health harms. Much as smoking on commercial aircraft now seems unthinkable, future generations may wonder why gas-powered leaf blowers remained commonplace long after their harms became clear.

The case for banning gas-powered leaf blowers is clear. The technology exists to begin their phase-out. The models are there to follow. The remaining question is no longer whether gas-powered leaf blowers should be phased out, but whether lawmakers are willing to overcome industry resistance and finish the job.

text:
Abstract

Carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries remain insufficiently addressed, with no unified international framework currently established to regulate and reduce these emissions. Given this, clarifying how carbon reduction responsibilities should be divided among states through appropriate normative principles is a prerequisite for collective international action. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) offers useful guidance for the dividing up mitigation obligations fairly and has become a fundamental principle of global climate governance. However, whether it applies to carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries remains uncertain. Examining where the CBDR principle came from and how it has developed gives us a solid basis for its application in this field. First, carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries create climate change risks that affect all states, which points to shared responsibility for mitigation under the principle of international cooperation. Second, developed countries’ historical responsibility for high-sea fishery emissions, along with developing countries’ relatively limited financial and technological capacities and the legal foundations established under the law of the sea, together justify differentiated mitigation responsibilities among states. Nevertheless, applying the CBDR principle to high-sea fisheries runs into several practical challenges, including selecting an appropriate implementation pathway, identifying responsible actors, and determining differentiated obligations. To address these challenges, this study proposes several recommendations, including better coordination between the climate change regime and the high-sea fisheries governance framework, factoring catch volume into the criteria for allocating mitigation responsibilities, and strengthening financial mechanisms to support developing countries in reducing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries.

1 Introduction

Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations have now hit record levels ( WMO, 2025), and achieving the Paris Agreement’s temperature goals will require emission reductions across a much broader range of sectors ( Williamson, 2016). The fishing industry, as a strategic sector closely linked to food security, international trade, and the marine environment, relies heavily on fossil fuels, thereby generating substantial carbon emissions. Although high seas fisheries account for only 4.2% of global annual marine capture fisheries production ( Schiller et al, 2018), they predominantly rely on large distant-water fishing fleets to exploit high-value transboundary and highly migratory fish stocks, resulting in relatively high fuel consumption and carbon emissions (). Carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries represent a global problem marked by significant negative externalities, yet the international legal framework has not established specific rules governing their mitigation. Collective action at the international level is essential for overcoming governance challenges these emissions pose, but any coordinated international action must first settle how mitigation responsibilities should be allocated among states. The evolution of global climate governance shows that disputes among states have frequently centered on how mitigation responsibilities should be shared. In fact, slow progress on collective international action owes much to persistent disagreements over burden-sharing arrangements (). Here, the international law of the sea regime, centered on the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), neither addresses carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries nor offers any principles for allocating mitigation responsibilities. In contrast, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), along with the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement, established CBDR as a founding principle for allocating climate-mitigation obligations. Since these instruments do not directly address carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, it is still unclear whether CBDR principle can be extended to this emerging area of international environmental governance ( Klerk, 2025).

Most existing scholarship has focused on how CBDR applies to areas such as high-sea environmental protection and international shipping, while its application to fishery-related carbon mitigation has received comparatively limited attention. Wang and Pan (2024) argued that CBDR has gradually become an important guiding principle in high sea environmental governance, although its implementation still faces challenges tied to inter-regime coordination and practical enforcement. Kopela (2013) noted that applying CBDR to emissions reduction in international shipping could bring about carbon leakage, regulatory avoidance, and distortions in market competition. Yang (2026) further noted that the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) legal culture and regulatory framework rest on developing uniform, non-discriminatory, and depoliticized technical standards, which are a key reason why the organization resists incorporating CBDR. Building on these discussions, a growing number of studies have begun asking whether CBDR can also offer a normative framework for fishery-related carbon mitigation. proposed applying CBDR to fishery emission reduction through a NDC mechanism. Zou (2021) also stressed the importance of examining CBDR’s potential applicability to fishery governance. More recently, Wang et al. (2025) argued that applying CBDR is essential to ensure equitable carbon mitigation across different regions within the global fishery system. However, the existing literature has not systematically examined the legal foundations for extending the principle to high-sea fisheries, or the specific ways such an application could work in practice. Limited scholarly attention has gone to the legal basis for applying CBDR to carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, the institutional constraints stemming from existing law of the sea and fishery governance regimes, and how differentiated mitigation responsibilities could be implemented in practice.

This study argues that CBDR, as a fundamental principle of international environmental law, applies to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries and should be the primary normative basis for allocating mitigation responsibilities among states. Against this background, the study is structured into three parts. The first part examines foundations for applying the principle of CBDR to carbon mitigation in high-seas fisheries. It begins by tracing the historical evolution of CBDR in international environmental law before assessing its legal applicability to carbon emission reduction in high-seas fisheries. The second part turns to the practical difficulties and governance challenges involved in implementing CBDR. It focuses on three interrelated questions: whether carbon mitigation should be pursued through the international climate regime or the high-seas fisheries governance regime, how mitigation responsibilities should be allocated among states, and how the substantive content of differentiated responsibilities should be defined. The third part offers recommendations for making a CBDR-based approach to carbon mitigation in high-sea fisheries more effective and feasible.

2 The principle of CBDR and carbon emission reduction in high seas fisheries

2.1 History of CBDR principle

The CBDR principle requires states to pursue common objectives while taking on differentiated obligations based on their socioeconomic circumstances and historical contributions to the environmental problems concerned ( Sands et al., 2012). This principle originated from the idea of equity in international law. In the field of international environmental law, the 1972 Stockholm Declaration is generally seen as the earliest international instrument to reflect the thinking behind CBDR ( Stone, 2004). Although the Stockholm Declaration never mentioned CBDR directly, Principle 12 set out two elements that later became central to the principle: first, recognition of developing countries’ particular circumstances and special needs, and second, the provision of additional financial and technological assistance from developed to developing countries ( Wang, 2025). This preferential treatment for developing countries is carried through into the 1974 United Nations General Assembly Declaration on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order. The most generally accepted formula of CBDR, though, comes from is the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, where Principles 6 and 7 address different aspects of CBDR. Principle 6 states that “the special situation and needs of developing countries, particularly the least developed and those most environmentally vulnerable, shall be given special priority.” Principle 7 further goes “States have common but differentiated responsibilities in view of the different contributions to global environmental degradation. The developed countries acknowledge the responsibility that they bear in the international pursuit of sustainable development in view of the pressures their societies place on the global environment and of the technologies and financial resources they command” ( United Nations, 1992). Rajamani breaks CBDR down into two interconnected dimensions: “common responsibility” and “differentiated responsibility.” The first comes from the notion of “common concern” and sits within the principle of international cooperation: since environmental challenges have gone global, all states face shared risks, which calls for collective efforts to prevent transboundary harm. The second reflects differences among states in their historical contributions to environmental degradation and their respective capacity to address it, thereby justifying differentiated treatment in how environmental responsibilities are allocated ( Rajamani, 2000). Compared with other principles of international environmental law, such as the polluter pays and precautionary principles, CBDR works to translate the concepts of intergenerational and intragenerational equity into interstate equity, particularly by addressing fairness concerns between developed and developing countries.

In global climate governance, developed countries have traditionally argued that all states should take on obligations to limit and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. However, developing countries have pushed back, insisting on common but differentiated responsibilities in addressing climate change. This position rests on three main points: the historical emissions of developed countries are a major driver of current global climate change; developing countries’ right to development deserves priority protection; developing countries generally lack sufficient financial resources and technological capacity to respond effectively to climate change. Ultimately, this principle made its way into the preamble and Article 3(1) of the UNFCCC, and was later reaffirmed, in different forms, by the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement. It should be noted that, as emerging economies’ share of GHG has grown, developed countries have become increasingly reluctant to accept a rigid, binary split between “developed countries” and “developing countries” ( Stone, 2004). Their argument is that emerging economies should now shoulder greater mitigation responsibilities. This pressure helped pushed the CBDR principle under the Paris Agreement toward a more dynamic approach, one grounded in states’ respective capabilities and national circumstances ( Rajamani, 2016). However, CBDR principle has not been abandoned. The rising emissions of emerging economies neither undermine the fundamental rationale that developed countries bear historical responsibility for climate change, nor do they mean developing countries’ development rights and adaptive capacities are now fully secured. Articles 2(2) and 4 of the Paris Agreement can still be understood as carrying forward the CBDR principle within today’s climate governance framework.

2.2 Applying the principle of CBDR to carbon emission reduction in high seas fisheries

Globally, there are 53 regional fisheries organizations, of which 17 regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs) hold management mandates for high-sea fisheries. These RFMOs include both developed and developing countries (see Table 1). As with the application of the CBDR principle in global climate governance, the fundamental basis for applying this principle to emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries still holds. States should not only share common responsibilities for reducing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries but should also recognize differentiated responsibilities among states based on their respective circumstances and contributions.

2.2.1 Governing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries globally means all states must share common mitigation responsibilities

First, carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries create climate change risks that affect all states. Existing scientific studies have shown that high-sea fishing activities produce both direct and indirect carbon emissions. Direct carbon emissions mainly come from fossil fuels burned by fishing vessels operating on high seas. A study on large-scale purse seine tuna fisheries in the Indian Ocean found that the global tuna fleet likely consumed around 2.5 million tonnes of fuel in 2009, producing around 9 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2 -eq) in GHG emissions. These emissions account for roughly 4.5%–5% of global fishing vessel emissions. Moreover, as climate change drives the geographical redistribution of fish stocks, fishing vessels increasingly have to travel longer distances, which could push fuel consumption and carbon emissions even higher ( Madin and Macreadie, 2015). Indirect carbon emissions result from the ecological impact of certain fishing practices. For example, bottom trawling in high-sea fisheries releases substantial GHG from marine ecosystems into the atmosphere (). Some studies suggest that such emissions may rival those from the international aviation sector ( Sala et al., 2021). Whether direct or indirect, these carbon emissions, in the absence of effective regulations, will contribute to global climate change and expose all states to climate-related risks. Second, collective action among all states to reduce carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries serves their common interests. Although only a limited number of countries carry out large-scale high-sea fishing operations, more than 100 countries take part in high-sea fishery activities to varying degrees. When it comes to addressing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, no individual state can solve the problem alone; collective action through international cooperation is essential. The global climate system, as a global public good, is non-rivalrous, meaning that one actor’s use or enjoyment of climate stability does not diminish what is available to others. However, without coordinated international measures to reduce carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, individual states may lack sufficient incentives to act in defense of shared interests. For these reasons, states should share common responsibilities for cutting carbon emissions in high-sea fisheries. This reflects the core rationale of the “common responsibility” dimension of the CBDR principle, namely that global environmental challenges require collective responses from the international community as a whole.

2.2.2 States should assume differentiated responsibilities when it comes to reducing carbon emissions in high-sea fisheries

First, developed countries have historically emitted far more carbon from high-sea fisheries than developing countries; therefore, they should bear responsibility for their historical emissions. Unlike other forms of marine pollution, carbon emissions are not merely mobile pollutants tied directly to vessels; they also build up in the atmosphere and cause long-term environmental effects. Therefore, historical accumulation of emissions has to be factored into how mitigation responsibilities are allocated (). Although high-sea fisheries are not currently exclusively dominated by developed countries in terms of catch volumes, global marine fishing activities has largely been controlled by a handful of industrialized countries since the mid-twentieth century. These countries gained major early advantages in distant-water fishing capacity, marine resource exploitation, and fisheries technology. In the 1960s, as coastal fishing grounds at home became overexploited, fishing fleets from the Soviet Union, Japan, and European countries began expanding into offshore and high-sea areas, thereby speeding up the development of modern distant-water fisheries (). This history indicates that developed countries produced substantially greater carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries than developing countries over time.

Second, developing countries generally do not have the financial resources or technological capacity to cut carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries. Low-carbon conversion of fishing vessels usually requires significant financial investment. In September 2024, a European Commission report found that converting fishing vessels to the most feasible biodiesel option would need an average funding gap of approximately EUR 357,000 per vessel, which is well beyond wat many developing countries can afford (). Meanwhile, key low-carbon fishing vessel technologies sit mostly in developed countries, leaving developing countries with little room for independent research, development, and large-scale deployment. Currently, the core technologies behind fishing vessel decarbonization are largely held by developed economies, with the European Union, Norway, United Kingdom, and Japan leading the way in low- and zero-carbon maritime innovation ( UNCTAD, 2023). Accordingly, financial and technological support from developed countries is a fundamental prerequisite for helping developing countries to reduce carbon emissions in high-sea fisheries.

Third, giving developing countries differentiated responsibilities for high-sea fishery carbon mitigation are supported by legal foundations. Articles 202 and 203 of the UNCLOS expressly require states to provide scientific and technical assistance to developing countries to protect and preserve the marine environment. These provisions also give developing countries a claim to preferential treatment when it comes to financial and technical assistance and access to specialized services from relevant international organizations. Therefore, applying CBDR to carbon mitigation in high-sea fisheries fits well within the existing legal framework of the law of the sea, which already recognizes the need to balance environmental protection obligations against differences in states’ historical contributions and capacities ( Wang and Pan, 2024). Article 202 of the UNCLOS recognizes that least developed and developing countries need help fulfilling their obligations to protect and preserve the marine environment. The provision requires states, either directly or through competent international organizations, to provide scientific and technological assistance to developing countries. This obligation reflects the concern raised in Article 194 of UNCLOS, which requires states to take measures to protect and preserve the marine environment using “the best practicable means at their disposal and in accordance with their capabilities” ( Nordquist et al., 2002). Specifically, the scientific and technological assistance envisaged under Article 202 falls into three categories. The first is assistance aimed at promoting scientific, educational, technological, and other forms of support for developing countries. To this end, developing countries can receive assistance from other states in areas such as the training of scientific and technical personnel, participation in relevant international programs, obtaining necessary equipment and facilities, and building capacity to manufacture such equipment. The second covers assistance designed to mitigate the impact of major incidents causing serious pollution in developing countries. The third provides appropriate assistance to developing countries in preparing environmental impact assessments. Consequently, states should help developing countries carry out environmental impact assessments related to reducing carbon emissions in high-sea fisheries. Such assistance would further strengthen developing countries’ ability to participate effectively in international efforts to cut emissions from high-sea fisheries.

Article 203 of the UNCLOS further provides that developing countries may be entitled to preferential treatment with respect to the allocation of financial resources and technical assistance, as well as access to specialized services provided by international organizations. This preferential treatment applies where assistance is intended to prevent, reduce, and control pollution of the marine environment, or to minimize its effects. The international community still disagrees over whether carbon emissions constitute “pollution of the marine environment” within the meaning of Article 1(1)(4) of UNCLOS; therefore, the legal characterization of carbon emissions from high seas fisheries remains unsettled. As a result, assistance aimed at enhancing developing countries’ capacity to reduce carbon emissions from high seas fisheries may not fully satisfy the objective of “preventing, reducing, and controlling pollution of the marine environment.” Nevertheless, such assistance may still help minimize the adverse effects of marine pollution. On this basis, developing countries should be entitled to preferential treatment under Article 203 of the UNCLOS for assistance related to carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries.

In addition, Article 5 of the 1995 Agreement for the Implementation of the Provisions of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982 Relating to the Conservation and Management of Straddling Fish Stocks and Highly Migratory Fish Stocks (Fish Stocks Agreement) requires states, in establishing conservation and management measures for straddling fish stocks and highly migratory fish stocks, to take into account the special requirements of developing states. Articles 24, 25, and 26 of the Fish Stocks Agreement go further, specifying obligations to consider the needs of developing states. However, this application rests on the assumption that carbon emissions reduction measures count as “conservation and management measures.” According to Article 1(1)(b) of the Fish Stocks Agreement, this term refer to measures designed and applied to conserve and manage one or more species of living marine resources and consistent with the relevant rules of international law reflected in UNCLOS and the Agreement. Read alongside Article 5(1)(b) of the Fish Stocks Agreement, the scope of “conservation and management measures” should be understood broadly: any measure capable of maintaining or restoring fish stocks to levels that can produce the maximum sustainable yield could qualify. Existing scientific evidence indicates that higher levels of global warming will reduce fishery productivity across an increasing number of marine regions (). In contrast, reducing carbon emissions help sustain higher levels of marine fishery productivity. This implies that carbon emission reduction measures in high-sea fisheries play an important role in maintaining and restoring fish stocks at levels capable of producing the maximum sustainable yield and should therefore count as “conservation and management measures” under the Fish Stocks Agreement (). Accordingly, Article 5 of the Fish Stocks Agreement offers a legal basis for applying the CBDR principle when adopting carbon emission reduction measures in high-sea fisheries. By requiring states to consider the special needs of developing countries when formulating and implementing fishery conservation and management measures, this provision reflects the broader normative logic of differentiated responsibilities within the international fishery governance regime.

3 Difficulties in applying the principle of CBDR to carbon emission reduction in high seas fisheries

Although the application of the CBDR principle to carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries rests on legal and normative foundations, several unresolved issues stand in the way of effective implementation.

3.1 Should the climate governance regime or the high seas fisheries governance regime serve as the implementation pathway?

There are two potential pathways for applying the CBDR principle to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries: extending the existing climate governance regime to cover the carbon emissions generated by high-sea fisheries or incorporating the CBDR principle into the existing high-sea fishery governance framework. However, both run into significant difficulties.

Starting with the first pathway: the UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol, and Paris Agreement have all established the CBDR principle as a fundamental principle for responding to climate change, and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) went further still, recognizing in its advisory opinion on Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change that “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” is a fundamental principle of the climate change treaty regime (). Even so, none of these climate instruments clearly define CBDR’s scope of application or provide a comprehensive framework for carbon emissions from transboundary activities (). Instead, they tend to treat certain international mobile sources of carbon emissions separately. The existing climate treaty regime is built largely around controlling and reducing GHG emissions within national jurisdiction, with mitigation responsibilities generally allocated based on where emissions occur. Consequently, activities that cross national borders, such as international aviation and shipping conducted over the high seas and airspace, have never really fit into the national mitigation framework set up under climate agreements. For example, the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories call for national inventories to include GHG emissions and removal within national territories and offshore areas under national jurisdiction, while Section 3.5.3 of the Guidelines explicitly states that emissions from international water-borne navigation should be reported separately from domestic emissions and excluded from national totals. This shows that these emissions have historically sat outside the mitigation framework under climate treaties. Ever since the first Conference of the Parties (COP) to the UNFCCC in 1995, how to treat carbon emissions from international aviation and shipping has remained highly contested (), largely because attributing emissions among states is so difficult. This became particularly contentious during the Kyoto Protocol negotiations. In its deliberations, the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) under the UNFCCC identified five possible allocation options as the basis for further work in 1996: no allocation; allocation to the state where marine fuel was sold; allocation to the state where the transport company was located or the aircraft or vessel was registered or operated; allocation to the state of departure or destination of the aircraft or vessel, with possible emission-sharing between such states; and allocation to the state of departure or destination of passengers or cargo, again with possible sharing arrangements (). Owing to the political impasse over emissions allocation ( Oberthür, 2003), UNFCCC Parties ultimately handed the issue off to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and IMO, with Article 2(2) of the Kyoto Protocol assigning responsibility to these two specialized international organizations. Similar to international aviation and shipping, high-sea fisheries carry strong international and transboundary dimensions. Therefore, incorporating carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries into the existing climate treaty regime would also raise difficult questions of fairness and feasibility of allocation methods, and could well stir up political disagreements among states. The specific allocation challenges are discussed in the following sections.

Now, for the second pathway, the main challenge is that there is no single competent international organization comparable to the ICAO and IMO for high-sea fisheries governance. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and numerous RFMOs are primarily responsible for high-sea fishery management. Every part of the high sea falls under the management of at least one RFMO (). In 1965, the Thirteenth Session of the FAO Conference established the Committee on Fisheries (COFI), which, as a subsidiary body of the FAO Council, regularly offers global recommendations and policy advice to governments, regional fisheries organizations, civil society organizations, the private sector, and other international stakeholders (). The 17 existing RFMOs responsible for high-sea fishery management each hold independent legal personalities under international law. They work independently from one another and have only decentralized and indirect guidance relationships with the FAO Committee on Fisheries. Because of this fragmented structure, applying the CBDR principle to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries would still require building consensus individually among the members of each RFMO. However, many differences in RMFO membership structures make it difficult to achieve uniform application of the CBDR principle in high-sea fishery carbon mitigation. For example, RFMOs, such as the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Organization (NAFO), where developed countries make up the majority of members, may place greater emphasis on the “common responsibility” side of CBDR. By contrast, RFMOs such as the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC), which has a larger proportion of developing country members, may give more weight to the “differentiated responsibility” side. Therefore, the decentralized and fragmented institutional structure of high-sea fishery governance is likely to lead to divergent interpretations and uneven application of the CBDR principle across different RFMOs. This institutional fragmentation stands as a significant obstacle to building a coherent and coordinated approach to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries.

Another challenge is that it remains unclear whether RFMOs have the authority to adopt carbon emission reduction measures. Although the constituent instruments of various RFMOs require them to protect marine ecosystems, their main goal is long-term conservation and sustainable utilization of specific fishery resources. For example, Article 9(2) of the Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR Convention) clearly states that the Commission may adopt “such other conservation measures as are necessary for the fulfillment of the objective of the Convention,” which could offer a legal basis for adopting carbon emission reduction measures in high seas fisheries. Nevertheless, this should only apply if climate change-induced impacts on marine ecosystems pose a serious threat to the conservation and sustainable utilization of marine resources in the high seas. However, in practice, clear criteria for determining the severity of such threats are lacking. Therefore, although certain RFMO mandates could be read as allowing climate-related measures under a broad understanding of conservation obligations, whether carbon emission reduction measures truly fall within existing RFMO mandates remains legally uncertain. This ambiguity could further limit the incorporation of the CBDR principle into the high-sea fishery governance framework.

Moreover, existing high-sea fisheries agreements do not include provisions for differentiated responsibilities among their parties. Even though RFMOs have the authority to adopt carbon emission reduction measures for high-sea fisheries, their ability to differentiate obligations among states is still limited by provisions of existing fishery agreements. Looking at the provisions in the constitutive instruments of the 17 existing RFMOs shows that none of these agreements provide specific preferential treatment or differentiated obligations for developing country parties when it comes to marine environment protection obligations (see Table 2). Instead, these agreements generally stress that all RFMO members should take on equivalent obligations to protect marine ecosystems. This means that the carbon emission reduction measures adopted by the RFMOs would, in principle, require equal compliance from all parties, leaving little legal room for incorporating differentiated responsibilities among states. Furthermore, RFMOs currently lack dedicated mechanisms to monitor how the CBDR principle is implemented. Unlike Article 15 of the Paris Agreement, which sets up a specific mechanism to facilitate implementation and promote compliance, existing RFMOs rely on various compliance mechanisms, including vessel-monitoring systems, observer programs, boarding and inspection procedures, and catch-documentation schemes. However, these mechanisms were mainly designed to prevent overfishing and ensure compliance with fishery conservation measures, not to monitor and facilitate differentiated carbon emission reduction obligations. As a result, they are unlikely to provide an effective institutional basis for overseeing CBDR implementation in the context of high-sea fishery carbon mitigation.
