text:
In the high desert of Emery County, Utah, the sun arrives hard and early. Nearly a million panels now catch it before most of the county has made coffee. The rows run so far in every direction that standing at the edge of the array feels less like visiting a power plant and more like watching the land itself turn to face the sky. Something else is visible from the edge of the field, though, and that detail changes everything about the story.

A county that ran on coal, and knew it

Emery County built its identity around coal. The Hunter and Huntington generating stations, two of Utah’s largest coal fired plants, anchored the local economy for decades, and the infrastructure they needed, roads, substations, high voltage lines strung across the canyon country, shaped the landscape as surely as the Colorado Plateau itself. When coal employment peaked in Utah in the early 1990s, Emery County was at the center of it.

That history left physical marks. The transmission corridors punched into this remote stretch of eastern Utah cost a fortune to build, and they were designed for one purpose: moving the output of burning coal west toward the cities. Nobody who drove a survey stake into this ground in 1970 imagined what those lines would eventually carry.

The solar half fills the batteries through the afternoon, and the batteries pay out through the evening hours when the sun is gone and demand is still climbing.

What it takes to fill 2,500 acres

Construction began in September 2024 and required 849,268 labor hours. That figure is abstract until you try to picture it: if a single worker put in a full 40-hour week without interruption, it would take more than 400 years. Hundreds of workers spread across two Utah desert winters and one fierce summer to get it done.

The Green River Energy Center now generates 800 megawatts from 996,000 solar panels across 2,500 acres, and the $1.6 billion project used steel and the vast majority of other materials made in the U.S. Every panel had to be driven into ground that routinely freezes and bakes within the same calendar year. The hardware footprint also includes 484 Tesla Megapacks, and those batteries are not decoration.

The battery trick hiding in plain sight

The center pairs 400 MW of solar photovoltaic generation with 400 MW and 1,600 megawatt hours of battery energy storage. The solar half fills the batteries through the afternoon, and the batteries pay out through the evening hours when the sun is gone and demand is still climbing. A plant that runs on sunshine can now keep the lights on after dark.

In 2024, rPlus Energies amended a power purchase agreement with PacifiCorp to quadruple the battery storage capacity at the project then under development. Someone decided halfway through that good was not good enough, and grid operators tend to read a number like 1,600 megawatt hours twice.

Coal’s wires, the sun’s electricity

Here is the twist that the county’s older residents notice first. The project has nearby access to transmission lines originally built for the Hunter and Huntington coal fired plants, making it an even better fit for the site. At Green River, that transmission bill was paid decades ago by coal, and the industry being replaced left behind the very infrastructure needed to replace it.

rPlus Energies announced commercial operations on June 23, 2026, and CEO Luigi Resta said at the commissioning ceremony: “This project exists because of this country, this community, and the long legacy of energy production here.” That is not a talking point; it is geography. rPlus Chief of Staff Theresa Foxley added that at any given moment the plant could be satisfying roughly 10 percent of Utah’s total load, enough to power some 110,000 homes, making it the largest solar and battery operation in Rocky Mountain Power’s six state footprint. On the day the ribbon was cut, the smokestacks of the Hunter Power Plant were visible in the background, still standing a few miles away across the scrubland.

What this means for the grid changing around it

In 2024, Utah Governor Spencer Cox announced Operation Gigawatt, an initiative aimed at doubling Utah’s energy production over the next ten years. As the largest solar and storage facility within PacifiCorp’s territory, Green River is the clearest signal yet that the state intends to reach that goal. The project is also investing locally through $375,000 in scholarships and a $45,000 donation to the Ferron Fire Department.

In the first quarter of 2026, 91 percent of all new grid capacity came from solar and storage, the highest quarterly share the duo has ever recorded. Green River’s location and its repurposed coal era wires give it a weight the raw numbers alone do not capture. It is proof that solar economics can reach deep into places that once seemed permanently beyond their range.

title: New Science Says Scrapping A Working Gas Car For An EV Is Usually Greener
description:
Their new study in Science compares continued operation of functional combustion vehicles with permanently scrapping them and replacing them with battery-electric vehicles.
They vary vehicle efficiency, annual mileage, battery manufacturing emissions, battery size and regional electricity emissions instead of assuming one conveniently favorable EV case.
The emissions from manufacturing the gasoline car are already in the atmosphere, so Campbell and Geyer treat them as sunk.
Keeping the gasoline car avoids one new manufacturing event, but it also preserves years of recurring fuel consumption and combustion emissions.
Destroying a working vehicle early can therefore remove a future rung from that used-car ladder.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

“The greenest car is the one already built” has been one of the more durable arguments against replacing internal combustion cars with EVs. It sounds sensible enough. Manufacturing a new vehicle has a carbon cost, while continuing to drive an existing car avoids another manufacturing event. But that framing quietly treats all of the gasoline the existing car will burn over the rest of its life as if it were free of emissions.

In 2024, I argued that a modern version of Cash for Clunkers should pay people to retire internal combustion vehicles early when they replace them with electric ones. I described that as a strong opinion, weakly held because the lifecycle objection was obvious. If a gasoline car has already been manufactured and still works, perhaps keeping it running until the wheels fall off really is greener than building another vehicle to replace it.

J. Elliott Campbell of UC Santa Cruz and Roland Geyer of UC Santa Barbara have now done the lifecycle work that question needed. Their new study in Science compares continued operation of functional combustion vehicles with permanently scrapping them and replacing them with battery-electric vehicles. They vary vehicle efficiency, annual mileage, battery manufacturing emissions, battery size and regional electricity emissions instead of assuming one conveniently favorable EV case. Their results make the environmental case for early retirement considerably stronger than I expected.

For a representative production-weighted SUV on the average US grid, retiring the combustion vehicle in its second year and replacing it with a battery EV reduced cumulative emissions over the study’s 16-year period by 44%. Manufacturing the replacement EV creates the expected carbon bump, but the lower operating emissions repay that manufacturing debt in about three years. Earlier retirement produced the largest cumulative benefit because more years of gasoline combustion were avoided.

The broader sensitivity analysis is more important than that single SUV example. Across the combinations the researchers tested, 92% of modeled scenarios produced lower emissions from early retirement, while fleet-average assumptions produced a 58% benefit. The full range ran from an 82% reduction to a 77% increase in deliberately extreme cases, so this is not an argument that replacement always wins. It does, however, make clear that avoiding a second manufacturing event is much less decisive than the familiar slogan suggests.

The biggest driver in the study was how much fuel the old vehicle would continue burning, not the manufacturing emissions of the replacement battery. Campbell and Geyer varied battery-production emissions from 52 to 173 kilograms of CO₂e per kilowatt-hour, a very wide range, and that shifted the net retirement benefit by only about 13 percentage points. Differences in vehicle operating efficiency created more than twice as much variability.

There is a fairly straightforward accounting reason for that. The emissions from manufacturing the gasoline car are already in the atmosphere, so Campbell and Geyer treat them as sunk. The relevant comparison starts today: how much future gasoline will the old vehicle burn, and how does that compare with the manufacturing and electricity emissions of the EV that replaces it? Keeping the gasoline car avoids one new manufacturing event, but it also preserves years of recurring fuel consumption and combustion emissions.

That does not make every functioning gasoline vehicle a sensible candidate for the crusher. The study finds annual mileage thresholds below which the replacement EV’s manufacturing emissions are not recovered: about 7,054 kilometers for cars, 6,837 kilometers for SUVs and 10,794 kilometers for trucks. Those are well below the roughly 20,000 kilometers in the researchers’ average case, but very lightly driven vehicles clearly exist and can be better left in service.

Efficient hybrids and some plug-in hybrids are also poor targets, as are cases where inefficient EVs are charged from particularly dirty grids. In the continuous analysis, the climate advantage can disappear when EV electricity consumption exceeds roughly 30 kWh per 100 kilometers and grid emissions rise above 500 kilograms of CO₂ per MWh. Under the assumptions tested, replacing a PHEV car with a BEV increased emissions by 11%, while the SUV result was close to neutral. A policy that simply rewarded people for destroying any running combustion vehicle would ignore exactly the distinctions the study makes visible.

High-mileage pickups, inefficient SUVs and other vehicles burning a lot of fuel are much more attractive targets. That also lines up with earlier modeling from Resources for the Future, which found that targeting scrappage payments at expected future emissions rather than simply vehicle age could roughly halve the public cost per ton of emissions avoided. A flat bounty pays just as much to retire a lightly driven efficient car as it does to remove a heavily driven gas guzzler, which is convenient administratively but poor climate economics.

The United States then runs into a second problem that lifecycle analysis alone cannot solve. Americans are unusually dependent on private automobiles, including in large cities where people elsewhere shift much more strongly toward public transportation. Prieto-Curiel and Ospina’s The ABC of mobility found that 91.9% of trips in its US and Canadian urban sample were by car, compared with 44.9% in Europe and 18.8% in East Asia. It also found that US car dependence barely changed as cities became larger.

For a large share of Americans, access to a car is therefore less a consumer preference than a practical requirement for working, shopping, taking children to school, seeing a doctor and participating in society. That dependence matters because the cheap cars bought by lower-income households usually began life higher up the income ladder. Federal Reserve survey data cited in the Briefing found that about two-thirds of lower-income people who had recently acquired a vehicle bought used, while 78% of privately purchased used vehicles cost less than $10,000.

New vehicles bought or leased by wealthier households, companies, rental fleets and governments eventually become six-year-old, ten-year-old and fifteen-year-old vehicles, moving down through progressively cheaper portions of the market. Destroying a working vehicle early can therefore remove a future rung from that used-car ladder. The emissions benefit may be real, but so is the possibility that someone years later has one fewer affordable car available to buy.

Campbell and Geyer acknowledge that vehicle resale creates system effects, although their study is primarily a lifecycle analysis rather than a model of household transportation affordability. The policy problem is therefore broader than deciding whether a particular ICE vehicle produces fewer lifecycle emissions if it is scrapped. The United States also has to ensure that households which would have bought those cars farther down the depreciation curve still have affordable transportation available.

A modern vehicle-retirement program should be designed around both issues. Scrappage incentives should reflect fuel economy, recent mileage, remaining expected life and the local electricity mix rather than simply the age of the vehicle. Used EVs should qualify fully as replacements, with additional support for households that otherwise could not afford one. Efficient, lightly driven combustion cars should often be repaired rather than scrapped, while high-mileage pickups and SUVs deserve much stronger incentives for early retirement.

Fleet turnover is important as well. Governments, rental companies, delivery fleets and corporations rack up kilometers quickly, so electrifying them early gets a large immediate emissions benefit while also putting three-to-five-year-old EVs into the used market relatively quickly. Battery-health certificates, dependable charging and reasonable financing would make those vehicles much more useful to secondhand buyers. If supplies of sub-$10,000 or sub-$15,000 cars start tightening sharply in a region, the retirement incentive can be reduced rather than continuing to subsidize vehicle destruction regardless of what is happening in the used market.

That approach is more complicated than another Cash for Clunkers program, but the underlying climate case is now much firmer. Campbell and Geyer show that retiring a functioning combustion vehicle early can substantially reduce cumulative emissions, and that the most useful targets can be identified from mileage, efficiency and electricity emissions rather than guesswork. A high-mileage pickup burning a lot of gasoline is an obvious candidate. A Prius traveling 5,000 kilometers a year on a dirty grid probably is not.

The harder task for US policy is making the fleet turn over faster without treating affordable transportation as somebody else’s problem. That means retiring the vehicles responsible for the most future combustion while accelerating enough new and used EV supply that the bottom of the market becomes electric too. The climate transition and the used-car ladder do not have to work against each other, but getting both right requires considerably more thought than simply paying people to crush old cars.

title: Lessons from Energy Politics for our Polarized America - The Fulcrum
description:
The Antiquities Act delegates to the president the power to create national monuments, but the power to diminish them belongs strictly to Congress.
China's position in clean energy manufacturing is not a policy choice that tariffs can alter in the near term.
Those materials are not optional for clean energy manufacturing.
The case for domestic clean energy manufacturing is not frivolous.
The supply chain for that deployment runs, in most critical components, through Chinese manufacturing.
text:
The Antiquities Act delegates to the president the power to create national monuments, but the power to diminish them belongs strictly to Congress. Trump’s attempt to slash these boundaries is an unlawful usurpation of legislative power that defies more than a century of legal precedent. But then, what else is new? Still, while Roosevelt explored the wild west and was inspired to designate lands worth protecting, Trump is stripping those protections, sight unseen, to harvest parts to sell to the highest bidder. He has already eliminated over 16 times more land than Teddy protected. It may be predictable, but it is despicable.

Perhaps Trump just has terrible taste when it comes to what is worth preserving for antiquity. His proclamations modifying the monuments, which condescendingly explain why 90% of the monuments were just not monument-worthy enough, are illuminating. He writes that the original designations as national monuments were “premised on the purported need to protect items that are not historic landmarks…or objects of historic or scientific interest.” He then mocks a list of what he calls “generic topographic and geologic features.” Of Grand Staircase-Escalante, they include: “‘vast and austere landscape[s],’ ‘sedimentary rock layers,’ and ‘bold plateaus and multihued cliffs.’” Of Bears Ears: “‘deep sandstone canyons, broad desert mesas, towering monoliths, forested mountaintops dotted with lush meadows’ and ‘low bluffs and high mesas.’” Trump concludes: “These generic features…do not become “landmarks,” “structures,” or “objects of historic or scientific interest” worthy of protection under the Antiquities Act simply because they are scenic.” It is the point of view one imagines ChatGPT, with its zero senses, might have.

To suggest that sedimentary rock layers are not objects of scientific interest is the mark of someone who has never cared for science. In reality, to quote the proclamation that Trump is reversing, the sedimentary rock layers are “unobscured by vegetation, offering a clear view to understanding the Earth’s geological development…[making it] one of the world’s great paleontological laboratories.” And to state there are no objects of historic interest is deeply dismissive, offensive, and inaccurate. These lands include a rich human history that begins with ancient indigenous people (documented even in petroglyphs and pictograph panels–another feature of these monuments). To imply otherwise is an erasure.

On that note, Trump’s desire to privatize these lands is merely the latest chapter in a legacy of American colonialism. Historically, treaties between the U.S. and sovereign Indian nations were routinely coercive, misleading, and signed under duress, and in several landmark cases, the Supreme Court invented loopholes in property law to diminish Native American land claims. Now, Trump tries once more to illegally claim land that is not his, turning to a tired trope. To add insult to injury, Bears Ears happens to be the very first national monument established at the request of a historic coalition of Tribal Nations. If we are not going to actively return this land through the “Land Back” movement, the absolute minimum we can do is treasure it and ensure it remains for future generations. Trump’s actions are unforgivable.

Fortunately, guess who supports protection for public lands: the public. Polling shows that 91% of Western voters support existing monument designations. Three in four Americans actively oppose expanded drilling and mining on our public lands (it’s bipartisan!). The fact is, nobody wants this except the beneficiaries of deals like these, who apparently can look upon “forested mountaintops dotted with lush meadows” and not see past the dollar signs. One of my favorite things about public lands is the spirit of equality in a place where everyone is sleeping in a tent and the campsites are first-come, first-served. Perhaps it is that exact spirit—or the distinct lack of thread count—which generates such contempt for the land among oligarchs.

It turns out, Trump may have only ever visited three national parks or monuments: Everglades, Mount Rushmore, and Gettysburg. He’s a billionaire and the leader of the free world, but with all that money and power, he’s never seen the sun rise at the Grand Canyon or a night sky peppered with stars in Joshua Tree. If he only looked into the bold plateaus and multihued cliffs of our planet, perhaps he would no longer find them generic and rather see the value in protecting them. Or not. In the meantime, he felt compelled to plaster his face on this year’s park passes, in violation of a federal requirement that the pass bear the winning wildlife scene from a national parks photo contest.

Still, this ongoing effort to loot the American commons begs the question: has anyone at the White House ever had a meaningful experience in nature? Been mesmerized watching a condor soar above a canyon? Or simply curious about the natural world? Pity for those people notwithstanding, given the evidence that they consider breathtaking natural wonders generic, at what point do they sell off the Grand Canyon, Yosemite, and Yellowstone for being mere scenery, too?

It should go without saying, but our grandest marvels are so much more than scenery. They are essential to our collective identity as a nation and to the health of our planet. They are also the backdrop for the history and culture of so many people in this country, from ancient tribes to college besties on a road trip. And they need our help. If we don’t want to see their destruction, we must sign petitions, support organizations like Veterans for Public Lands, and show up. It is exactly this kind of people-led advocacy that helped restore protections to these lands after 2017. We can do it again. We can also visit these vistas ourselves and share stories about the cactus wren and the Saguaro, or the wonder of watching a desert tortoise cross the road. We can spread the gospel: nature is worth protecting.

Julie Roland was a Naval Officer for ten years, deploying to both the South China Sea and the Persian Gulf as a helicopter pilot before separating in June 2025 as a Lieutenant Commander. She has a law degree from the University of San Diego, a Master of Laws from Columbia University, and is a member of the Truman National Security Project.

China's position in clean energy manufacturing is not a policy choice that tariffs can alter in the near term. It is the accumulated result of two decades of investment. Chinese renewable energy products now reach over 200 countries and meet more than 80 percent of global demand for photovoltaic modules and 70 percent of global demand for wind power equipment. In batteries and electric vehicles, the position is similar.

When the US raises tariffs on Chinese-made solar panels, Chinese manufacturers do not stop producing them. It is to route them through Malaysia, Vietnam, and Cambodia, sometimes with additional value-added steps to satisfy rules of origin. The Columbia analysis found that this transshipment pattern accelerated significantly after the 2025 tariff escalations. The result is that American solar projects import the same Chinese components, pay more for them, and wait longer for delivery.

The Busan trade deal included a notable concession on this front: China agreed to suspend its export controls on rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony, and graphite, and to issue general licenses for US end users. Those materials are not optional for clean energy manufacturing. They go into everything from battery cathodes to inverters to EV motors. When China restricted them in late 2025, US energy project timelines came under immediate pressure. The suspension bought time. It did not solve the underlying dependency.

US electricity consumers and grid operators absorb the downstream cost of supply chain friction. Solar project developers facing higher panel costs and longer lead times either delay projects, accept higher financing costs, or both. Utilities pass those costs into rate structures. The households that stand to benefit most from affordable clean energy, lower-income renters and homeowners in sun-belt states with high cooling costs, are precisely those least able to absorb higher electricity rates.

Meanwhile, China's position is strengthening regardless of the US tariff policy. China's 15th Five-Year Plan targets 3,600 gigawatts of wind and solar capacity by 2035, six times 2020 levels. The technology, the manufacturing scale, and the cost curves all point in one direction. American tariff policy cannot reverse that, but it can determine whether the US benefits from Chinese manufacturing capacity or pays a premium to partially avoid it.

The case for domestic clean energy manufacturing is not frivolous. Brookings Institution analysts have argued that grid-connected hardware with Chinese software or remote access capabilities raises legitimate cybersecurity concerns. A solar inverter that can be disabled remotely is a different category of risk from a pair of shoes. Those concerns warrant specific, technology-focused policy responses.

What they do not warrant is blanket tariffs on solar panels and battery cells that delay grid buildout without addressing the security concern. A Chinese-made panel with no connectivity hardware is not a cybersecurity threat. A Chinese-made inverter with embedded firmware and remote access capability may be. Policy should reflect that distinction. It currently does not.

There is also a competitive cost that rarely enters this debate. The IRA's 45X manufacturing tax credit has been the single most effective tool in building genuine domestic solar capacity, far more so than tariffs. Canary Media's analysis of the 2026 solar manufacturing landscape found that companies such as First Solar, Qcells, and Heliene have made real upstream progress, not because of import barriers, but because of investment incentives. Tariffs on Chinese panels have instead led to a perverse outcome: raising costs for the same domestic manufacturers they are meant to protect, since those manufacturers still depend on Chinese-origin cells and wafers with no adequate domestic substitutes at scale. Industrial policy that builds capacity and trade policy that raises costs for that capacity are working against each other. Washington has not resolved that contradiction.

The US has set energy independence and carbon reduction as simultaneous goals. Achieving both requires large-scale deployment of solar, wind, and battery storage in a compressed timeframe. The supply chain for that deployment runs, in most critical components, through Chinese manufacturing. A policy framework that acknowledges this reality and manages it through targeted security requirements, rather than blanket tariffs that raise costs without producing domestic capacity, is the only approach that serves both goals. The alternative is slower deployment, higher consumer energy costs, and continued dependence on the same Chinese supply chains, just routed through more countries and at greater expense.

Hugo Balta is the executive editor of The Fulcrum and the publisher of the Latino News Network.

text:
August has not been a good month for Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta. That’s good news for the rest of us.

Courts have dealt Zuckerberg major legal losses for his company’s failure to reckon with the harm that Facebook and Instagram have caused young people. Last week, a New Mexico state judge ordered Meta to pay $567 million for youth treatment and prevention programs. That’s on top of a $375 million penalty after a jury held Meta accountable for child safety failures. New Mexico prosecutors showed in court that the company’s design features enabled predators to sexually exploit children online.

These penalties against Meta add up to nearly $1 billion — an eye-popping figure for most of us but pocket change for a company valued at $1.5 trillion. Still, a panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals dealt Meta another blow last week when it said that more lawsuits against the company could proceed. Meta had argued that it was protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which says tech companies are not responsible for what their users post.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Not so fast, said the court. It explained that Section 230 is a defense against liability — not immunity from suit. Twenty-nine states led by California have sued Meta, accusing the company of promoting addictive behavior in young people. Meta disputes the claims and said damages could reach $1.4 trillion.

What strikes us about all this is that judges and juries are the ones stepping up to hold Big Tech accountable in light of Congress’ ongoing failure to regulate social media.

We’re holding out hope that lawmakers will do the right thing. The Kids Online Safety Act, a bill that would create social media parental controls and allow minors to opt out of personalized algorithms, recently cleared a committee to advance to the full Senate floor, where it has strong bipartisan support. The problem is the House, where a watered-down measure is preferred.

We urge our Texas delegation — particularly Sen. Ted Cruz, who has championed this cause — to keep at it. If the latest court rulings against Meta tell us anything, it’s that the drive for accountability is gaining momentum.

text:
TUCKER COUNTY, W.Va. -- Tucked in a deep-red district in West Virginia, two tiny tourist towns rest high up in the Allegheny Mountains along the Blackwater River, nestled alongside grand waterfalls, winding hollows and scenic overlooks.

And soon, 10,000 acres between the towns of Thomas and Davis and spanning into neighboring Grant County could become home to one of the "largest data center campuses in the world," its developers told the Wall Street Journal, including a new natural gas power plant with diesel backup generators and a solar facility -- although its public details keep changing.

Nikki Forrester, a resident and organizer with Tucker United, a group leading the charge against the data center and power plant, sat on a bench in early July along the few-block stretch of downtown Thomas, about a mile and a half away from the proposed site.

Almost every store window brandished signs opposing the data center complex, and Forrester estimated hundreds of citizens support her group, citing concerns about air and water pollution. Families with young children are especially concerned -- the elementary and middle school is nearby.

"It's the most energized ... and unified I've seen anyone about an issue before," Forrester said. "(It's) been frustrating, but we're also like, we can't stop if we are the only line of defense in terms of getting answers ... because no one else is."

Tucker County is just one of thousands of communities across the country searching for answers amid a data center boom. While the majority of Americans oppose data centers in their areas, many of the lawmakers representing them in Washington argue the U.S. can't afford for the rapid buildout to slow.

Republicans especially seem to be in a tight spot, party aides and lawmakers said. As the Trump administration pushes for AI adoption, many GOP lawmakers aren't sure how to walk the tightrope between backing their data center-wary constituents and the AI industry.

Most new data centers are also cropping up in rural areas, according to Pew Research Center, which have grown increasingly Republican during the past decade.

"The locals aren't particularly happy because there's not local input. They can say something, but there's not an approval or disapproval process at the local level," said Rep. Riley Moore, R-W.Va., who represents Tucker County.

Moore referred to a state law that aims to attract business but overrides local control: "Part of that reasoning was the critical nature of data centers and the AI race between us and China, and the necessity to expedite these projects, which I certainly can understand. But I also understand the frustration of the locals feeling like they don't have control."

Since the discord is only just starting to trickle into Washington, Republicans are getting somewhat of a break this election cycle, said a national GOP operative, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. But by 2028, they expect it to be among the top issues.

"This election cycle may be the first election cycle where data centers are a huge issue on voters' minds, and I think that's a good thing," said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., whose district is no stranger to data center proposals. "I've been talking about data centers since I got into politics ... and how we need to be really deliberate and careful about where we put them and the impact it would have. And now people are starting to see it more viscerally."

"No good solution"

Democrats are also wrestling with messaging on the data center issue, and Subramanyam said the party could still "do better." But Democrats seem to be faring better than Republicans, he added.

"Republicans seem to be tied with industry on this, and protective of the industry. And the president himself has called data centers 'liquid gold,'" he said. "On the Democratic side, we have developed more of a platform of being with the communities and with the people affected by them, and that's a good place to be politically right now."

It's undeniable that data centers have a PR problem, said Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn.

"I think the data center people are totally off their game, they're terrible at messaging, and there's talk that the Chinese are putting it out because they're the ones that want to be in the business of it," he said, pointing to "a lot of misinformation out there."

Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden represents a sprawling southwestern Wisconsin district where there are plans to build a data center. He also said a lot of information opposing the project is "from the Chinese companies" who are "paying people to say this stuff."

Van Orden faces a Toss-up race this fall against Democrat Rebecca Cooke, whom he defeated by 3 points in 2024.

Cooke released an ad accusing Van Orden of "selling out" to AI companies and, like some progressives in Congress, has thrown her support behind a data center moratorium. Van Orden called the ad a lie but has taken a more nuanced approach to data centers, stipulating he won't support them unless they have local buy-in and avoid farm land, among other factors.

That largely tracks with initial Republican messaging on the data complexes, although the GOP operative said there "really is no good solution." For now, many candidates are stressing competition with China and touting job opportunities, while also acknowledging constituent concerns, such as the centers driving up utility rates.

Aside from progressives advocating moratoriums, Democrats are largely doing the same. Both Republicans and Democrats in Congress have introduced legislation aiming to foster local control in the data center proposal process and stabilize energy prices, but the bills are still in the early stages.

"They're starting to see the environment, the water impacts affect them," Subramanyam said. "If the data center industry does not collaborate with us as public officials and collaborate with the public more, then they're going to have trouble building those data centers."

Ridgeline resistance

In Thomas, Forrester said she has never done advocacy work before but felt that residents were the "only line of defense" against the proposal. Fundamental Data LLC, the Virginia-based company behind the so-called Ridgeline data center complex, has not been consistent with details, she said, and many in the community don't trust it.

Fundamental Data did not provide Roll Call with answers to emailed questions.

"People haven't forgotten what natural resource extraction has done to our communities in West Virginia -- we've seen this playbook before, we've heard all the lines," Forrester said. "It's like, 'Oh, we're gonna host a public meeting so we can check the box and say we engaged the community.' But it doesn't matter what people say, because it's the same outcome."

Forrester said Tucker United has reached out to members of Congress who represent the area but hasn't received a response. When asked about communications with the group, Moore's spokesperson said his office has not been in contact.

"I've heard from hundreds of constituents across the Second District who are sharing their concerns about the impacts data centers are having on our communities," Moore said in a statement. He added he wants to see how the state's new data center development plan might address those concerns.

A spokesperson for Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said in a statement she has "emphasized the importance of local involvement, responsible stewardship, and the protection of utility payers along with prospects of job creation and community development."

"She remains in touch with local leaders on this," the spokesperson added.

The office of Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va. did not respond to a request for comment.

Residents have heard the "AI race with China" argument for data centers, Forrester added. But it's been hard for them to relate, "like at the auto parts store in Thomas, where they're like, 'I don't like seeing all this AI video stuff, I can't tell what's real or what's not anymore.'"

"People live here for a reason ... it's because we like being outside in nature," she said. "In many ways, this AI tech world feels so distant from our daily lives here ... like, we still struggle to get basic internet."

She pointed to the president of Utah's state Senate, J. Stuart Adams, who was ousted in a June Republican primary after backing a data center near the Great Salt Lake. When asked whether the anti-data center fervor was strong enough in Tucker County to yield similar political outcomes, Forrester said: "It feels that way."

"Here and across the country, the resistance has grown so much, movements have sprung up everywhere," she said. "There's a real possibility they could build out all this infrastructure and it'll be obsolete in a few years ... so, it's like, what is it going to be next?"

title: California planned a nuclear exit. Now it's reconsidering - Los Angeles Times
description:
Diablo Canyon doesn’t look like a nuclear power plant that’s getting ready to retire.
Nuclear power produces no greenhouse gas emissions, the primary driver of climate change.
Experts say the abrupt about-face on California’s once-heralded nuclear exit reflects a broader trend as the state grapples with an electricity future almost no one saw coming.
The California Energy Commission projects that demand for electricity will increase by roughly 50% through 2045 after decades of remaining relatively flat.
But some experts say keeping Diablo online is actually slowing the growth of renewable energy in California.
text:
Diablo Canyon doesn’t look like a nuclear power plant that’s getting ready to retire.

Beneath its twin concrete domes here on the edge of the Central Coast, neutrons slam into uranium atoms billions of times each second, workers respond to blinking lights in a seafoam-green control room, and thunderous turbines generate steady electricity for nearly 4 million Californians.

At the building’s entrance, a massive banner celebrates the plant’s recently renewed federal operating license, proclaiming “You Made This Possible” above a photograph of smiling staffers.

It wasn’t supposed to be this way. A decade ago, the plant’s operator, Pacific Gas & Electric, agreed to methodically shut down Diablo’s reactors in 2025, replacing its 2.2 gigawatts of power with a portfolio of wind farms, solar arrays, battery storage and just plain using less electricity.

But as that deadline neared, state officials, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, waved a white flag. They weren’t ready to shut down an energy source that consistently provides up to 9% of California’s electricity. They extended its life to 2030.

Now there’s a growing movement to extend Diablo’s life once again — this time to 2045. Nearly 50 groups have joined a coalition that includes chambers of commerce, labor unions, nonprofits and the San Luis Obispo County Board of Supervisors to argue that the plant is a critical bridge to the state’s clean energy future. Nuclear power produces no greenhouse gas emissions, the primary driver of climate change.

Opponents of the plant, many of whom live in the area, are livid and say it is the latest in a string of broken promises. Extending the plant’s life through 2045 means 15 more years of nuclear waste and seismic risk as the 1980s-era plant gets older and more brittle.

Experts say the abrupt about-face on California’s once-heralded nuclear exit reflects a broader trend as the state grapples with an electricity future almost no one saw coming.

Like the rest of the nation, California has seen a remarkable explosion in demand for electricity, driven in large part by the rise of artificial intelligence data centers, electric vehicles and building electrification. The California Energy Commission projects that demand for electricity will increase by roughly 50% through 2045 after decades of remaining relatively flat.

At the same time, the state is legally mandated to switch entirely to 100% carbon-free energy by 2045, meaning it must produce more electricity while simultaneously cleaning up the electricity it produces.

The question of how California is going to make major emissions reductions while keeping electricity affordable and reliable “starts in the 2030s and goes all the way to 2045,” said David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at UC San Diego. “And shutting down Diablo in the middle of all that was always going to be a stretch.”

It’s a conversation happening across the United States. Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania — the site of the worst commercial nuclear accident in U.S. history — is slated to reopen in 2027 as part of a 20-year deal to power Microsoft data centers. The Duane Arnold plant in Iowa will start back up in 2029, nine years after its closure, to help power data centers for Google.

In California, extending Diablo’s life through 2045 requires an act of the Legislature, and Newsom has punted the question to the next administration. But the plant’s federal license, which was renewed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in April, technically gives it permission to power on until 2045, when it would be 60 years old.

“It doesn’t make any sense to go through that process of extension and only do it for five years,” Victor said. He said he wouldn’t be surprised if PG&E requests another 20-year extension down the road, because there are “several reactors in the country that already have 80-year licenses, and there may be life even beyond that.”

That’s not to say California hasn’t made great gains in renewables. The state has added an impressive amount of solar power and battery energy storage in recent years, surpassing more than 21,000 megawatts of battery capacity, the largest such fleet in the nation, according to the Energy Commission. It used more solar than natural gas during the first half of 2026 for the first time.

But the grid is missing round-the-clock power to replace Diablo Canyon, said Conor Doyle, chief of strategic initiatives at PG&E, during a recent tour of the plant.

“We have an abundance of renewables, and we’re doing good with procurement, but the sun sets, the wind doesn’t blow, and that’s where reliability and stability come into question,” Doyle said. He noted that there is “not one electron” of always-on power, sometimes referred to as baseload, in the California Independent System Operator’s interconnection queue.

In his opinion, if Diablo were to shut down in 2030 as currently scheduled, it would largely be replaced with natural gas.

Arne Olson, a senior partner with Energy and Environmental Economics who consults on California’s energy planning, said replacing the plant with clean energy may have looked “eminently doable in 2016,” and is probably feasible today. But it becomes much more challenging as the state gets closer to its 2045 target, when the entire grid must be clean.

Offshore wind power, a complement to solar because it blows overnight, is lagging in California in the face of powerful political opposition. While the state had been aiming for 2 to 5 gigawatts of offshore wind power by 2030, none has yet been built, and the Trump administration recently struck deals with three of the state’s offshore wind leaseholders to walk away from their plans and instead invest in fossil fuel projects.

Geothermal, which involves tapping into Earth’s underground heat to spin turbines, looks a lot like nuclear in that it can produce clean electricity 24 hours a day. But it’s not yet clear how many geothermal megawatts are available, and few projects are ready, Olson said.

And replacing Diablo’s steady power with a combination of solar and batteries would be technically possible but increasingly expensive, particularly during the periods of highest demand, he said.

The difficulty and expense of the various alternatives increases “the attractiveness of a resource that’s already operating and producing clean energy around the clock,” he said.

But some experts say keeping Diablo online is actually slowing the growth of renewable energy in California. The plant cannot be turned off during periods of high solar power production, so the state ends up cutting back on its solar power or giving it away for free, said Mark Jacobson, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Stanford.

“So it’s become like an inflexible albatross that causes a lot of waste of electricity,” he said.

Jacobson said the state can — and should — shut Diablo Canyon down on time and still meet its climate goals through a combination of wind, geothermal, rooftop solar and imported supplies. He pointed to the massive SunZia wind farm in New Mexico, which recently came online and is already sending clean electricity to California’s grid, and a major Google-backed geothermal project underway in Utah that aims to supply 500 megawatts by 2028.

“There’s nothing necessary about keeping it open,” he said.

Some who live in the shadow of Diablo Canyon say a 2045 extension feels increasingly inevitable. At a recent information session hosted by the county, about half of the people who delivered public comments were in favor of keeping the plant open, and half were vehemently opposed.

Among them were plant employees who said they can’t imagine a world in which California doesn’t need Diablo’s electricity, and environmental groups who said they’re concerned about threats to marine life. Diablo Canyon uses 2.5 billion gallons of ocean water for cooling each day, discharging hot water directly into the nearby cove.

Others worry about a Fukushima- or Chernobyl-style meltdown. The plant sits near more than a dozen earthquake fault lines.

“It’s a low probability, but the consequences are so enormous that you’ve got to factor it in,” said Jane Swanson, president of Mothers for Peace, a San Luis Obispo-based nonprofit, in a recent phone call.

She and the group’s vice president, Linda Seeley, question PG&E’s arguments for keeping Diablo open, noting that plant officials often point to the rolling blackouts of 2020 as evidence that the state still needs nuclear to meet peak demand. But California hasn’t seen rolling blackouts since that year in large part due to its massive increase in battery energy storage, Seeley said.

The push to extend Diablo Canyon’s life, she contends, “has nothing to do with whether we need the power. It has everything to do with money, and it has everything to do with political will.”

Plant officials maintain that Diablo is safe and subject to constant seismic studies and layers of redundancies to prevent a nuclear meltdown. Its major components, including reactor vessel heads, steam generator parts and low-pressure and high-pressure turbines, were all recently updated as part of the 2030 extension, said Maureen Zawalick, chief risk officer at PG&E.

She said the facility has the capacity for at least 60 years of nuclear waste storage — including 40 years in dry concrete casks and 20 years in spent fuel pools — which would carry it right up to 2045, although she is optimistic about the prospects of a federal fuel repository offsite.

Asked if there’s any scenario in which a 2045 extension doesn’t make sense, Zawalick said no. Given the forecast for future electricity usage and demand, “Diablo is in a unique situation and position to provide and support that,” she said.

For now, the ball is in the Legislature’s court.

Sen. John Laird (D-Santa Cruz), whose district includes Diablo Canyon, said in a statement last week that he’s not surprised Newsom has pushed the question to next year. Important issues must be addressed before any decisions are made, including PG&E’s repayment of an existing state loan, seismic and nuclear reactor safety, spent fuel storage and continued revenues to local government and schools, Laird said.

“I look forward to having the opportunity in 2027, over a full nine-month legislative session, to thoughtfully consider Diablo Canyon’s future and ensure that the community is protected during any additional years of operation,” he said.

description:
We currently give tax credits for clean energy use and production.
We also have a program called Hawaii Energy.
The rebates in the Hawaii Energy program don’t come from taxes.
These include the fuel tax, which is applied to fuel for vehicles using the highways, and the barrel tax, which started off as a tax on imported petroleum but has since been expanded to include many different kinds of fossil fuels.
We then have a special registration fee surcharge, soon to be replaced with a road usage charge, for electric cars and other vehicles using the highways but don’t use fuel subject to the fuel tax.
text:
Clean Energy Schizophrenia

by Tom Yamachika, President, Tax Foundation Hawaii

This week, I wanted to give some additional context in depth to a commentary by new Civil Beat columnist Olin Lagon entitled “A Subsidy Is a Statement About Who Matters.”

Our state does a lot of giving and taking when it comes to energy use.

We currently give tax credits for clean energy use and production. I say “currently” because a bill enacted in this year's legislative session terminates the tax credit for renewable fuels production as of the beginning of 2029, and imposes significant new limits on the renewable energy technologies credit now before doing away with it as of the beginning of 2030.

We also have a program called Hawaii Energy. That program provides rebates and other incentives for people who are getting rid of old energy-using appliances, from light bulbs to water heaters and air conditioning units, and are replacing them with newer light bulbs or other appliances that are demonstrably more efficient than the old ones.

The rebates in the Hawaii Energy program don’t come from taxes. Rather, they come from a state-mandated fee, known as the Public Benefits Fund surcharge under HRS section 269-121, that is charged to all electric consumers. This includes renters, except perhaps for the few renters whose rent includes utilities.

Also on the taking side, we have special taxes that apply to energy consumption. These include the fuel tax, which is applied to fuel for vehicles using the highways, and the barrel tax, which started off as a tax on imported petroleum but has since been expanded to include many different kinds of fossil fuels.

We then have a special registration fee surcharge, soon to be replaced with a road usage charge, for electric cars and other vehicles using the highways but don’t use fuel subject to the fuel tax. Considered by itself, it looks like a penalty for using electric cars or alternative fuel vehicles.

With a new Legislature (well, mostly old but with a few fresh faces) coming in 2027, there are a few policy questions they might want to look at. Mr. Lagon makes the point that contributions of renters (because they use electricity and are forced to pay in to the Public Benefits Fund) fund the rebates that are then made available to homeowners or property owners. That sounds like a distribution of wealth away from the poor and to the rich(er). But that impression isn’t quite right because the rebates reward the replacement of inefficient appliances, and the renters probably don’t own those appliances and so are in no position to effectuate the goal of pushing out old, inefficient appliances in favor of newer ones.

text:
Invest in trees

Re: "Taking the bluff out of Bluffview — Residents, property owners clash over redevelopment of northwest Dallas land," by Robert Wilonsky, Wednesday Opinion.

It’s shameful to read about the destruction of trees and topography in Bluffview. Dallas has long been a city that does not take enough interest in its limited natural beauty, and it falls far short of doing what is required to protect the native landscape.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

While I favor a pro-business climate and understand that the success of Big D is due in part to our embrace of development, there is a way to achieve both. City planners — or whatever passes for city planning in Dallas nowadays — should look to Austin and their strict enforcement of tree preservation rules. In Austin, trees with a diameter of 19 inches or greater require a permit for removal or significant impact during construction.

Additionally, if your project involves working near these trees, you must follow specific tree protection measures to ensure their preservation. Yes, this slows down the process and potentially increases project costs, but it preserves trees that cannot be reliably replaced, replanted, nor grow to canopy height overnight.

Trees, it hardly needs saying, provide so much more than shade, beauty and habitats. A successful city should invest in them.

Beverly Lowry, Dallas/Old Preston Hollow

What are we doing?

Re: "NOAA: Contiguous U.S. breaks record for hottest month," Tuesday news story.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Amazon’s decision to build the largest polluting natural gas power plant in the country to power its new AI center in West Texas should alarm all of us. At a time when we’re facing an accelerating climate crisis, adding massive new sources of carbon emissions is moving us in the wrong direction.

The timing couldn’t be more troubling. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration just reported that July was the hottest month ever recorded in the United States. Extreme heat is already threatening our health, straining our electric grid, damaging agriculture and wreaking havoc on communities.

AI and economic growth do not have to come at the expense of a livable planet. Texas has abundant sunshine and wind that can provide reliable, affordable electricity without locking us into decades of additional fossil fuel emissions.

We can’t keep building gas-powered electric infrastructure while the planet continues to heat. If we’re serious about protecting ourselves and future generations, we must demand cleaner energy choices now.

What are we doing? The climate is telling us we have run out of time for business as usual. This November we must vote for candidates who will work to protect our planet. Our very lives may depend on it.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Andrea Christgau, Keller

She's appalled

Re: "Electric shock gloves draw outrage," Thursday news story.

I am appalled that electric shock gloves are being planned for distribution to ICE agents. My first thought was, where are the body cams they were supposed to start wearing to be more transparent in their actions?

Now, this transparency is skipped, and we move straight to a new way to assert power and possibly injure more people, many of whom are not the vicious criminals that we were promised would be arrested and deported.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

How many more Renée Good and Alex Pretti tragedies do we need before these agents are reined in?

Irene McCleskey, Carrollton

Our broken immigration system

Republicans' anxiety over immigration is misplaced. The United States needs legal immigrants to grow and prosper, as stagnant populations create economic and social strain.

Of course, the border must be secure, illegal immigration stopped and entry managed through a fair, lawful process that welcomes contributors while maintaining order.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

American universities can be magnets that attract the brightest young people from around the world when they can be vetted and provided a path to work toward citizenship if they qualify. Not doing so wastes an incredible opportunity to fuel our country for future growth and prosperity.

The country also needs legal pathways for foreign workers in labor-short industries such as agriculture, construction and other essential sectors.

Republicans had two years to overhaul the broken immigration system, but failed to act. Yes, executive orders tightened the border, but they are not a permanent solution.

Bipartisan reforms have often been attempted in the past and always failed. If Republicans lose the House or Senate this November, comprehensive reform is unlikely, making this missed opportunity especially disappointing.

Jack Gibson, North Dallas

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Don't mess with stockyards

Re: "Stockyards expansion dropped — Developer cites market conditions in halting $1B second phase of development," Aug. 6 Metro & Business story.

The story detailing the plans for the Fort Worth Stockyards throws me into, yes, a small fit of regret and a call to stop the madness. The more change corporations bring to that area, the more likely they are to destroy the essence of why people want to go there in the first place. Big corporations can never leave well enough alone when there is money to be made.

I grew up in the stockyards area, sorta. My grandfather, Will Cornutt, operated a hotel around the corner and several other businesses in what was, back then, close to a dangerous, no-go area. Our mother insisted we spend time every summer, no matter that we lived about 1,400 miles away, with her relatives in Texas. We had a grand time going to the Isis Theatre and trying to stay out of serious trouble.

The plans to change things are exactly what I feared would be on the horizon when we last visited a few years ago.

Just like the president's plans to disrupt Washington, D.C., these kinds of changes should be carefully considered, widely reviewed and, if necessary, turned down flat.

Don't mess with it when you have something grand. The halfway rundown character is part of its charm. Don't wreck it. Please.

title: AI data centers are reshaping Texas. How did we get here? - Houston Chronicle
description:

text:
Data centers are taking over Texas politics. How did we get here?

Texas has offered tax breaks and other incentives to attract data centers for more than a decade. But it wasn’t until artificial intelligence took off that the industry started to boom here.

Now lawmakers and local officials are confronting the consequences of its explosive growth as residents in rural communities across the state push back on the energy and water-guzzling centers.

At least 335 data centers are operating in Texas, with another 225 planned, according to the Houston Chronicle’s data center tracker.

Here’s how Texas went from welcoming data center developers with open arms to playing catch-up with regulations:

Texas’ first data center tax break takes effect

Abbott signs tax breaks for larger projects

ChatGPT launches

Trump announces $500 billion Stargate Project

Regulations for the powergrid and restrictions on local control

Abbott calls Texas the "epicenter" of AI development

Local efforts to halt data centers falter

Miller calls for moratorium

Abbott directs regulators to protect residential ratepayers

San Marcos becomes first Texas city to ban data centers

Abbott says no data centers in "rural neighborhoods"

Texas Democrats demand moratorium

Lawmakers revisit the tax breaks

Abbott pauses data center permits with call for an audit

September 1, 2013

Texas’ first data center tax break takes effect

Lawmakers passed House Bill 1223, creating a state sales tax exemption for data center projects that invest more than $200 million to build in Texas with the equipment they needed to operate, including electricity, cooling systems and emergency generators. Former Gov. Rick Perry signed the tax breaks into law.

The legislation was part of an effort to make Texas more competitive with states already offering incentives to the industry. The reasoning was clear-cut. If Texas gave companies a reason to build here, then investments, jobs and economic activity would follow.

Advertisement

June 10, 2015

Abbott signs tax breaks for larger projects

Lawmakers expanded the incentives for data centers, creating a new exemption for hyperscale data centers in 2015. House Bill 2712, signed by Gov. Greg Abbott, applied to facilities of at least 250,000 square feet, with $500 million in capital investment and 20 megawatts of transmission capacity.

The law exempted electricity and equipment used to operate these projects from state sales tax. It was the first major expansion of the incentives. More would follow.

By 2020, data center developments were accelerating. The Dallas-Fort Worth market saw a 30% net increase in data center leasing transactions between 2020 and 2021.

When the first incentives were passed in 2013, the state’s fiscal analysts estimated the exemption would cost about $14.6 million through 2015. That estimate has now ballooned to $3.3 billion for the 2028-9 budget cycle.

Novermber 30, 2022

ChatGPT launches

OpenAI released ChatGPT, introducing generative artificial intelligence to the public. It helped spark the AI boom that is fueling the data center rush in Texas.

The company is now one of several tech giants, including Google and Meta, with data centers planned here.

January 23, 2025

Trump announces $500 billion Stargate Project

President Donald Trump announced the Stargate Project, a $500 billion federal partnership with OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank to build infrastructure across the country. The first site for the companies’ massive data center campus was in Abilene.

Advertisement

June 20, 2025

Regulations for the powergrid and restrictions on local control

As data centers started to sprout up in small towns across the state, lawmakers in Austin passed Senate Bill 6, which set new rules for large electricity users and gave the state more power over their connection to the grid.

At the same time, they placed new limits on how cities and counties can regulate the developments. The law, House Bill 2559, made it more difficult for cities to temporarily pause development while considering their effects.

Abbott signed both bills into law on the same day.

Novermber 14, 2025

Abbott calls Texas the "epicenter" of AI development

The governor appeared alongside Google CEO Sundar Pichai to tout the company’s plans to invest $40 billion into artificial intelligence data centers and related workforce training in Texas, Google’s largest such investment in the U.S.

“We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen,” Abbott said.

The investment would expand Google’s AI and cloud infrastructure in Texas, adding to a wave of new AI-related projects in the state.

February - June 2026

Local efforts to halt data centers falter

As data center proposals rolled in across rural Texas, some local governments tried to put the brakes on them.

In February, Hood County commissioners denied two attempts at placing a countywide moratorium on data center development after state Sen. Paul Bettencourt warned doing so would flout the law passed last year. Bettencourt asked Attorney General Ken Paxton to weigh in. His office has yet to issue an opinion.

Hill County imposed its own moratorium in May, but commissioners rescinded it in June after developers filed a $100 million lawsuit against the county.

May 26, 2026

Miller calls for moratorium

Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller called for a temporary moratorium on new data center development, arguing the state should first study long-term effects on the power grid, water supplies, agricultural land and rural communities.

“I’m not saying we don’t need them, that we don’t have to have them, but we have to take a pause,” Miller said. “There’s no guidelines, no parameters. Zero regulation.”

Miller was the first statewide elected official and the highest-ranking Texas Republican to push back on data center development.

June 10, 2026

Abbott directs regulators to protect residential ratepayers

Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas to develop measures protecting Texans from infrastructure costs associated with large data centers.

The governor also urged lawmakers to strip the lucrative tax breaks and set new rules on where the centers can be built when they return to Austin next year.

It was the first sign of the governor’s shift from wholeheartedly embracing the data center boom to calling for new guardrails.

At the time, more than 480 data centers had sought to connect to the grid through 2032, according to ERCOT.

June 16, 2026

San Marcos becomes first Texas city to ban data centers

San Marcos voted to prohibit data centers within city limits, becoming the first Texas city to effectively ban the developments. The vote followed months of debate over their effects on electricity, water, land and surrounding neighborhoods.

June 30, 2026

Abbott says no data centers in "rural neighborhoods"

At a campaign stop in Bullard, Abbott called for a ban on AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods.

“We must prohibit them from building AI data centers in rural Texas neighborhoods,” Abbott said.

The governor’s comments came as lawmakers acknowledged the growing political pressure on them to do something about the boom. During a House committee hearing, lawmakers expressed outrage that data center operators had largely ignored requests by state agencies to report their water use. Of 341 data centers required to report their water use to the state, only 17% complied.

July 14, 2026

Texas Democrats demand moratorium

Democrats running for statewide offices held a news conference calling for a temporary pause on data center development as they looked to seize on the growing opposition.

State Rep. Vikki Goodwin, running for lieutenant governor, state Sen. Sarah Eckhardt, running for comptroller, and Clayton Tucker, the party’s candidate for agriculture commissioner, were among those pushing the moratorium.

“This issue isn’t left vs. right. It’s not city vs. county. It is organized people vs. organized money, and only organized people can beat organized money,” Tucker said.

State Rep. Gina Hinojosa, an Austin Democrat running for governor, also eventually called for a moratorium — and for Abbott to bring lawmakers back for a special session to set new rules for data center development.

July 27, 2026

Lawmakers revisit the tax breaks

The Senate Finance Committee examined the cost of Texas’ data center tax exemption as lawmakers prepared for the next state budget.

Texas had three tax-exempt data centers in 2013. By 2021, there were 17. In 2026, 59 were certified before July ended.

“What we thought we were voting for back in 2013, it’s a much different animal these days,” said state Sen. Joan Huffman, a Houston Republican who chairs the Senate finance committee.

Lawmakers appeared to be on board with ending the tax exemptions. But they cannot do so until the legislature reconvenes next year.

August 3, 2026

Abbott pauses data center permits with call for an audit

Abbott ordered state regulators to conduct an audit of all data center projects seeking permits in Texas before they give any more the green light, a move the governor has cast as a statewide pause on data center construction.

“Our top priority is to protect Texans’ safety and quality of life,” Abbott said. “Texans must come first.”

It was unclear how long the pause would last. The governor's letter to regulators did not detail what the audit should include or how long it should take.

ERCOT was already studying the first batch of large projects — known as “batch zero” — for approval to connect to the grid. It announced that the process was on hold and said it would consult with the PUC on next steps.

authors: Derek Harrison, Liza Gross, photos  Michael Kodas, Gabriel Matias Castilho
