title: Growing Renewable Energy in Trinidad and Tobago - The Borgen Project
description:
This article will explore why the country is transitioning toward renewable energy, the organizations supporting these efforts and how renewable energy investments could strengthen the economy while improving long-term sustainability.
Why Trinidad and Tobago Is Diversifying Its Energy Sector Oil and natural gas have been a significant part of Trinidad and Tobago, especially economically.
Additionally, the global transition toward renewable energy and the impacts of climate change are prompting Trinidad and Tobago to diversify its energy sector and invest in cleaner energy sources.
Trinidad and Tobago also joined the International Renewable Energy Agency in 2014, giving it access to the agency’s technical expertise and policy guidance to help accelerate its transition to renewable energy.
Organizations such as Renewable Power Caribbean are helping support this transition by installing renewable energy systems, providing energy management services and educating communities about clean energy solutions.
text:
In Trinidad and Tobago, there has historically been a large dependence on oil and natural gas usage and production. Traditionally, reliance on these nonrenewable energy sources drove the country’s economy, accounting for about 36% of its nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2022. In 2021, 99% of Trinidad and Tobago’s electricity was generated from natural gas. This highlights the country’s heavy reliance on fossil fuels and the growing need to diversify its energy sector. Renewable energy, however, offers an opportunity to strengthen energy security while supporting long-term economic sustainability. Government initiatives and growing investments in renewable energy aim to reduce the country’s dependence on fossil fuels while expanding opportunities for cleaner energy production.

Through renewable energy initiatives, green hydrogen development and support from international organizations, Trinidad and Tobago is working to build a more diversified, resilient and sustainable energy future. Expanding renewable energy could also create new jobs, encourage economic growth and strengthen long-term opportunities for the communities most affected by changes in the traditional energy sector. This article will explore why the country is transitioning toward renewable energy, the organizations supporting these efforts and how renewable energy investments could strengthen the economy while improving long-term sustainability.

Why Trinidad and Tobago Is Diversifying Its Energy Sector

Oil and natural gas have been a significant part of Trinidad and Tobago, especially economically. For decades, the country has relied on oil and natural gas production, yet now the gas fields are mature, creating a decline in production. According to the International Monetary Fund, natural gas production fell by 17% between 2010 and 2019, while crude oil and condensate production declined by 40% during the same period. As production has decreased, exports of liquefied natural gas and petrochemicals have also declined.

The government has encouraged the development of new oil and gas fields; however, the projects are expected to be very timely. Additionally, the global transition toward renewable energy and the impacts of climate change are prompting Trinidad and Tobago to diversify its energy sector and invest in cleaner energy sources.

Because the country’s economy is so closely tied to the energy sector, fluctuations in oil and natural gas production can affect economic stability. The World Bank notes that efforts to expand renewable energy are part of the country’s broader transition toward a low-carbon economy. This can help build a more resilient economy that better supports communities over the long term. A stronger renewable energy sector could also create employment opportunities in construction, maintenance and clean energy industries while supporting more stable incomes for families.

Expanding Renewable Energy Opportunities

The International Monetary Fund explains that expanding renewable electricity generation could reduce the country’s reliance on oil and natural gas, while lowering greenhouse gas emissions. Trinidad and Tobago’s own authorities have set a target of generating 30% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030. Trinidad and Tobago is also investing in green hydrogen as part of its long-term energy strategy. The government has developed a plan for the next 35 years to create a green hydrogen sector based on renewable energy sources. That sector will be used to produce products like ammonia and methanol. The goal of this program is to decrease the country’s carbon footprint and allow it to export additional amounts of natural gas to meet increasing worldwide demand for cleaner energy.

Organizations are also supporting the country’s transition to renewable energy. The Inter-American Development Bank has partnered with the government through its Sustainable Energy Program by providing financing and technical assistance to advance renewable energy and energy efficiency initiatives. The United Nations Development Programme supports renewable energy development through clean energy projects and policy assistance. Trinidad and Tobago also joined the International Renewable Energy Agency in 2014, giving it access to the agency’s technical expertise and policy guidance to help accelerate its transition to renewable energy.

Looking Toward a More Sustainable Future

Trinidad and Tobago’s warm climate and long dry season provide favorable conditions for expanding renewable energy, particularly solar power. Organizations such as Renewable Power Caribbean are helping support this transition by installing renewable energy systems, providing energy management services and educating communities about clean energy solutions. These efforts can lower energy costs over time and expand access to reliable electricity, creating more economic opportunities for local communities. The country is exploring opportunities to expand wind energy as well. According to the Caribbean Climate Network, a national roadmap identified nine potential onshore locations for future wind projects. That roadmap estimated Trinidad and Tobago has more than 2.5 gigawatts of onshore wind energy potential.

Conclusion

These initiatives could help diversify the economy beyond oil and natural gas while improving long-term energy security, as long as the country keeps investing in renewable energy. A more diversified energy sector may result in a more stable economy that can better support jobs, public services and sustainable development. It could also reduce the country’s susceptibility to changes in the production of fossil fuels and international energy markets. As renewable energy industries continue to grow, they also have the potential to create jobs and strengthen local economies. Continued investments in clean energy and economic diversification have the potential to improve community conditions and create a more resilient future for Trinidad and Tobago.

– India Hairston

India is based in Malvern, PA, USA and focuses on Good News and Politics for The Borgen Project.

text:
The ability to tap into the energy locked inside your car’s battery to power tools, lights, campground gear, and essential home appliances during an outage has quickly become one of the most desirable EV features.

The problem? Many electric vehicles already on the road – including millions of Teslas (Model S, Model 3, Model X, and Model Y)! – were never sold with native vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability. The new D2 power adapter from WETOX changes all that, using the car’s native charge port and turning more EVs into portable power stations.

WETOX might be a new name to Western EV buyers, but the company has been developing V2L adapters for over four years, building deep expertise in the growing vehicle-to-everything (V2X) market through its established GB/T adapters for Teslas, NIOs, and other EVs. Leveraging this mature supply chain, their newest product, the D2, is a next-generation adapter specially developed for North American and European markets—designed to bring portable V2L capability to Tesla, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and other EVs that didn’t originally ship with bidirectional power baked in.

The company is using Kickstarter as a launch platform for the D2 adapter, with the campaign serving as both an early-access sales channel and a way to introduce the brand to a broader Western audience. The campaign is currently underway and gaining traction, with backers

pledging over $120,000 as of this writing

Advertisement - scroll for more content

Safety is standard

IPX5 waterproof design; via WETOX.

WETOX builds safety into the D2’s design from the start, and the adapter’s custom-molded internal structure ensures every part fits perfectly for superior stability, safety, and the sort of tight seals required to achieve an impressive IPX5 waterproof rating – but they didn’t stop there. WETOX developed a “full-chain” waterproof solution, ensuring that every part from the connector and main unit (IPX5) to the 10 ft (3m) extension power strip (IPX6) is safe for use, even in heavy rain.

Water isn’t the only safety hazard V2L adapters face, however. Many have a fatal flaw: they trigger Tesla’s battery heating mechanism.

“You might waste 5% of your battery just boiling a kettle, or suffer from phantom drain even with no appliances running – dragging the overall energy efficiency down to a miserable 52%,” reads the official Kickstarter copy. “The WETOX D2 solves this. Our advanced software protocol completely bypasses the vehicle’s heating trigger. You only consume the power your devices actually draw. No unnecessary noise, no phantom drain.”

To back up those claims, WETOX offers a global product insurance plan that not only covers standard accidental damage to the D2 (including the adapter, the vehicle, personnel, and connected appliances), but explicitly includes coverage against voiding your EV’s warranty.

WETOX underscored their confidence in the D2 recorded a 13-hour, uncut, one-take stress test and put it on YouTube, running a continuous, 3600W max load and drawing the car’s battery from 93% down to 19%. At the same time, the WETOX D2 proved to be as much as 40% more efficient than the other V2L adapter brands on the market. (!)

Longest Tesla V2L test EVER

Safety is obviously the first hurdle when tapping into the high-voltage battery pack of a modern EV, but compatibility and convenience are close behind.

To tackle both, WETOX avoided off-the-shelf third-party SECC modules and instead fully mastered and proprietary-engineered the low-level code for the ISO 15118 and DIN 70121 protocol stacks. Fully owning the source code allowed WETOX to custom-design the circuit board for a significantly smaller footprint, while giving engineers deep control over battery handshake messaging to optimize vehicle-to-load interactions. This complete mastery over the underlying protocol stack also enables WETOX to continuously adapt and tune software protocols for new vehicles—with plans to unlock V2L compatibility for a new EV model every quarter, delivered seamlessly to existing owners via over-the-air (OTA) updates.

While vehicle limitations currently cap the D2 at ISO 15118-2, WETOX is already future-proofing its technology, earning the world’s first ISO 15118-20 certification report from SGS, a milestone that marks a key step forward in pushing V2X communication toward standardized, large-scale commercialization.

Awarded the world’s first certification report for next-gen V2X communication protocol standards by SGS

WETOX’ app solves for the convenience piece, allowing EV owners to customize discharge limits, set power-off timers, and access full system diagnostics directly from your smartphone.

Owners can use the app to set how much of the vehicle’s battery they are willing to use, monitor the system, and configure the adapter for different situations, whether that’s powering tools at a job site, running equipment during a camping trip, or keeping essential appliances running when conventional power isn’t available. The D2 is also designed for a broad range of regional charging standards. WETOX’s Kickstarter campaign includes NACS, CCS1, and CCS2 variants, opening the door to V2L applications across North America, Europe, and other markets.

WETOX’ Kickstarter campaign is set to run through August 30th, and includes NACS, CCS1, and CCS2 variants designed to deliver V2L power to a variety of regional markets. If you can’t wait, search “WETOX” on the App Store or Google Play to download and experience the app now, or by visiting WETOX’ official website.

You can watch WETOX’ official Tesla V2L adapter videos, below – and remember that all the safety and convenience features shown on the Tesla D2 for the NACS connector are also there for your Ford Mustang Mach-E with CCS connector, and more vehicle compatibility will be announced on the official WETOX website in the future.

Tesla / Mach-E WETOX D2 Videos

For EV owners who have wanted to turn their car into a portable power station but didn’t want to buy a new vehicle just to get factory-installed V2L, that’s perhaps the biggest appeal of the D2: you may already have the battery — WETOX is giving you another way to use it.

title: Lithium Mining Companies Survive a Transition — Why Sentiment Could Shift Fast
description:

The result is that lithium demand growth, while positive, is insufficient to absorb the increase in supply coming online.
Balance Sheet Impact on Mining Companies Lithium mining companies entered with optimistic assumptions about future profitability and cash generation.
Many had approved expansion projects, committed to shareholder distributions, and increased guidance for operational metrics based on assumed lithium prices.
Winnowing of the Producer Base As lithium prices remain under pressure, the least efficient producers will face mounting challenges.
text:
Highlights

Global lithium supply is expected to exceed demand for the first time in multiple years, marking a major shift from previous undersupply conditions

Lithium carbonate prices have fallen to six-month lows, reflecting both increased production and moderating demand growth

Major lithium producers are cutting capital expenditure plans as profitability forecasts deteriorate in response to lower price expectations

The investment thesis for lithium stocks for much of and rested on a simple premise: the world did not have enough lithium to satisfy demand from electric vehicle manufacturing and battery storage deployment. This scarcity would persist for years, supporting prices and making lithium miners extraordinarily profitable. That thesis is now breaking down with surprising speed.

August marks an inflection point where lithium supply is expected to exceed global demand. This is not a modest surplus but a meaningful reversal from the deficit conditions that characterized markets just a year ago. The causes are multiple: new lithium production capacity has ramped faster than anticipated, battery recycling is beginning to offset some mined supply, and demand growth has moderated from pandemic-era peaks.

The result is a commodity market in the early stages of a potentially prolonged period of price weakness. Lithium prices have already retreated significantly, and there is limited catalyst for recovery if supply remains elevated relative to demand.

The Capital Expenditure Cliff

Mining companies are responding rationally to changing market dynamics by curtailing expansion plans. A lithium mine expansion that looked economically viable when lithium carbonate prices were elevated no longer makes sense at current or projected future prices. Companies that committed capital to expansion projects now face the prospect of bringing new capacity online into an oversupplied market.

This creates a classic overcapacity scenario. Existing production remains in place, demand is not growing fast enough to absorb existing supply, and new capacity additions turn what would be a tight market into a surplus market. When that occurs, commodity prices typically decline to levels where only the lowest-cost producers remain profitable.

This dynamic is already unfolding in lithium. Companies are announcing delays, deferrals, or cancellations of expansion projects. Each such announcement signals that management expects lithium prices to remain under pressure, contradicting the bull case that drove lithium stock valuations higher through.

Electric Vehicles Still Growing, But Not Explosively

It's important to note that electric vehicle adoption is still expanding and battery manufacturing is still growing. The issue is not that demand is declining in absolute terms, but that demand growth is moderating from peak rates. Earlier forecasts sometimes assumed electric vehicle adoption would accelerate exponentially. Reality is showing growth, but more linear growth than the most bullish scenarios anticipated.

Additionally, the efficiency of battery manufacturing is improving. Each battery requires slightly less lithium as manufacturing processes improve and battery chemistry advances. This structural demand headwind is not captured in headline electric vehicle unit growth figures but is meaningful for lithium demand.

The result is that lithium demand growth, while positive, is insufficient to absorb the increase in supply coming online. This supply-demand mismatch creates the pricing pressure now evident in commodity markets.

Balance Sheet Impact on Mining Companies

Lithium mining companies entered with optimistic assumptions about future profitability and cash generation. Many had approved expansion projects, committed to shareholder distributions, and increased guidance for operational metrics based on assumed lithium prices. The rapid deterioration in the price environment is forcing recalibration of these plans.

Companies are reducing capital expenditure and potentially cutting or eliminating shareholder distributions to preserve cash. This has direct implications for total shareholder returnseven if earnings per share grows, total returns suffer if capital expenditure is cut and dividends are eliminated.

The margin compression is occurring faster than typical commodity cycles. Normally, supply overcapacity develops gradually as multiple projects come online. In lithium, the speed of capacity additions and the suddenness of demand moderation is creating a sharp transition rather than a gradual shift.

Winnowing of the Producer Base

As lithium prices remain under pressure, the least efficient producers will face mounting challenges. Junior explorers and developers dependent on high lithium prices to justify economics will likely be forced to abandon projects or seek merger partners. The result will be consolidation in the lithium mining space, with a smaller number of large producers capturing most of the supply.

This consolidation process creates opportunities for sophisticated investors to identify quality assets at distressed valuations. However, it also creates significant risks for investors in junior lithium explorers or companies with high-cost production. These operators may face substantial shareholder losses if lithium prices remain depressed for an extended period.

The Multi-Year Repricing Ahead

What makes the current lithium situation particularly challenging is the likelihood that price recovery will take years, not quarters. If supply exceeds demand by meaningful amounts, reducing this surplus requires either production cuts (which companies resist) or demand growth accelerating to absorb supply. Battery demand growth may not accelerate sufficiently to quickly clear oversupply.

This suggests a multi-year period where lithium prices remain under structural pressure. Companies and investors who positioned for scarcity and high prices will need to reset expectations substantially.

text:
The Strategic Emerging Engines for Disruptive (SEED) initiative, led by South Korea’s ministry of science and Information and Communications Technology (ICT), is aimed at advancing innovation in seven key areas across three fronts – securing clean energy, next generation technologies and the foundations for the future.

A statement from the ministry states that in a rapidly changing technological environment, it is difficult to guarantee sustainable growth for Korea with the current gap in key industries.

“With this awareness of the issue, the government aims to sow the seeds of advanced technology now and foster them from a long-term perspective to secure Korea's next-generation growth engines 10-20 years from now,” says the statement.

“This is a national project aimed at fostering 'advanced technology', a core asset of security as a future growth engine for South Korea.”

Also of interest

Rolls-Royce SMR advances plans at two more Czech sites

How different approaches are driving fusion development

Nuclear advances

The aim of the clean energy thrust is to simultaneously address the surging electricity demand driven by the AI revolution and the challenge of carbon neutrality, with three projects focussed on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), nuclear fusion and breakthrough renewables.

Specific targets are the commercialisation of light water type SMRs in 2035 and the construction of non-hard water SMRs to begin in 2030.

With SMRs considered an easy option to meet increasing power demand with their modular assembly onsite, the government has been supporting the development of SMR designs, in particular for non-hard water SMRs.

It is proposed to accelerate these activities utilising advanced technologies such as digital twins and the government proposes to launch a public-private special purpose vehicle to oversee development and launch the technology into the global SMR market.

Additionally, by 2030, it is proposed to have in place a regulatory framework for the design and implementation of SMRs, both for utility power generation and for sectors such as industry, marine and defence.

On fusion, the goal is to develop on a public-private basis a national reactor to deliver first power generation by 2035 and commercial power in the 2040s.

To accelerate this, activities include the advance of a supply chain and establishment of a regulatory framework to resolve bottlenecks.

The Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute has been very much at the forefront of SMR development since the late 1990s first with the SMART, then the SMART100, and now the next generation i-SMR, which is expected to gain standard design approval in 2028.

The SMART100 is designed for 110MWe and 365MWt and a lifetime of 60 years and is undergoing feasibility for deployment in various markets and settings, including Indonesia, Czeck Republic and Canada.

The i-SMR is planned for 170MWe and an 80-year lifetime, which is due to come into operation in 2035.

In fusion, the Institute is a partner in San Diego-based Energy Matter Conversion Corp’s Polywell fusion development expected to pilot in 2038.

The Korea Institute of Fusion Energy (KFE) is the country’s representative in ITER and is advancing the KSTAR project as the basis for a future fusion device, for which full scale design efforts were launched in June.

As part of its contribution to ITER, KFE is responsible for delivering the tritium storage and delivery system, which also should support the growth of expertise of the national industry.

Clean electricity

The third project in this area is to accelerate the expansion of clean electricity, with several sectors in which the government anticipates the country can secure technological leadership.

In the solar sector the focus will be on the commercialisation of perovskite tandem cells (with efficiency over 35%) and the development of technology for space data centres, while in the wind sector it will be on building a domestic manufacturing capacity for ultra-large 20MW+ turbines and floating systems.

Additionally, through industry-academia research cooperation, water electrolysis capability in the 50-100MW class will be developed for the supply of clean hydrogen in a timely manner.

For the grid HVDC and superconducting technologies will be demonstrated and promoted, as also will be the integration of AI into grid planning.

Other innovations

In the area of next generation technologies the projects include securing 100-qubit class domestic quantum computers by 2029 and ranking first in quantum chip manufacturing capability by 2035, achieving a moon landing by 2030 and an independent low Earth orbit satellite communication network by 2035, while establishing an AI bio infrastructure by 2030 and commercialising brain-computer technologies by 2035.

In the third area of foundations for the future, the focus is advancing supply chains for core minerals and other materials and equipment that will be required through advancing local capabilities or for items that cannot be produced domestically by extended stockpiling.

To advance this SEED initiative, the government plans to develop detailed roadmaps and monitoring for each project and to expand and strengthen research capabilities, with division of responsibilities among industry, academia and research institutes and including investment of 10 trillion South Korean won ($7.1 billion) in R&D of key equipment over the next five years.

But this isn’t about black or brown, it is about blue — that blue flame of natural gas. Inside Climate News reports that state Sen. Phil King, a Republican from Weatherford, is asking the leaders of ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission of Texas to set a quota for gas plants rather than just letting the market keep picking cheap solar. description:
Envision Energy has commissioned the Galaxy Campus in Ulanqab, a facility that could redefine how AI infrastructure interacts with power grids.
Renewable energy as primary architecture The facility integrates dedicated renewable generation with large-scale energy storage and transmission infrastructure.
Grid constraints drive infrastructure design The project addresses a constraint facing AI infrastructure developers globally.
According to Envision, the project is the world's only planned gigawatt-scale green data centre.
Ulanqab serves as the first demonstration of Envision's plan to combine renewable generation, power infrastructure and AI compute in locations where energy resources can support data centre expansion.
text:
Envision Energy has commissioned the Galaxy Campus in Ulanqab, a facility that could redefine how AI infrastructure interacts with power grids.

The site is designed to scale beyond 2 GW of capacity, with renewable generation, storage and transmission infrastructure built as core components rather than afterthoughts.

Renewable energy as primary architecture

The facility integrates dedicated renewable generation with large-scale energy storage and transmission infrastructure.

According to Envision, the campus is designed to support up to one million AI accelerators once fully built out.

The company claims the site can deliver one million PFLOPS of AI computing while generating up to 10 times more compute output per square metre than conventional data centres.

Ricky Zheng, General Manager of Envision's AIDC (AI Data Centre) says: "Supporting a million accelerators requires a purpose-built AI Power System that integrates renewable generation, dedicated transmission infrastructure and large-scale energy storage to deliver stable, low-cost green power."

He adds: "This enables the facility to deliver up to ten times more compute output per square meter than conventional data centres."

Grid constraints drive infrastructure design

The project addresses a constraint facing AI infrastructure developers globally.

Conventional data centre expansion can encounter limits around grid capacity.

AI workloads are driving higher power requirements per facility, which could mean energy availability becomes a bottleneck for computing capacity.

Envision's approach treats the energy architecture as part of the data centre itself.

The company has designed the power system to provide stable electricity directly from renewable sources without relying on grid infrastructure alone.

Ulanqab's location provides access to wind and solar resources.

The grassland city has developed into a digital infrastructure hub, offering network performance suited to AI clusters containing hundreds of thousands of accelerators.

Regional advantages support deployment

The region's renewable energy resources align with the facility's power requirements.

According to Envision, the project is the world's only planned gigawatt-scale green data centre.

Dedicated renewable assets are combined with transmission infrastructure and AI-focused power management to support the campus at gigawatt scale.

Ricky says: "The next frontier of AI is infrastructure."

He continues: "As AI models become larger and more compute-intensive, the limiting factors are increasingly power availability, network performance and energy efficiency."

Global expansion targets desert regions

The Galaxy Campus is the first project under Envision's Mission Gobi initiative, unveiled at VivaTech in Paris in June 2026.

The initiative targets 5 GW of green AI computing capacity in desert and arid regions worldwide by 2030.

Ulanqab serves as the first demonstration of Envision's plan to combine renewable generation, power infrastructure and AI compute in locations where energy resources can support data centre expansion.

Ricky says: "Envision Galaxy Campus combines energy, networking and physical infrastructure at unprecedented scale, enabling hyperscalers, technology companies and AI innovators to deploy and scale the next generation of AI workloads."

The model could show whether renewable-powered AI infrastructure can operate at scale without grid dependency.

Desert and arid regions with high solar and wind potential may offer locations where energy generation and computing demand can coexist without competing for existing grid capacity.A data centre complex in Inner Mongolia now covers 120,000 square metres and runs entirely on renewable electricity.

# Pakistan Launches ‘Made in Pakistan’ Clean Energy Manufacturing Drive

**SUZHOU:** Pakistan has launched an **“E-Cluster” model** aimed at building an integrated clean-energy manufacturing ecosystem and positioning the country as a regional hub for clean-energy technology and production, according to China Economic Net.

Qasim Kamal, Group Director of Suzhou IBI Engineering (Belt & Road Economic and Trade Centre), said the initiative would progressively introduce and localise advanced technology, manufacturing expertise, quality standards and supply-chain capabilities across major industrial hubs in Pakistan.

“At the heart of the initiative is the transfer and localisation of Chinese technology and industrial expertise,” Kamal said. “The goal is to build Pakistan’s own production capabilities and develop competitive ‘Made in Pakistan’ products and brands.”

Under a phased localisation strategy, manufacturing will initially follow a **completely knocked down (CKD) assembly model**, enabling production to begin while local technical and manufacturing capabilities are developed. The level of localisation will gradually increase, with key components eventually produced domestically to establish a comprehensive local supply chain.

Kamal said Pakistan was also introducing a **“3+3” cooperation model**, under which Chinese partners would provide technology transfer, research and development support, manufacturing lines and integrated supply-chain expertise, while Pakistani partners would contribute land, regulatory approvals, market development and sales capabilities.

The initiative also includes joint R&D programmes involving Pakistani universities and local industry partners, with the aim of strengthening indigenous research capabilities and developing locally adapted clean-energy technologies.

The programme is further exploring **hydrogen fuel-cell technology**, with the objective of developing commercially competitive solutions as the technology matures.

Conceived in 2022, the initiative entered its implementation phase in 2026 and currently involves four to five partners working across **battery manufacturing, electric vehicles and energy-storage systems**. Large-scale production is expected to commence within the next five to six months.

Pakistan’s rapidly expanding clean-energy market has created growing opportunities for domestic manufacturing. According to Renewables First, the country’s cumulative solar photovoltaic capacity reached **38 GW by FY25**, compared with less than 2 GW three years earlier. Meanwhile, lithium-ion battery energy-storage system (BESS) imports surged **220 per cent year-on-year to 4.6 GWh in 2025**.

Earlier this month, Federal Minister for Power Awais Leghari unveiled a roadmap targeting an increase in the share of clean electricity to **90 per cent by 2035**, from around 55 per cent currently.

“For long, Pakistan’s renewable market has been driven by imports. Through this initiative, we aim to transform Pakistan into a regional clean-energy manufacturing and technology hub, creating local jobs and added value,” Kamal said.

The E-Cluster initiative is therefore expected to support Pakistan’s transition from an import-dependent clean-energy market towards **local manufacturing, technology development and export-oriented production**.

By China Economic Net

text:
Leo ICT Cables PLC has upgraded its lithium-ion battery pack manufacturing facility with advanced automation, robotics and modern production technologies, marking a significant step forward for Bangladesh's domestic energy storage industry.

The company has integrated automated production systems and robotic technologies at its manufacturing plant located in the Kaliakair Hi-Tech Park in Gazipur. The investment is expected to enhance the quality, precision, safety and production capacity of its HQ brand lithium-ion battery packs. According to the company, it has been manufacturing and marketing HQ lithium-ion battery packs in Bangladesh for the past two years. With domestic demand for lithium-ion batteries growing steadily, the latest technological upgrade aims to ensure internationally competitive manufacturing standards while expanding production capacity.

The automated production line will manufacture lithium-ion battery packs for renewable energy storage systems, electric vehicles (EVs), UPS and IPS solutions, data centres, electric three-wheelers, and various industrial applications. The facility is capable of producing approximately 400 lithium-ion battery packs per day across nearly 40 different product categories.

Industry stakeholders believe the investment represents an important milestone for Bangladesh's emerging lithium-ion battery manufacturing sector. The adoption of automated production is expected to improve product consistency, operational safety, manufacturing precision and overall productivity.

The global lithium-ion battery market continues to expand rapidly, driven by accelerating demand for electric vehicles and renewable energy storage solutions. Bangladesh is also witnessing rising demand for advanced battery technologies, making increased domestic production capacity strategically important for the country's industrial development.

Sector experts note that expanding local manufacturing could reduce dependence on imported battery products, save foreign exchange, encourage investment in technology-driven industries and create skilled employment opportunities. It is also expected to support the development of ancillary industries within the country's manufacturing ecosystem.

The company said its continued investment in advanced manufacturing technologies is aligned with the government's broader initiatives to promote renewable energy, strengthen domestic industrial capacity and generate employment. Through internationally standardised production, Leo ICT Cables PLC aims to reduce import dependence, contribute to industrialisation and support Bangladesh's GDP growth.

Experts, however, emphasise that long-term global competitiveness will depend not only on increasing manufacturing capacity but also on sustained investment in research and development (R&D), international quality certification, product safety, technology transfer and the development of a highly skilled workforce.

15/08/2026 11:38

Email Print 369

KPL Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone has instructed the Investment Promotion and Management Committee to strengthen efforts to promote investment that is robust, environmentally friendly and sustainable, with a focus on renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, resilient infrastructure, and green production and processing.

The Prime Minister issued the instruction while attending the First Meeting on Investment Promotion and Management on August 12, 2026.

He called for the implementation of investment policies that support climate resilience and sustainable development, while identifying three priority areas, including addressing labour shortages and ensuring that workers possess the necessary skills and maintain discipline.

Prime Minister Sonexay also stressed the need to further improve the investment environment to make it more convenient, transparent, predictable and competitive in terms of costs.

He called for a shift from attracting investment based primarily on quantity to prioritising quality investment that generates greater added value, creates employment, develops skills and careers, facilitates technology transfer, promotes innovation and accelerates digital transformation.

The Prime Minister further urged relevant authorities to facilitate stronger integration between domestic businesses and foreign markets, improve investment-related regulations and procedures, and streamline services by moving from multiple points of contact towards a single-window system.

He also called for improvements to non-tariff measures and regulations governing imported goods, infrastructure and public services to strengthen logistics competitiveness and improve national connectivity.

The meeting identified eight general priority tasks for strengthening investment promotion and management.

First, authorities were instructed to improve access to credit by introducing more flexible collateral arrangements.

Second, efforts should continue to maintain currency stability, which is essential for strengthening investor confidence and improving the overall investment environment.

Third, the single-window administration should be upgraded and connected through integrated data systems extending to the final service destination.

Fourth, a digital land database system should be developed, supported by internationally standardised application, assessment and approval procedures, clear timelines for each stage, and appropriate safeguards to ensure data security and prevent adverse social and environmental impacts.

Fifth, business registration procedures should be made more convenient and streamlined, while informal trade and business activities should be addressed strictly and fairly in accordance with the law.

Sixth, authorities should establish databases and programmes to develop domestic suppliers and create effective business-matching mechanisms, enabling local enterprises to participate more fully in investment and supply chains.

Seventh, monitoring, inspection and post-approval support mechanisms for investors should be established and strengthened to ensure effective implementation and continued facilitation after investment approval.

Eighth, the organisational structure of the Investment Promotion and Management Committee at all levels should continue to be strengthened and consolidated to improve coordination, efficiency and accountability.

The Prime Minister's instructions underscore the government's intention to improve the quality and effectiveness of investment while ensuring that investment contributes to economic growth, employment creation, technological advancement, environmental protection and long-term sustainable development.

text:
August 15, 2026

Dear Friends,

Across our nation today, countless families are feeling the effects of a global energy crisis — a crisis caused and subsequently worsened by President Trump’s reckless war with Iran and by record-breaking heat waves around the globe. These crises have stretched our energy infrastructure to the brink, and working Americans are paying the price with higher utility costs and skyrocketing gas prices.

Before Trump started his senseless war with Iran in February, gas prices were averaging under $3 per gallon. Now, the national average is over $4 per gallon. In these past 6 months, Americans here in our region and beyond have paid hundreds of dollars more for gas and other goods, including a combined $41 billion for gasoline at the pump.

With Iran blocking ships from the Strait of Hormuz — where about 20% of the global oil supply was shipped prior to this conflict — there seems to be no end in sight for this economic pain. It’s clear the president completely failed to understand the ramifications of starting this reckless war. But instead of fixing the problem or investing dollars here at home to help struggling families, Republicans are pushing for a budget that would sink billions more taxpayer dollars into Trump’s war.

I’m doing all I can in Washington to force Congress to act to bring real relief to working families and to stop funding this war. That means supporting affordable housing, cutting health care costs, and lowering energy bills. Addressing the latter requires passing common-sense legislation like my Regional Energy Hubs Act. This soon-to-be-introduced legislation would authorize the Department of Energy to set up and maintain regional hubs — like our own Capital Region Clean Energy Hub — across the nation that help residents navigate and access energy efficiency incentives and affordability programs. This week, I held a roundtable discussion with representatives from the Clean Energy Hub, contractors, and beneficiaries of the program to highlight the vital role these hubs play in lowering costs for residents, and to emphasize how our region can benefit from the resources they provide.

One of the major challenges that came with the clean energy initiatives enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 was making certain that people knew about the benefits available to them and about how to navigate the complex system of grants, rebates, and tax credits established by the IRA. The hardworking folks at our region’s Clean Energy Hub serve as a trusted local source of information to help people navigate these opportunities, upgrade their homes, and save hundreds on their energy bills.

While we work to expand existing benefits, we also need to continue looking to the future and investing in energy solutions that create jobs, bolster our domestic supply chains, and cut costs for consumers. One clear and proven solution is offshore wind development.

Offshore wind provides real and extensive opportunities to cut energy costs and strengthen our local economies. But that has not stopped Trump from waging his own personal war on wind. Trump’s misinformation-fueled vendetta is doing nothing to support American manufacturing, create jobs, or lower energy prices for families. Since March, the administration has announced multi-billion-dollar corporate buyouts for offshore wind leases, spending nearly $4 billion in taxpayer money to pay companies to walk away from projects that could have produced more than 21 gigawatts of clean, dependable energy — enough to power millions of homes and support more than 50,000 jobs. These attacks are taking good-paying, union jobs off the table and driving electricity bills even higher for everyday Americans.

Even as Trump continues his attacks on offshore wind, there are still significant benefits that come with investment in the industry — something recognized even by Trump’s own Republican Party. These benefits give us an opportunity to push back against this administration’s assault and forge ahead with legislation like my Offshore Energy Modernization Act, which provides a comprehensive blueprint to ensure the long-term viability and success of U.S. offshore wind development and allows our nation to reap the benefits of this powerful economic driver.

The American people deserve so much better from their government than funding endless wars and fueling petty vendettas. Know that I’m continuing to work day in and day out to help deliver an America where you can afford to buy a home, go to the doctor when you need to, take care of your loved ones, and pay your grocery and utility bills without breaking the bank. The need and will is there. Let’s get it done.

As always, thank you for reading.

text:
Given America's political environment, you would be forgiven for thinking the country has slipped into a dark age of energy recidivism; burning oil, gas and coal left and right; and tossing wind and solar farms on the scrap heap.

In reality, this is looking a lot like a golden age for renewable energy in the U.S., not just in spite of the political winds but partly because of them.

The country is on track to install nearly 85 gigawatts of electrical generating capacity in the next 12 months, according to preliminary Energy Information Agency data on planned projects. And of that new capacity, about 90% will be generated by solar, wind and batteries. Natural gas, currently the country's biggest energy source, will account for just 9% of new capacity. Geothermal and hydropower are tiny parts of the "other" category.

Despite President Donald Trump's vigorous efforts to revive coal, the antiquated fuel will make up exactly 0% of the new capacity. In fact, the renewables boom is happening despite Trump's whole-of-government approach to pretending climate change doesn't exist, squashing clean energy and boosting fossil fuels (until they start to become too profitable for political comfort, anyway).

And between Trump's on-again, off-again attacks on Iran and his cheerleading of an unfettered AI rollout, his own policies have made renewable energy more attractive. It can't get stuck in the Strait of Hormuz, for one thing. And if you are hastily slapping together a data center to satisfy the world's appetite for hallucinations and bad advice, then you need electricity quickly and preferably cheaply. Solar, batteries and even wind are satisfying those requirements.

Fossil gas is still relatively plentiful, cheap and popular. But demand for gas turbines has stretched wait times out for years. And a recent study by Penn State University engineers, funded in part by Tesla Inc., found that the rapid start and stop of AI training in data centers is wearing out turbines that were intended for steadier output, drastically shortening their lifespans. Meanwhile, the first new nuclear facility on the horizon, Kemmerer Power Station in Wyoming, isn't due to come online until December 2030.

It's little wonder, then, that solar and batteries made up 80% of the 53 gigawatts of capacity the U.S. added in 2025 and 76% of the 25.3 gigawatts installed this year through May (the latest data available). Even Trump's hated wind energy, which he claims causes cancer and kills whales, has added 6.3 gigawatts of capacity so far this year, including 800 megawatts of offshore power.

This is all more evidence for the growing sense that renewables, contrary to what skeptics often claim, can stand on their own without government support. In fact, the green businesses so derided by Trump and his fellow conservatives, including clean energy, efficiency and water management, are now a $10 trillion global industry, according to a recent London Stock Exchange report.

Investors noticed long ago. Green stock market gauges like the S&P Global Clean Energy Transition Index consistently trounce the broader market. And cleantech companies pulled in $60 billion in equity funding in the first half of 2026, according to BloombergNEF, the best six months since the good old Inflation Reduction Act days of 2022.

Much of this enthusiasm comes from the AI boom and is therefore vulnerable to an AI bust. Planet-heating fossil fuels are still a dangerously large share of America's energy mix. But every new solar array or wind farm that gets built today might prevent another coal plant or gas turbine from being built next year. Time is money, and both are on the side of renewables right now.

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

HENDERSON, N.C.—On a recent summer evening Mitzi Parrott, who lives in Vance County, saw a television commercial on the evening news that gave her pause. Kathie Hamm and Bobbie Lequire, also of Vance County, saw it, too, streaming on Sling and posted on Nextdoor.

The ad extolled the purported economic benefits of data centers, including the claim that these enormous power-hungry facilities pay their own energy costs so "North Carolina families don't have to."

"I knew it wasn't true, and it concerned me that other people wouldn't know the other side," said Parrott, whose land could back up to a proposed data center. "I figured somebody in the data center industry had to be behind it."

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

Parrott was right.

Over the last two months, to counter the souring public sentiment, a group called North Carolina Connects has been running ads on TV, radio and social media promoting data centers.

What the ads don't disclose is who's behind North Carolina Connects: The Data Center Coalition, a powerful trade group composed of some of the largest tech corporations—Amazon, Microsoft and Google—as well as smaller companies that build, support or operate the facilities.

The Data Center Coalition is based in Virginia, which has the largest number of data centers in the U.S., 674, according to market intelligence firm Data Center Map. The coalition launched as a nonprofit group in 2019, federal tax records show, with total revenues of $304,000. As the data center industry expanded, the coalition's fortunes grew: In 2024, the group reported $4.6 million in revenue.

The DCC has formed similar nonprofit groups in several states, such as Ohio, Virginia and Texas. The websites look alike and contain no contact information aside from an online form.

During a video interview with Inside Climate News, Dan Diorio, DCC's executive vice president of state policy and government affairs, kept his camera off. He did not answer questions about the link between North Carolina Connects and the larger organization. Instead, he directed Inside Climate News to a company statement that reads in part:

"North Carolina Connects represents stakeholders from the data center ecosystem, including the Data Center Coalition, working to inform North Carolinians about the benefits of data centers. … Through North Carolina Connects, the industry seeks to better explain the role of data centers to the public—including how they operate, why they are important to our daily lives and the 21st-century economy, as well as information about the industry's responsible usage of water and its commitment to paying for the energy it uses."

The coalition touts the windfalls they say data centers deliver to communities. In North Carolina, the DCC says data centers generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue, based on public documents. However, without fuller public disclosures it's difficult, if not impossible, to verify some of the claims.

Diorio acknowledged that data centers keep some operational details confidential, but "what you're seeing now is very much a concerted effort for the industry to get a better handle on what information is proprietary and confidential, and then how do we release the information."

Developers frequently require local governments to sign non-disclosure agreements. They don't release their energy and water use and their wastewater discharges. Amazon recently asked the state Division of Air Quality to keep confidential details of its air permit application, but relented after the regulators questioned the company's reasoning.

Opposition to data centers is increasing nationwide, according to a recent survey conducted by the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania. Of the 1,320 U.S. adults polled in mid-June through mid-July, 61 percent said they opposed the construction of new data centers in their area.

That figure is 12 percentage points higher than a similar survey conducted by the APPC in February and March.

The public relations push isn't working, said Jeremy Solomon, president and founder of Learnewable. His company uses AI to analyze government ordinances, moratoria and public comments about data centers, renewable energy and electric transmission projects in each of the nation's 3,144 counties.

Nationwide, approximately one in seven counties now has some form of restriction, Solomon said, and advertising won't win the public's trust.

"The real counter to a moratorium wave is disclosure," he said. "Publish the energy load, the water and the actual value of the tax breaks."

Microsoft announced last spring that it would no longer require local governments to sign NDAs, and the company terminated any existing ones, such as one with Person County officials over a planned data center north of Roxboro.

Data centers emerge as top Alabama election issue as community concerns grow

The Data Center Coalition has tried to counter public concerns about rising electricity prices and the facilities' voracious appetite for energy. In the PJM territory, which includes northeastern North Carolina and a dozen more states, data center demand, coupled with a recent heat wave, tripled energy prices, according to Oil.com.

"We pay for every single kilowatt hour," the North Carolina Connect ad says. "That's building responsibly."

It's also common. Most businesses, such as factories, restaurants, hair salons and banks, as well as homeowners and renters also pay for all of their energy usage. What the North Carolina Connects ad omits is that until early July, when the legislature repealed an exemption for data centers, most paid no sales tax on electricity.

Under that exemption, a large project that consumed 100 megawatts of energy avoided paying as much as $2.2 million a year, state Commerce Department figures show.

"The legislature agreed to remove the data center's sales tax exemption for electricity, so you and I will no longer be subsidizing their energy consumption," Gov. Josh Stein said at a press conference in July as he signed the bill.

Lawmakers kept data centers' sales tax exemption on certain equipment, worth more than $45 million that would otherwise go to state and local governments each year.

Anne Harvey David is chief counsel for environmental justice with the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, which has represented residents fighting data centers.

"There are just so many unanswered questions with every single one of these projects that I think it's really a big part of why people are so opposed to having these data centers in their communities. It has a very cloak and dagger feel," Harvey David said. "You don't even know when there is an NDA, and communities don't have a chance to oppose these data centers until it's nearly a done deal for their community."

Job creation, trade secrets

The data center industry promises local governments that the facilities will create dozens, if not hundreds, of good-paying jobs. Amazon told Richmond County officials that 500 people will eventually work at its hyperscale data center in Hamlet.

In North Carolina, data centers aren't required to publicly disclose their employment numbers, even if they receive tax breaks. Last year Google signed an agreement with the City of Lenoir designating the company's job figures as a trade secret.

The Data Center Coalition commissioned a report by PWC, a research, management and consulting firm, to estimate the economic impact of data centers in the U.S. Using federal labor data, PWC calculated that the industry created 1 million direct jobs in 2024. Of those, 24,000 were in North Carolina.

Another 4.5 million "indirect and induced" positions were supported nationwide; 56 percent were service jobs, and 10 percent were in real estate, finance and insurance. North Carolina accounted for 107,000 of the indirect and induced positions.

The report doesn't have a breakdown of the pay scales for the types of positions. The figures also include part-time workers, the self-employed and contractors, who might not qualify for company-supported health insurance or retirement plans.

DCC said that while it paid for the study, it did not dictate how PWC conducted its research or the results.

Diorio provided Inside Climate News with an example of how data centers can spark new or expanded companies. In Northern Virginia, two veterans started a portable toilet company and added data center construction sites to their clients. They're now in five states, Diorio said, with 70 employees. "It's been a huge part of how they've been able to expand."

So far, those success stories aren't resonating with many North Carolina residents and their elected officials.

Ten counties, 17 cities and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians have enacted their own temporary moratoria on data centers, according to information compiled by Frank Muraca, a former analyst with the N.C. Department of Commerce. Two local governments rejected a moratorium.

The terms range from one year to 32 months, the maximum allowed under state law. Local governments can't pass a permanent development moratorium without legislative approval.

Data center developers encounter greater resistance in counties with more people, Solomon said. Learnewable's most recent figures show developers are shifting toward lower-population counties in the Upper Midwest, Colorado, Wyoming and Alaska.

These areas have fewer restrictions, simpler permitting processes and could be lured by promises of additional tax revenue and employment benefits, according to Solomon. Fewer people could also mean fewer conflicts involving traffic, noise, water consumption and competing land uses.

Vance County, a rural area that borders Virginia, doesn't have any data centers yet. That could change. Despite public opposition, the county commissioners in April rezoned land to allow Natelli, a Maryland real estate company, to develop the land potentially for a data center. If built, the facility would be near five rural neighborhoods, a school and a church.

Natelli had planned to develop a data center site near Apex, in southern Wake County, but withdrew the proposal because of local opposition.

Kathie Hamm, who lives in Vance County, said the county hasn't shared any information about the Natelli project. "Nothing but secrecy," said Hamm, who is co-organizing her community against the proposals. "I'm not a protester, but this is what we're faced with."

The situation in Vance County illustrates what Learnewable's analysis has shown.

"It doesn't even take a finished building," Solomon said. "Once a proposal shows up in a county's public record, sentiment turns negative and the odds of maximum hostility nearly triple."

There is no goodwill dividend for doing it well, Solomon added. Counties where past projects were positive and successful still score worse than counties that never had one.

"The most favorable counties are favorable," he said, "because nobody has proposed anything there yet."

text:
Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) energy office has a message for all of the Maryland counties with temporary data center moratoriums: Make your wish list.

“Use the time that you have bought yourselves with your local moratorium, talk to other communities that have figured this out,” said Ian Ullman, deputy director of the Maryland Energy Administration. “And make your wish list. This is the time.”

If one thing was clear after the second major panel focused on the issue at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference, it was that data centers are not going anywhere — at least not any time soon. So counties should start preparing.

“Counties willing to negotiate can extract meaningful investment in their community’s futures while mitigating impact to their communities and residents,” Ullman said. “New schools, road upgrades, community centers, long-term support packages for local initiatives — it’s all on the table.”

Constellation Energy, represented on the panel by senior vice president of government affairs Mason Emnett, agrees.

“Engage, roll up your sleeves, identify what matters to you, what matters to your community, and in our experience, you’ll find partners who come forward and want to be in the solution space and get to yes,” Emnett told the audience in Ocean City.

Just over a week ago, Constellation learned that data center developer Amazon Web Services was pulling out from its planned project at the company’s Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Southern Maryland. It came after voters unseated three members of the county council amid data center backlash. Now, the county is considering a moratorium of its own.

Though the response of many Maryland counties — representing the majority of Maryland residents — has been to enact time-limited bans amid fierce pushback from voters to data center proposals, the demand for AI among consumers seems persistent. Data centers “aren’t going away,” said Jason Stanek, executive director of governmental services at PJM Interconnection, the electric grid serving Maryland and about a dozen other neighboring states.

“We need all levels of government: county government, state government, to address this situation because we see this train coming and it’s coming fast,” Stanek said.

And Maryland, which does not have a large volume of high voltage transmission lines, is in a precarious position as data centers outside the state continue to place pressure on the PJM grid. The Eastern Shore does not have any high voltage transmission, only one such line crosses the Western panhandle, and only a few lines exist near the Interstate 95 corridor.

“We have 14 states, and Maryland is one of the most concerning,” Stanek said. “We see challenges on the horizon in the near term. Next year, we expect possible disruptions of the grid in the state of Maryland.”

But efforts to add new lines can be fraught, said Stanek, who formerly led the Maryland Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities and power equipment in the state. For instance, PJM commissioned the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project, a new high-voltage line for rural Central Maryland, and it’s been the subject of significant pushback from hundreds of landowners practically ever since. It currently sits before the PSC.

“It doesn’t take very long to build a data center: 18, 24 months,” Stanek said. “Try building a new power plant. Five years? Maybe, if you’re lucky. A transmission line? When I chaired the PSC, I approved every line that came across my desk. Not one got built because we couldn’t get it across other state lines.”

Now, PJM is challenging its member states to approve power plants in one year, and transmission lines in one to two years, Stanek said.

On Thursday, PJM filed a proposal that would allow new data centers to connect to the grid — but if they do not bring their own power generation, they would be first in line to be shut off in a power emergency, forcing them to rely on back-up generators. The proposal would have to be approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

“When electricity supply on the grid approaches dangerously low levels, a new emergency procedure would notify utilities to reduce or transfer the electricity demand from new Large Load customers ahead of any action that would serve to shut off traditional consumers, including residential consumers,” reads a news release from PJM.

Still, the demand growth projections — fueled largely by possible data centers — remain immense, said Maryland People’s Counsel David Lapp, who represents residential utility ratepayers in the state.

“By 2046, PJM forecasts adding [the power demand of] about seven states of Maryland to the region. This is not normal growth in electric demand,” Lapp said. “It’s almost entirely due to data centers projected to arrive in record time and in concentrated locations.”

Most of this data center demand growth isn’t coming from Maryland. In fact, 93% of it is coming from Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Illinois, Lapp said during his presentation.

His office has been working to shield Maryland customers from paying for the energy buildout that data centers are requiring, because, currently, the costs of expanding and maintaining the system are shared by all ratepayers. But processes are underway at PJM, at FERC and at the state level to change the paradigm, Lapp said. That’s why slowing down on data centers — even slightly — has a lot of value, he said.

“These efforts should — if they’re done right — should provide good, solid protections for residential customers,” Lapp said. “But they take time.”

text:
A train track used to run underneath the Holland Tunnel that links lower Manhattan and Jersey City, New Jersey. The thing is, when it was designed in the 1920s, the Holland Tunnel wasn't built for trains. Instead, the track that covered a good stretch of the 1.6-mile-long tunnel was added much later, in 1954, for cops to be able to patrol the byway and report on accidents. It ran adjacent to traffic on a thin, elevated catwalk that sits a few feet above the lanes, and the sole train that went to and fro between the mouths of both ends was a single-seat electric machine just 2 feet wide.

This 1,300-pound choo-choo was powered by a three-horsepower electric motor capable of a maximum of 12 mph. Once it got to one end of the line, the machine couldn't turn around. Instead, the seat swiveled (no doubt, to the chagrin of the cops' knees), so the driver could rotate their body and roll back into the Holland. It's almost as interesting as how the ceilings of tunnels get cleaned.

According to Popular Mechanics' coverage at the time, the justification for needing this system was to enable four rather than six police officers to patrol the entirety of the tunnel. A retrospective at the Hoboken Historical Museum in 2012 — the 85th anniversary of the Holland Tunnel and the 75th anniversary of the Lincoln Tunnel –was covered by The New York Times. The piece noted that the justification for a tunnel was that it was cheaper: $11 million versus $42 million. Yes, the cost ballooned to $48.5 million upon completion in 1927. Just for context, that's more than $1 billion today, and no way should you believe we could pull this off for a mere $1 billion in 2026.

Probably out of jealousy, the Lincoln Tunnel also got its own skinny not-rods in 1960. Theirs were gas-powered, open-top, and could rocket to 35 mph. They weren't made of plastic, but instead, of steel and aluminum. But, in an emergency, the Holland Tunnel cars could handle up to three officers, whereas the ones darting through the Lincoln were strictly solo jobs. Rather shockingly, according to the New York Times, catwalk cars weren't retired until 2011.

You'd guess that the cops who had to ride the railway cars back and forth in these tunnels would be gasping for air. However, the Holland tunnel has four huge buildings — two on each side of the Hudson River — which house 84 fans that run constantly, exchanging the air in the tunnel every 90 seconds. According to the Times' reporting about the 2012 exhibit in Hoboken, that innovation was later used in the Lincoln Tunnel as well.

Here's something else you probably didn't know. The Holland Tunnel isn't named for the country — and fortunately, it doesn't have a dumb and clunky name like the Convention Center Loop Tesla Tunnel, which remains hilariously bad. We've never had a president Holland, so unlike the Lincoln Tunnel, it's not named after a president either. As a tribute, it bears the name of its first chief engineer, Clifford M. Holland, who came up with the design. But Holland died before the tunnel's completion, and so did his successor, Milton Freeman, less than a year later. Lastly, Ole Singstad — the third chief engineer who spearheaded the Holland Tunnel's completion — later went on to design the Lincoln Tunnel.

The police aren't the only folks who've walked the tunnel on foot. Just before it opened to cars, thousands of spectators poured through the tunnel upon its inauguration. Several hours later, at the stroke of midnight, November 13, 1927, the gridlock began. And charging people to drive into Manhattan became a grudging tradition that's now nearly a century old.

text:
Kimberly-Clark is widening its search for alternatives to conventional wood pulp, with a new research program examining whether hesperaloe, a drought-tolerant desert plant, could supply fiber for future tissue products.

The research adds another option to the company's long-running work on alternative fibers. According to the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), Kimberly-Clark has invested about $250 million over roughly two decades in research aimed at reducing its dependence on traditional forest-derived materials.

The company has also reported reaching an interim goal of cutting its use of natural forest fiber by half as it works toward removing the material from its product portfolio.

For tissue manufacturers, the significance goes beyond one plant species. Wood pulp remains a core raw material across the sector, but concerns around forestry practices, carbon emissions, raw-material availability and supply-chain resilience are putting more attention on what else can realistically feed high-volume tissue operations.

Hesperaloe is now one of the materials being put to that test.

Why Hesperaloe Is Being Considered for Tissue Production

Native to dry environments, hesperaloe has attracted research interest partly because it can grow with comparatively low water requirements while producing long fibers that may be suitable for pulp and paper applications.

Previous academic work on Hesperaloe funifera found alpha-cellulose content of about 52% alongside relatively low lignin levels. Researchers concluded that those characteristics could make the plant suitable as a raw material for cellulosic pulp.

Low lignin content matters because lignin must typically be separated from cellulose during pulping. A lower concentration can potentially influence chemical requirements, processing and pulp brightness, although laboratory advantages do not automatically translate into commercially viable tissue production.

Earlier experiments have already shown that hesperaloe can be converted into pulp.

In one body of research, dried and ground plant material was treated in a reactor using diethanolamine under different temperatures, chemical concentrations and processing times. Researchers then separated and washed the resulting pulp before mechanically fiberizing, refining and screening it.

Paper sheets produced from the pulp were evaluated for properties including tensile strength, tear strength, burst strength, stretch and brightness.

Pulp yields generally ranged from around 50% into the upper-50% range depending on processing conditions, with temperature identified as an important factor affecting yield.

Those results establish technical potential, but Kimberly-Clark faces a much broader commercial test.

A tissue manufacturer cannot judge a new fiber on cellulose yield alone. Any alternative must support attributes including softness, absorbency, wet and dry strength, appearance and machine runnability while performing consistently across large manufacturing volumes.

Cost is another hurdle. Fiber pricing, chemicals, energy use, logistics and processing requirements all contribute to the economics of finished tissue. Research has also suggested that some characteristics of hesperaloe fiber could require additional refining energy to achieve targeted paper-strength properties.

As a result, the central question is shifting from whether hesperaloe can be made into paper to whether it can be made into the right paper, at the right scale and price.

Scaling Alternative Fiber Means Rethinking the Supply Chain

A purpose-built integrated park moving into production rollout suggests the cost and lead-time picture is shifting.
What the convergence means for utility operators and procurement teams Three separate announcements in a single week would normally be noise.
The supply chain, the connection hardware, and the utility incentive structure are moving in the same direction at the same time.
text:
Three developments landed in the electrical utilities sector this week that, taken together, tell procurement and operations teams something concrete: the infrastructure build-out supporting distributed and long-duration energy storage has shifted from aspiration to funded, operational reality.

HiTHIUM opens the first LDES integrated industrial park

Shandong HiTHIUM held its Production Rollout Ceremony at the Heze Base on August 8, 2026, marking what the company describes as the world's first long-duration energy storage integrated industrial park to enter commercial production, according to a PR Newswire release issued the same day. The Heze Base is designed to consolidate LDES manufacturing and delivery under a single campus, a model the company says enables scalable output that isolated cell factories cannot match.

For utility equipment buyers, the operational significance is supply-side: LDES has spent years in demonstration mode, with per-unit costs that made large procurements hard to justify. A purpose-built integrated park moving into production rollout suggests the cost and lead-time picture is shifting. Teams evaluating multi-hour storage for grid stabilization or renewable firming should be tracking HiTHIUM's delivery timeline and capacity allocations as a benchmark against other vendors in their next RFP cycle.

ConnectDER's $35M raise brings institutional weight to grid-edge hardware

On the distribution side, Philadelphia-based ConnectDER closed a $35 million Series D round led by Decarbonization Partners, the venture fund jointly established by BlackRock and Temasek, according to Electricity Today. ConnectDER's core product is a metering socket adapter that installs between a utility's existing meter and the meter socket, letting utilities manage rooftop solar, battery storage, and EV chargers without running new service infrastructure or replacing meters fleet-wide.

The practical appeal for utilities is cost containment. Grid-edge connection upgrades are one of the largest friction points slowing DER adoption, and ConnectDER's approach sidesteps much of that capital outlay. The involvement of Decarbonization Partners, backed by two of the largest institutional investors in the world, puts a clear stamp of long-term confidence on the grid-edge hardware category. Utility operations teams still evaluating whether socket-level adapters belong in their DER integration stack now have a clearer answer on vendor financial staying power.

Duke Energy announced in August 2026 that it was activating programs to help North Carolina customers manage energy costs during an expected extreme heat period, according to PR Newswire. While the specific program mechanics for commercial accounts were not fully detailed in the announcement, the deployment pattern is familiar: utilities use heat emergencies to stress-test and publicize demand response infrastructure before making it a permanent rate feature.

For large commercial and industrial accounts, this is a planning signal. Utilities that deploy demand management tools reactively during heat events tend to formalize those tools into time-of-use structures, demand charge revisions, or mandatory curtailment tiers within one to two rate cycles. Facilities and energy managers who have not yet audited their peak demand exposure, or enrolled in available demand response programs, are behind the curve relative to where Duke's rate design is likely to land.

What the convergence means for utility operators and procurement teams

Three separate announcements in a single week would normally be noise. What makes this cluster meaningful is the directional consistency. Institutional capital is flowing into both the manufacturing scale (HiTHIUM's Heze Base) and the grid-edge connection layer (ConnectDER), while operating utilities are activating the customer programs that create demand for both. The supply chain, the connection hardware, and the utility incentive structure are moving in the same direction at the same time.
